World.title: Liberia: Climate Change and Liberia: What It Means and What We Must Do
World.content:
When floodwater enters a home, a farmer loses a harvest, or the sea washes away land, families suffer. Children miss school, businesses lose income, and communities struggle to recover. Climate change increases these risks. Understanding it helps us protect ourselves and our country.

By Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo

Executive Director, Environmental Protection Agency of Liberia

Climate change means lasting changes in the Earth’s temperatures and usual weather patterns. Weather is what happens today: sunshine, rain, or wind. Climate is the pattern we expect over many years, including our rainy and dry seasons.



The Earth is warming mainly because human activities release gases that trap heat in the atmosphere. Burning coal, petrol, diesel, and gas produces these gases. Cutting and burning forests adds to the problem because trees absorb carbon dioxide, one of the main gases warming the planet. These gases act like an extra blanket around the Earth, holding in more heat.

Liberia contributes very little to global emissions, yet we are highly vulnerable. Many Liberians depend on farming, live near the coast, or lack strong roads, proper drainage, and reliable basic services. These conditions make climate pressures harder to withstand.

Along our coast, rising sea levels increase the danger of flooding and erosion, threatening homes, roads, businesses, and livelihoods. For farmers, changing rainfall makes planting decisions harder. Heavy rain, dry spells, and higher temperatures can damage crops and reduce harvests. When farmers produce less, their incomes suffer and food supplies come under pressure.

Health and daily work are also affected. Extreme heat makes outdoor work more difficult. Floods can contaminate drinking water and damage roads, disrupting access to clinics, schools, and markets. Families with fewer resources often have the greatest difficulty recovering.

Not every flood or damaged shoreline is caused by climate change alone. Blocked drains, poorly planned construction, and destruction of wetlands can worsen the damage. We must address both climate change and the local practices that make communities more vulnerable.

We cannot end climate change overnight, but we can slow it down and reduce its harm. This means cutting the gases that cause warming while preparing for changes already happening. Cleaner energy, forest protection, stronger infrastructure, and better weather warnings all have a role.

The Government of Liberia, through the EPA and its partners, is already acting. Coastal protection projects in Sinoe County and metropolitan Monrovia are being implemented to reduce risks from coastal flooding and erosion and protect livelihoods. The Climate Information Systems project is strengthening weather monitoring and early warnings so that farmers, fishermen, and communities can better prepare for dangerous weather.

Government is also turning waste into a resource. Working with the Monrovia City Corporation, the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, and international partners, the EPA has helped establish a composting facility in Fiamah. It is designed to turn food scraps and other organic waste into compost that improves soil for farming. This shows how better waste management can support cleaner communities and agriculture.

The EPA is also enforcing environmental laws. Nationwide inspections have covered mining operations, industrial sites, coastal areas, and waste facilities across all 15 counties. Actions include stopping illegal operations, ordering corrections, and imposing fines. Protecting rivers, forests, wetlands, and farmland also helps communities withstand climate pressures. Development must provide jobs without sacrificing people’s health and livelihoods.

However, the needs exceed available resources. Coastal protection, drainage, weather services, and nationwide monitoring require sustained funding, equipment, trained personnel, and maintenance. Families also need affordable alternatives to activities that damage the environment.

Large emitters carry a greater responsibility. Countries and industries that have released the most warming gases, especially over many decades, should make deep and rapid emissions cuts. Financing tree planting elsewhere should accompany real reductions from their own factories, power plants, and transport systems.

Wealthy developed countries also have responsibilities to help poorer countries respond. The Paris Agreement requires developed countries to provide financial support to developing countries for reducing emissions and preparing for climate impacts. Liberia needs accessible funding, useful technology, and training that reach communities most at risk.

Major emitters should also support people facing losses that cannot be prevented, including destroyed homes and lost livelihoods. Liberia should not carry an unfair financial burden for a crisis it contributed little to creating. This is a matter of fairness.

Our small contribution to global emissions does not remove our own responsibilities. Citizens should join government’s efforts by reporting pollution, protecting public facilities, keeping rubbish out of drains and streams, avoiding waste burning, saving electricity, and following official weather warnings. Keeping drains clear will not stop global warming, but it can reduce local flood damage.

Businesses must respect environmental permits, reduce waste, and correct damage from their operations. Schools, religious institutions, traditional leaders, and the media can explain climate issues in everyday language and local languages. Communities should help shape projects affecting their homes and livelihoods, while holding government accountable for results.

Every Liberian deserves a safe home, clean water, dependable food, and a secure future. Government is taking action, but lasting progress requires citizens, businesses, and international partners to contribute. Large emitters must fulfil their responsibilities, and we must fulfil ours. Protecting Liberia is a shared responsibility.

World.title: Liberia: Chief Justice Gbeisay Calls for Unity Among Liberians, Particularly People in Gompa City, Nimba County
World.content:
Liberia’s Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr.

MONROVIA – Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr. has called on all Liberians, particularly the People of Nimba County to remain united and respect the rule of Law.

Speaking during the opening of the Supreme Court October Term on Monday, October 12, he said, “I want to use this occasion to call on all Liberians, especially my fellow Citizens in Gompa City, Nimba County, to unite irrespective of tribe or ethnic background. Tribalism destroys national unity and peace, and further triggers violence and war. Liberia has traveled down that road before and we know where it led us. We must not go there again. The Gbeisay’s Bench will enforce all legitimate judgments without fear or favor and irrespective of its consequences.’’

Chief Justice Gbeisay pointed out that the law is blind and the only tribe recognized before a court of competent jurisdiction is Justice. He expanded on the court’s enforcement of judgments, particularly in Montserrado and Nimba Counties.



He said that as the court works to expand access to justice across the country, enforcing court judgments remains a daunting challenge. The Chief Justice pointed to an incident of the court’s final judgment at the 8th Judicial Circuit Court in 2018, wherein some members of the Mandingo Ethnic Group in Gompa mobilized and violently obstructed the enforcement of judgment against a member of their tribe.

Speaking further, he said the spokesperson of the group, Mark Jabateh, took to the media and openly declared that he could kill the former Chief Justice, Francis Korkpor, if he had laid eyes on him. “The past government took no action; instead, the present government rewarded him with a ministerial position in government.’’

On the recent incident in Gompa City, he said that, in an effort to enforce the final judgment, the former Gompa City Mayor used tribal sentiment, claiming that Mandingo people have no land rights in that city.

Accordingly, the former Mayor of Gompa City mobilized some members of the Mano and Gio Communities against the court and especially against him as Chief Justice.

“Up to and including today, my family remains under threat and subject to constant attacks. Some individuals have vowed to kill me for allegedly giving their land to Mandingo people.’’

Among other things, he added, ‘‘the Judgments of our courts are based on evidence and the applicable laws. This is the oath I took and continue to hold.”

World.title: Peter Bon Jallah Trial Nears Showdown as Defense Rests; Verdict Expected October 22
World.content:
Prosecution Set to Present Rebuttal Witnesses Next Week as Court Moves Toward Closing Arguments in High-Profile Sexual Assault Case

By:Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia-The trial of Peter Bon Jallah, alleged rape defendant, at Criminal Court “E” at the Temple of Justice in Monrovia is approaching a decisive stage, with the defense having rested its case and the court expected to hear prosecution rebuttal witnesses next week before closing arguments and a possible verdict on Thursday, October 22.



The case, being heard by Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr. without a jury, is expected to conclude, if the remaining proceedings proceed according to the current schedule.

Following the defense’s presentation of eight witnesses, including Jallah himself, the court convened for the appearance of representatives from three institutions subpoenaed by the defense.

These institutions include, Orange GSM, the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, and the John F. Kennedy Memorial Hospital, JFK.

The defense sought the institutions’ participation in connection with documents relevant to issues raised during the proceedings.

Their appearance forms part of the final evidentiary steps before the case moves into its rebuttal and closing-argument phases.

The court is scheduled to resume on Monday, October 19, and Tuesday, October 20, when the prosecution is expected to present rebuttal witnesses in response to evidence introduced by the defense.

Sources familiar with the trial indicate that the prosecution could call as many as eight rebuttal witnesses, although the final number will depend on how the proceedings unfold.

If the prosecution completes its rebuttal evidence within the anticipated period, the parties are expected to present their closing arguments on Thursday, October 22.

Judge Wesseh Aphansus Wesseh could then deliver a verdict the same day, determining whether Jallah is guilty or not guilty of the charges against him.

The projected timeline, however, remains dependent on the completion of the outstanding proceedings and the court’s directions.

A Trial Marked by Contested Testimony and Forensic Evidence

Jallah’s trial has drawn attention because of the seriousness of the allegations, the testimony of the 16-year-old alleged victim, and the competing arguments over forensic evidence, medical findings and the circumstances surrounding the alleged incidents.

The defendant is facing allegations involving rape, gang rape or statutory rape, and kidnapping in connection with the case. He has pleaded not guilty and denied the allegations.

During the prosecution’s presentation, the alleged victim testified about alleged sexual encounters involving Jallah between November 2025 and January 2026.

The prosecution also presented police investigators, medical personnel and forensic evidence in an effort to establish its case.

The prosecution’s witnesses included Rwandan forensic examiner Pascal Bavugirije, whose testimony concerning DNA analysis became one of the central evidentiary issues in the trial.

Bavugirije testified that DNA profiles recovered from clothing submitted for examination were consistent with a match to Jallah’s profile.

His testimony also addressed the limitations of the forensic findings, including the fact that DNA evidence alone cannot establish when or how a sexual act occurred or independently determine whether force, consent, penetration or criminal intent was involved.

The handling of the samples also became a point of dispute, with questions raised about collection, packaging, transportation and the chain of custody.

Those issues featured in the defense’s challenge to the prosecution’s forensic evidence.

Defense Challenges Prosecution’s Account

Throughout the trial, Jallah and his lawyers have disputed the prosecution’s account and questioned whether the evidence presented established his criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt.

Jallah denied the alleged encounters and challenged aspects of the alleged victim’s account, including the circumstances surrounding the reported incidents.

He also raised an alibi involving the Du-Port Road and Mikey Gray areas.

The defense questioned the significance of the medical evidence, arguing that the findings presented should not automatically be treated as proof that the alleged crimes occurred as described.

Jallah also disputed the circumstances under which biological samples were collected, alleging that the police planted saliva DNA evidence.

That allegation remains a defense claim and has not been established as a finding of the court.

Questions concerning mobile-phone records were another feature of the defense case.

Defendant Jallah had sought records covering January 1 to 3 and the Christmas period, arguing that the information could help address disputed issues about his movements and the allegations against him.

The defense’s presentation of eight witnesses, including Jallah, marked the conclusion of its main evidentiary case, although the scheduled appearance of institutional representatives and the prosecution’s anticipated rebuttal evidence remain important steps before the matter can be submitted for a final decision.

Judge Previously Rejected Acquittal Motion

The approaching conclusion follows an earlier critical ruling by Judge Wesseh, who on September 30, rejected a defense motion seeking Jallah’s acquittal after the prosecution had presented 12 witnesses.

At the time, the court determined that the prosecution’s evidence was not “wholly insufficient” to warrant allowing the case to proceed.

That ruling required Jallah to present his defense but did not constitute a determination of guilt.

The defense had challenged several aspects of the prosecution’s case, including the identification of the alleged crime scene, the interpretation of medical findings and the reliability and handling of the DNA evidence.

The rejection of the acquittal motion allowed the trial to proceed into the defense phase, culminating in Jallah’s testimony and the presentation of additional defense witnesses.

With the defense now having rested, the prosecution will have an opportunity to respond to relevant defense evidence through rebuttal witnesses before both sides make their final submissions.

October 22, A Potential Turning Point

The next two scheduled court days could prove decisive in determining whether the case reaches closing arguments and a verdict within the anticipated timeframe.

The prosecution is expected to use Monday, October 19, and Tuesday, October 20, to present rebuttal witnesses.

If the proceedings are completed as planned, the lawyers will argue their respective cases on Thursday, October 22, after which the judge could make a decision.

Unlike a jury trial, the final determination in this case rests with the presiding judge, who must assess the evidence admitted during the proceedings and apply the relevant law to determine whether the prosecution has proved the charges.

For the prosecution, the remaining task is to respond to the defense’s challenges and establish that the evidence satisfies the applicable criminal standard of proof.

For the defense, the closing arguments will provide an opportunity to consolidate its challenges to the credibility of the testimony, the interpretation of the forensic and medical evidence, and the prosecution’s overall case.

Until the judge delivers a verdict, Jallah remained entitled to the presumption of innocence, and the allegations against him remain allegations to be determined through the judicial process.

The scheduled conclusion on October 22 would bring the trial to a major turning point in a case that has tested the court’s consideration of witness testimony, forensic evidence and competing accounts of the alleged events.

World.title: What Has Become Of Some Catholic Priests?
World.content:
As humans, it would be folly for us to expect to be loved by everyone in society as if we’re money! It’s therefore normal to have an adversary or enemy here and there. However, it’s sickening and shocking for a man of the cloth, a Catholic priest for that matter take to social media to disparage or profess their aversion of others, Frank Bwalya in particular, a former Catholic Priest!

As many of us know, resigned from PF, which has since transitioned into Tonse, to join the ruling party, UPND after the elections. The gentleman was almost in tears as he recounted reasons for calling for a press briefing in Kitwe.

“I have for a long time tolerated insults and abuse over my 15-year political career. But I can no longer ignore these actions, especially because they involve my family,” cried Bwalya. “I have a family and personal reputation to protect, hence the reason I have made this difficult decision to sue and report the young priest to the police.”

He went on to reveal that a Father Henry Tyola, assistant priest at St Joseph Mukasa Parish in Kwacha, Bulangililo, Kitwe has been posting malicious statements alleging that he is mad and that mental illness runs in his family!

“I had tried to engage the priest privately despite having messages on my phone in which the priest was allegedly insulting me. I have spoken to at least three priests to restrain the said priest from posting malicious statements,” lamented Bwalya.

Shockingly, Bwalya’s entire family including his aging mother belong to the same congregation as the said Priest. His blood brother even plays the guitar in the Church choir!

What SIN has Bwalya committed for him to deserve to continue to be ‘baptized’ in insults or calumny? Is it because he chose to join the ruling party? Does such a decision constitute madness, honestly?

What has become of some these Catholic Priests? While some can be seen shamelessly propping up certain opposition political parties, others are having a field day insulting and scandalizing innocent victims! One of them was even suggesting rigging in favour of the former ruling party.

Aikona man!

Father Tyola had no right whatsoever to take pleasure in defaming, maligning, scandalizing or humiliating Bwalya or his entire family. Does he think he’s above the law?

During the days of expatriate priests such as Father Umberto, we never saw Priests becoming very personal or championing the cause of the opposition. They remained above board and genuinely spoke for the poor.

We’d conclude by encouraging Bwalya to please go ahead and sue the said Priest for defamation, and equally report him to the police for cyber bullying.

Until next time!

Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

Political/Social Analyst

Zambezi

World.title: Open Letter To Rev Godfridah Sumaili On The Merger OF National Day Of Prayer!
World.content:
We hope you’ll spare part of your precious time to absorb and comprehend the gist of issues raised herein and respond accordingly, devoid of any emotions, malice, naivety, worst of all, hypocrisy.

This is equally applicable to Brebner Changala, Rev. Walter Mwambazi and all doomsayers who have joined the chorus condemning government’s decision to merge the National Day of Prayer and Fasting with the Christian Nation commemoration.

Madam, if we may quote you correctly, you said: “It’s a betrayal, it’s a satanic betrayal. Zambia has been surrendered to Lucifer.”

Are you being fair? What do you mean Zambia has been surrendered to Lucifer? For whose benefit? Or are you simply preying on our people’s ignorance as has become the norm with politicians in clerical collars?

If we may revisit our history, Zambia was declared a Christian nation on December 29, 1991 by President Frederick Chiluba. It was done amidst vehement opposition from the Zambia Catholic Bishops Conference, Council of Churches in Zambia, UCZ and other mainline churches who said they were not consulted apart from the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia.

Would you insist Chiluba made that declaration genuinely or for political expediency?

Let us be honest — while this nation closed her eyes in prayer, the leadership of the country at the time — the President, his aides at State House, Cabinet Ministers and Permanent Secretaries — went into overdrive plundering the resources of this nation. From paupers walking in flip-flops, many became millionaires overnight.

And yet every Sunday, the leadership was occupying the front pew in Church shouting Hallelujah!

What tangible benefits accrued to this nation from that declaration? Did corruption end? Did tribalism end? Did poverty end?

In a case of history repeating itself, on September 18, 2015 during the ceremonial opening of Parliament, President Edgar Lungu proclaimed October 18 as the Day of National Prayer, Fasting, Repentance and Reconciliation. The first observance was on October 18, 2015 at Lusaka Showgrounds, and through Statutory Instrument No. 78 of 2015, it became an annual public holiday.

May you for once be honest and answer: Did that declaration help the country in any way? If so, how?

Wasn’t it in President Lungu’s tenure that criminality took root and became commercialized? While we were praying on October 18th, cadres were reigning terror and fear — taking over markets and bus stations, beating traders in Ndola and Lusaka. While we were fasting, leaders who were previously known to be paupers and scroungers were signing inflated contracts, $1 million fire tenders, mukula and gold scandals, and endless debt that our children are still paying.

So we ask you, Reverend, what is Christian about a holiday that co-existed with gassing, political violence and daylight plunder?

GOVERNMENT HAS NOT SURRENDERED ZAMBIA TO LUCIFER!

Government has merged two Christian observances — December 29th and October 18th — into one, Christian Heritage Day, to save resources and avoid duplication. The Christian identity in the preamble of the Constitution has not been removed. The duty to pray has not been abolished.

If anything, if Zambia was ever surrendered to Lucifer, it was when we used the name of Jesus to cover theft, and called it Christianity.

You served as Minister of National Guidance and Religious Affairs. You know Zambia needs substance, not dates. True Christianity is not shown by how many holidays we keep, but by ending corruption, ending caderism, ending political violence!

Calling government satanic for an administrative decision to consolidate holidays is exactly the politicization of the pulpit Zambians are tired of.

So we ask you plainly: Tell us without emotion — what did October 18th deliver apart from speeches?

If you cannot answer that, then let government do its work, particularly during a crucial time such as this one when President Hichilema is trying to transform this nation through his Grow Zambia Agenda which is aimed at doubling our economy as well as transforming our nation the breadbasket of Southern Africa.

Did you know that despite boasting of 30% of world’s minerals, 60% of uncultivated arable land and a youngest population, the very young people the likes of you seek to mislead, Africa remains the poorest continent? It has the lowest average Human Development Index (HDI)! The 30 lowest-ranked countries in the world are almost all in sub-Saharan Africa. In terms of GDP per capita, Africa is lowest — around $2,000 average vs ∼$50, 000 in North America, ∼$38, 000 in Europe. What a shame!

Even if this may be the case though, at least our country now ranks amongst those that are far ahead of others in Africa – Seychelles, Mauritius, Botswana, Rwanda, South Africa and Egypt.

We look forward to a reasonable response from you.

Thank you,

Prince Bill M. Kaping’a

Political/Social Analyst

Zambezi

World.title: Copper Queens thump Uganda to advance in Olympic race
World.content:
Zambia’s Copper Queens are through to the third round of the 2028 Olympic Games qualifiers after thrashing Uganda 4-1 at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola.

Zambia overturned a 2-1 first-leg deficit from Kampala to advance 5-3 on aggregate in front of a jubilant home crowd on a hot Tuesday evening.

Captain Barbra Banda led the charge with a brace, while Natasha Nanyangwe and Eneless Phiri added a goal each for coach Charles Haalubono’s side.

Nanyangwe sent the home fans into celebration with an 8th minute opener, but Uganda silenced the stadium six minutes later when Sylivia Kabene equalised.

Phiri restored Zambia’s lead in the 20th minute after being set up by US-based Prisca Chilufya.

Banda then took charge, scoring in the 50th minute before sealing the win deep in stoppage time.

After the game, forward Rachael Kundananji was ecstatic.

“We told Uganda that we will beat them at our home ground. We know well our stadium Levy Mwanawasa. They thought we were joking,” Kundananji said.

Zambia will now face Ghana in the third qualifying round in February next year.

Ghana booked their place after thrashing Mauritius 7-0 today to complete a 10-0 aggregate victory.

World.title: Chinsali farmers urged to keep their redemption codes confidential
World.content:
The Chinsali District Agriculture Office has expressed concern over reports that some farmers in the district are losing their redemption codes that could enable them access farming inputs under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

‎Chinsali District Agriculture Coordinator, Frank Sindazi, disclosed that unscrupulous people have allegedly acquired redemption codes for some farmers and used them to redeem inputs without farmers’ knowledge.

‎Mr Sindazi says preliminary checks on the system have confirmed that some of the reported codes had already been redeemed through local agro-dealers.

He said this in an interview with the Zambia News and Information Services (ZANIS) in Chinsali District.

‎‎Mr Sindazi has promised that his office will investigate the issue and establish how the codes were obtained and identify those responsible for the alleged malpractice.

‎‎He also encouraged farmers to keep their redemption codes confidential to prevent unauthorised access to their farming inputs.

‎‎“Farmers must be very careful with their codes and ensure that they do not share them with anyone, because doing so can lead to other people redeeming their inputs without their knowledge,” Mr Sindazi said.

Meanwhile, the DACO has confirmed that farmers in Chinsali have started accessing farming inputs under FISP.

Mr Sindazi said out of the 8,466 targeted beneficiaries in the district, 5,072 farmers have accessed their farming inputs from various agro-dealers, leaving 3,394 yet to benefit from the programme.

‎Mr Sindazi said the programme is progressing well, although some farmers are experiencing challenges related to blocked mobile phone numbers which is making it difficult to update their details and access inputs.

‎‎He said the technical challenges need to be addressed urgently to enable the remaining beneficiaries to access their farming inputs.

‎‎“We hope that these challenges will be resolved quickly so that the remaining farmers can also access their inputs in good time,” Mr Sindazi said.

‎ Mr Sindazi further explained that farmers accessed the inputs after delivering maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) and selling their produce to designated agents, with K400 deducted from their proceeds.

World.title: Luanshya district exceeds maize production target
World.content:
Luanshya district has exceeded its maize production target for the 2025/2026 farming season, recording a harvest of 37,900 metric tonnes against the projected 35,000 metric tonnes.

The achievement represents approximately 108 percent of the district’s production target, surpassing the projected harvest by 2,900 metric tonnes.

This came to light during the Third Quarter District Development Coordinating Committee (DDCC) meeting held in Luanshya, where the agriculture sector presented its performance report.

The meeting further heard that the district had sold 178,600 bags of maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA), against a target of 18,000 bags.

The development represents a significant achievement in maize marketing and highlights the district’s contribution to national food security and agricultural development.

Meanwhile, the agriculture sector disclosed that Luanshya has 7,521 beneficiaries under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP), aimed at enhancing agricultural productivity among small-scale farmers.

Of the total beneficiaries, 4,387 have so far redeemed their farming inputs from participating agro-dealers, representing approximately 58 percent of the beneficiaries.

The meeting also heard that 4,766 farmers supplied maize to the Food Reserve Agency during the marketing season.

And District Commissioner, Paul Malele, who is also Committee Chairperson, outlined measures being undertaken to transform small-scale farming into commercially viable enterprises through farmer training, improved agricultural marketing and business development.

Mr Malele emphasised the need for farmers to move beyond subsistence production and embrace farming as a business in order to improve household incomes and contribute meaningfully to economic growth.

He highlighted the importance of strengthening market linkages and improving farmers’ access to competitive prices for their agricultural produce.

The District Commissioner further challenged government departments and other development stakeholders to ensure that their activities translate into tangible economic benefits for communities.

Mr Malele emphasised that development performance should not merely be measured through cumulative figures but through the actual contributions made towards improving people’s livelihoods.

He called for greater collaboration among government institutions, the private sector and individuals in driving the district’s development agenda.

World.title: Zambia elected to the UN Human Rights Council for 2027–2029 Term
World.content:
Zambia has been elected to the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) for the 2027–2029 term.

The election was held on Tuesday at the United Nations headquarters in New York during the ongoing 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

This is according to a press statement issued to the media by Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister, Mulambo Haimbe.

Mr Haimbe stated that Zambia’s membership would provide an opportunity to contribute to international efforts to promote and protect human rights, strengthen cooperation among member states and advance the principles of equality, justice, democracy and the rule of law.

He stated that during its three-year term, Zambia will seek to promote constructive dialogue, cooperation and consensus among Member States, while contributing to a more effective, inclusive and responsive Human Rights Council.

Mr Haimbe noted that the country will also champion the rights of women, children and vulnerable groups such as the disabled, advance the right to development, and strengthen the links between human rights, climate resilience and sustainable development.

The Minister also stated that it would seek to encourage dialogue, cooperation and consensus among UN member states, with the aim of making the Human Rights Council more effective, inclusive and responsive to the needs of different countries, particularly developing nations.

Mr Haimbe cited Zambia’s domestic policies and reforms, including the abolition of the death penalty, protections for women, children and persons with disabilities, and expanded access to education and social support programmes, as evidence of the country’s commitment to human rights.

He stated that the election presents an opportunity for Zambia to strengthen human rights protection at home while contributing to the council’s work internationally.

He linked the achievement to President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda, which he said places people at the centre of national development and emphasises that economic progress should be accompanied by the protection of fundamental rights and inclusive opportunities.

Mr Haimbe further expressed government’s appreciation to UN member states that supported Zambia’s candidature and said the country looked forward to working with the international community to advance human dignity, equality, justice and respect for human rights.

World.title: Kabwe Mayor calls for collaboration in waste management
World.content:
Kabwe Mayor, Gary Domingo, has called for enhanced collaboration among stakeholders in waste management.

Mr Domingo says maintaining a clean environment is a collective responsibility requiring commitment from the local authority, the private sector and residents to promote a clean and healthy environment conducive to economic growth and development in the district.

Speaking during a familiarisation tour of NATSAVE Bank’s Kabwe Branch, Mr Domingo said the Council is ready to partner with other stakeholders such as NATSAVE to address waste management challenges and improve the cleanliness of the district.

“The local authority remains committed to clearing accumulated waste and, companies and other organisations should support its efforts through Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives,” he said.

He appealed to corporate entities to support the Council’s campaign to create a clean and green Central Business District through donations of waste bins and other essential waste management equipment.

Mr Domingo disclosed that Kabwe District has an estimated 4,000 metric tonnes of uncollected waste, highlighting the need for concerted efforts to address the challenge.

He said partnerships with the private sector would contribute significantly to the Council’s vision of making Kabwe a cleaner and healthier town while improving the well-being of residents and creating an environment that attracts economic opportunities.

Meanwhile, NATSAVE Kabwe Branch acting Manager, Winnie Zulu, said the Mayor’s visit has provided an opportunity to highlight the importance of stakeholder collaboration in addressing waste management challenges.

Ms Zulu welcomed the call for collective action and assured the Mayor that his appeal for CSR support would be communicated to the bank’s headquarters in Lusaka for consideration.

World.title: Zambia Elected To UN Human Rights Council For 2027-2029 Term
World.content:
Zambia has been elected to the United Nations Human Rights Council for the 2027-2029 term. The Government said the seat gives the country a voice in shaping the global human rights agenda and reflects its long-standing commitment to protecting fundamental freedoms.

The United Nations General Assembly held the election on October 13 at UN headquarters in New York, during its ongoing 81st Session. Zambia now takes a seat on the 47-member council.

Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Mr Mulambo Haimbe, SC, announced the result in a statement. He described the election as a milestone in Zambia’s multilateral diplomacy.

The Minister said the seat gives Zambia the opportunity to contribute meaningfully to the global human rights agenda, strengthen international cooperation and advance human dignity, equality, justice, democracy and the rule of law.

He said the country’s membership rests on the conviction that human rights, good governance and the rule of law are fundamental to sustainable development and lasting peace.

Mr Haimbe pointed to reforms at home as evidence of that commitment. They include the abolition of the death penalty, stronger protection frameworks for women, children and persons with disabilities, and expanded access to education and social support programmes.

The Government linked the election directly to President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda. The statement said the agenda puts people at the centre of development and holds that economic progress must go hand in hand with protecting fundamental rights, creating inclusive opportunities and improving livelihoods.

The Minister said the Head of State has consistently positioned Zambia as a beacon of peace and stability and a champion of fundamental freedoms.

On its plans for the term, the Government said Zambia would promote constructive dialogue, cooperation and consensus among member states, and work towards a more effective, inclusive and responsive council.

Zambia intends to champion the rights of women, children and vulnerable groups such as persons with disabilities. It will also advance the right to development and push for stronger links between human rights, climate resilience and sustainable development.

Mr Haimbe said the seat offers what he called two-way impact. Zambia would strengthen the promotion and protection of human rights at home while helping build a council that responds more effectively to the needs of all countries, particularly developing nations.

That idea was central to Zambia’s campaign for the seat. Mr Haimbe led the country’s delegation to the General Assembly, and during the campaign he argued that council membership could bring the body closer to citizens and give developing countries a stronger voice within it.

The Government thanked the member states that backed the bid. “The Government expresses its sincere appreciation to all United Nations Member States that supported Zambia’s candidature and looks forward to working with the international community to advance dignity, equality, justice and respect for human rights for all,” the statement reads.

Zambia’s three-year term on the council begins in 2027.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 13, 2026
World.content:
WHO Launches Five-Year Strategy to Detect Health Threats Faster

The World Health Organization (WHO) has launched a new five-year strategy to help every country detect and understand emerging health threats within 24 hours of their appearance by 2030. The strategy builds on the work of the WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, established in 2021 after the COVID-19 pandemic exposed gaps. Since its creation, the Hub has worked with 160 WHO member states, 190 partner organisations and thousands of scientists and policymakers to strengthen global disease surveillance. The plan focuses on five key initiatives, including using artificial intelligence to identify potential health threats, strengthening genomic sequencing to track emerging pathogens and connecting experts in data science and disease modelling. It will also support countries in sharing health data securely and improving cooperation between human, animal and environmental health systems. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the strategy provides a clear path towards a world where countries can respond to health threats before they develop into major crises. The organisation says sustained investment and international partnerships will be essential to achieving this goal.

South Africa's Deputy Police Chief Resigns Amid Criminal Charges

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

South Africa's Deputy National Police Commissioner, Lieutenant General Shadrack Sibiya, has resigned from the police service three weeks after being charged with sexual offences. His lawyer submitted the resignation letter during a disciplinary hearing. Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said his departure would be treated as a dishonourable discharge because he was still facing disciplinary proceedings at the time of his resignation. Sibiya has been in custody since his arrest in September. Sibiya faces several serious allegations, including the sexual grooming of a 16-year-old girl, rape, human trafficking and links to organised crime figures. He denies the allegations of criminal links and sexual grooming. He admits having sex with an 18-year-old woman but maintains that it was consensual. Allegations against him also emerged during the Madlanga Commission, a public inquiry investigating claims of police corruption and collusion with criminal networks. He has been accused of interfering with investigations into political killings in KwaZulu-Natal and receiving cash and 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract. Sibiya has denied the allegations.

Renewed Fighting in Tigray Raises Fears of Wider Regional War

Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region is raising fears of a wider conflict involving Eritrea and other neighbouring countries. Tensions escalated after reports that Eritrean forces crossed into Ethiopia, prompting Ethiopian forces to launch drone strikes against troops and equipment. Eritrea has denied reports of the incursion, while accusing Ethiopia of using the allegations as a pretext to pursue its ambitions for access to the Red Sea port of Assab. Local sources, however, reported clashes involving Eritrean forces at several locations in Tigray. The renewed violence follows the collapse of a fragile peace agreement that ended the 2020–2022 war. The conflict is unfolding amid shifting alliances between rival armed groups and growing tensions between Ethiopia and its neighbours. Tigray's ruling Tigray People's Liberation Front has vowed to continue fighting after federal forces and a pro-government militia captured the regional capital, Mekelle, on 3 October. The TPLF has also aligned with other opposition groups seeking to challenge Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Analysts warn that the conflict could develop into three possible scenarios: the proliferation of armed groups, a prolonged military stalemate, or a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. The humanitarian consequences could be severe, particularly in Tigray, where about one million people remain displaced, and nearly four million need urgent assistance. Drought, food shortages, and difficulties delivering aid are adding to the crisis.

Drought and Conflict Push Sudan Closer to Famine

The risk of famine is growing in parts of Sudan as severe drought worsens the humanitarian crisis caused by ongoing conflict, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a global food security monitoring partnership supported by United Nations agencies. A new alert warns that malnutrition is worsening in several areas, particularly in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Aid organisations are struggling to reach affected communities because of insecurity, restricted access and a severe shortage of funding. In Eastern Jebel Marra, South Darfur, surveys in two displacement camps found acute malnutrition among children at 38% and 30.8%, both above the threshold associated with famine. More than half of Sudan has been affected by the drought, destroying crops and leaving families without enough food or income. In North Darfur, 64% of cropland is showing poor plant growth and late rains have not managed to save most cereal crops. Food prices are expected to continue to rise. There has also been mass displacement in Greater Kordofan, where since October 2025 more than 300,000 people have been forced to flee their homes. Attacks and insecurity are putting aid workers at risk, while many children are going without life-saving treatment for severe malnutrition. By 8 October, less than half of Sudan's humanitarian appeal had been funded. The IPC has called for an end to the fighting, safe access for aid agencies and a major increase in funding to prevent further loss of life.

Close 

Lagos Court Clears Way for Inquest into Chimamanda Adichie's Son's Death

The Lagos State High Court has cleared the way for a coroner's inquest into the death of Nkanu Esege, the son of renowned Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie. Justice Aishat Opesanwo dismissed an application by Eurapharma Care Services Nigeria Limited, which operates Euracare Multi-Specialist Hospital, seeking to stop the inquiry. The hospital argued that the cremation of Nkanu's body made a post-mortem examination impossible and deprived the coroner of the authority to proceed. Nkanu died on 7 January 2026 following medical procedures, prompting an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death. In her ruling, Justice Opesanwo said the law requires an inquest when the circumstances of a death meet the conditions set out in the Coroners System Law of Lagos State 2007. She said that the absence of the body did not automatically prevent the inquiry from taking place or make it speculative. The judge also rejected the hospital's arguments concerning the handling of statements and evidence from medical personnel, saying the coroner has discretion over how the proceedings are conducted. She stressed that a coroner's inquest is a fact-finding exercise intended to establish who died, and how, when and where the death occurred. It is not a criminal trial to determine guilt or assign blame. The ruling allows the inquest to proceed.

World.title: South Africa: Road Accident Fund to Receive No Additional Govt Funding - South African News Briefs - October 13, 2026
World.content:
press review

Road Accident Fund to Receive No Additional Govt Funding

Transport Minister Barbara Creecy has ruled out additional government funding for the Road Accident Fund (RAF), reports EWN. Creecy also rejected its proposal to increase the fuel levy to R3 per litre. She said motorists are already under financial pressure and that the priority is to address the fund’s management and financial challenges. A new CEO has been appointed, while the process of appointing a permanent board is underway. The RAF has been under financial pressure, with concerns over its ability to meet claims obligations. Creecy also said legislative changes are needed to establish a clear schedule of benefits.

Court to Rule on Sibiya’s Bail Application

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Randburg Magistrate’s Court is set to deliver its ruling on former Deputy National Police Commissioner Shadrack Sibiya's bail application, reports SABC News. During the proceedings, the court heard that a man identified as "Mr M" contacted Sibiya's wife, Sizakele Dlamini, expressing dissatisfaction with how Sibiya had portrayed him in court. Dlamini submitted an affidavit in support of her husband’s bail application. Sibiya has been in custody since his arrest last month and faces charges including the alleged sexual grooming of a 16-year-old girl, rape, human trafficking and firearms-related offences.

AKA Murder Suspect Challenges State’s Evidence

Suspected hitman Eddie Myeza has challenged the State's evidence in the trial over the murders of rapper Kiernan "AKA" Forbes and chef Tebello "Tibz" Motsoane, reports EWN. A Tactical Response Team officer testified that he recovered a firearm from Myeza during his arrest in Umlazi in April 2023. The weapon is believed to have been used to kill one of the victims. However, Myeza’s lawyer argued that his client had no knowledge or control of the firearm, raising the possibility that it was planted. The trial continues in the Durban High Court, with another State witness expected to testify.

World.title: Africa: To Finance Africa at Scale, Build Its Capital Markets at Home
World.content:
Ovidiu Bujorean, chief executive officer of OviBees Ventures, spoke with Wasim Tahir, Senior Advisor at ODI Global and Research Fellow at the Harvard Center for International Development, for the third conversation of Wave 2 of the RootsToFoods Capital Series.

In a RootsToFoods Capital Series interview, Wasim Tahir, Senior Advisor at ODI Global and former director at British International Investment, explains how development finance actually moves private capital into emerging markets, and why the lasting answer lies in deep domestic capital markets and national development banks.

Ovidiu Bujorean, chief executive officer of OviBees Ventures, spoke with Wasim Tahir, Senior Advisor at ODI Global and Research Fellow at the Harvard Center for International Development, for the third conversation of Wave 2 of the RootsToFoods Capital Series. Tahir spent six years as a director at British International Investment (BII), the UK’s development finance institution, where he developed the institution’s mobilization strategy for bringing private capital into emerging markets. His argument: most of the instruments needed to move capital already exist. What matters is how precisely they are aimed, and whether receiving countries build markets deep enough to finance themselves.

Tahir places private capital on a spectrum. Grant capital from governments and philanthropies sits at one end; development finance capital must earn a return but exists for impact first; impact investing reverses that order; and purely return-seeking capital sits at the far end. Only the last two, he said, count as private capital. With aid budgets cut in the United States, France, the United Kingdom and elsewhere, development finance institutions (DFIs) can keep investing at scale only by bringing private investors with them.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

At BII, that meant moving from buy-and-hold to originate-to-share, a shift he describes as largely cultural: the institution once held a stake in a Ugandan bank from the 1960s until its final sale. A DFI adds value by lending for seven to ten years where commercial lenders offer four or five. Once such a loan has aged, it matches what the market provides, and the DFI can sell it and recycle the capital into new deals. Tahir led BII’s first secondary loan sale to an institutional investor, mobilizing $30 million of private capital and setting the template for later sell-downs. The incentives do not always line up, he cautioned: seasoned loans and operating assets past construction risk earn better risk-adjusted returns, creating a pull to keep them on the books.

“It’s like saying you’ve got quite a spicy soup and you drop a bit of milk in to cool it down so more people can eat it. Everyone sort of benefits in some ways.”

Wasim Tahir, Senior Advisor, ODI Global

That is how Tahir describes blended finance. Concessional capital changes the risk-return profile of a whole deal, so it rarely maps onto a single risk, but pools can be ring-fenced for specific purposes, such as demonstrating new technologies or covering country risk. He distinguishes mobilization strategies, which bring private investors over the line, from frontier strategies, which bring DFIs themselves into low-income and fragile states. He wrote the technical proposal for the UN Capital Development Fund’s Investing for Peace initiative, which blends DFI and donor capital into peace-positive companies.

Guarantees, he said, work like scalpels: the risks covered, the amount and who gets paid can all be tailored to make a specific deal happen. And because DFIs cannot reach small businesses directly, a guarantee covering a portion of losses gives a local bank that has only served corporates the confidence to lend to SMEs.

With a growing share of Africa’s investment now coming from the Gulf, he expects more Gulf capital blended with Western philanthropy, citing the five-year, $500 million partnership between the Gates Foundation and the Qatar Fund for Development.

Tahir also argues that the field needs structured, hands-on training rather than another blended finance report, the kind he has delivered to Saudi EXIM Bank and teaches at the Harvard Center for International Development.

Asked which instrument the field still lacks, Tahir gave a deliberately unfashionable answer: many “new” structures repeat what investment banks have done for decades. There is not enough concessional capital to de-risk every deal, and many enabling environments still need work. The lasting solution is to stimulate domestic capital markets, so that savings held by banks, pension funds and insurers flow into local infrastructure, projects and companies. “That is the ultimate holy grail here,” he said.

He would also champion national development banks. DBS, Singapore’s largest bank, began as the Development Bank of Singapore, and the model is returning: Nigeria has established the Development Bank of Nigeria, and the United Kingdom created the UK Infrastructure Bank, now the National Wealth Fund. He also points to borrower-led institutions such as the Africa Finance Corporation, owned by its member countries, and to South-South flows as traditional aid declines.

Close 

A DFI is genuinely mobilizing private capital, not just investing alongside, Tahir said, “when it is actively and intentionally engaged with the institutional investor community.”

Wasim Tahir spoke with Ovidiu Bujorean , chief executive officer of OviBees Ventures and host and designer of the RootsToFoods Capital Series, for Episode 8 of the series, the third episode of Wave 2. Tahir is Senior Advisor at ODI Global and Research Fellow at the Harvard Center for International Development, and previously served as a director at British International Investment. The views expressed are his own. RootsToFoods Capital Series is produced by OviBees Ventures, with AV Ventures, an ACDI/VOCA affiliate, as founding partner, and is distributed in partnership with AllAfrica Global Media. Wave 2 continues October 20 with Alexia Latortue of the Future of Development Coalition.

Follow the rest of Wave 2 by subscribing to the Capital Deployment newsletter on LinkedIn, and find every episode and Capital Insight Brief at rootstofoods.com.
