“To me, that speaks volumes for what Jamaica has produced and presented to the Caribbean and to the world,” he added. Jones also credited the company’s workforce, noting that Sandals employs close to 20,000 people across the region, the overwhelming majority of whom are from the Caribbean.

“For us to be able to show that you give the Caribbean people the opportunity to show up in a big way, they’ll make you proud every day of the week,” said Jones.

Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett, responding to the company’s performance, said the awards reflected both the strength of the Jamaican tourism product and the sector’s resilience following Hurricane Melissa which hit Jamaica’s western third with devastating effect last October.

“It’s a tremendous performance of the destination, and certainly Sandals as a brand was outstanding. No question about it,” Bartlett said. He also pointed to Jamaica’s ability to compete against destinations across the Americas despite the devastation caused by the hurricane, describing the results as evidence of the industry’s resilience.

Jamaica’s major wins included the Caribbean’s Leading Destination, Caribbean’s Leading Cruise Destination, Caribbean’s Leading Cultural Destination, Caribbean’s Leading Family Travel Destination, Caribbean’s Leading Festival and Event Destination, and Caribbean’s Leading Meetings and Conference Destination, among other honours.

The Jamaica Tourist Board also secured the Caribbean’s Leading Tourist Board award. For the 18th consecutive year, Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay was voted the Caribbean’s Leading Airport, maintaining its long-standing regional distinction.

Adventure tourism also featured prominently in Jamaica’s award tally, with Chukka Ocean Outpost winning Caribbean’s Leading Adventure Tourist Attraction, while Chukka Caribbean Adventures took home the Caribbean’s Leading Destination Experience award.

Hosts Princess Senses The Mangrove and Princess Grand Jamaica also enjoyed success, with the former capturing the Caribbean’s Leading Adult- Only All-Inclusive Resort and Caribbean’s Leading Resort titles.

World Travel Awards founder Graham Cooke praised Jamaica’s role as host destination partner for the 2026 regional ceremony, saying the arrangement reinforced the island’s international tourism profile.

“Jamaica’s positioning as 2026 World Travel Awards host destination partner cements its stature as one of the world’s most exciting and inspirational tourism destinations,” Cooke said.

He also commended the Jamaica Tourist Board for its work in bringing the event to the island. “I don’t believe that I have ever met such a dedicated and hard-working team than the one on the Jamaica Tourism Board,” he said.

Cooke noted that the awards recognise excellence across the global travel and hospitality industries, with winners selected following an extensive international voting campaign involving tourism professionals and consumers. His remarks came against a backdrop of continued global travel demand.

Citing figures attributed to UN Tourism, Cooke said international tourist arrivals worldwide rose by 9.4 per cent during the first half of 2026, with approximately 900 million international trips recorded between January and June.

International arrivals to the Americas increased by two per cent over the corresponding period in 2025, which Cooke described as five times the global average.

The annual World Travel Awards recognise outstanding performance across destinations, hotels, attractions, airports, and other tourism-related businesses, providing regional and international exposure for recipients.

World.title: Burnham pledges ‘rock-solid support’ for Ukraine as Zelenskyy makes UK trip
World.content:
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe. It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do. Russia's aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.”

Downing Street said the U.K. prime minister has asked ministers to draw up proposals for further sanctions, military aid, and fiscal packages to support Ukraine in the coming weeks.

Britain will deliver £45 million of surface-to-air missiles and implement a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.

Britain will also accelerate deliveries of more than 5,000 Lightweight Multirole Missiles to Ukraine over the next four years with £1.6 billion funding, Downing Street added.

Chancellor John Healey will use meetings at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok to urge other countries to impose an equivalent LNG ban, arguing it would “curtail the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants.”

European leaders are expected to use a European Council summit Thursday to back stronger sanctions on Moscow after Trump struck a deal with Russia to ease restrictions on its diesel exports.

World.title: From no cards to many: Europe warns Trump not to waste Ukraine’s leverage
World.content:
Trump’s recent demand that Zelenskyy “better damn well stop” Ukraine’s refinery attacks, and his call for Ukraine to install a new leader, amount to a recognition that Kyiv does indeed have significant leverage in the fight.

Kyiv’s refinery campaign is helping create a growing fuel shortage across Russia and is also harming the Kremlin's ability to finance the war. But European leaders fear that Trump's desperation to lower fuel prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv to stop its attacks could weaken Ukraine’s hand without persuading Russia to end the war.

Sybiha’s comments drew loud applause at the Warsaw conference and underscored growing tensions among Kyiv, Washington and Ukraine's European allies after Trump said the U.S. had agreed with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel.

The dispute between Washington and Kyiv overshadowed a Warsaw event that is normally strongly pro-American, given Poland's status as a key U.S. ally.

"Ministers and heads of state won’t say so outright what they think about the Americans, but they certainly think a lot of things — the negotiations with Putin are yet another stab in the back for the Ukrainians," said a French lawmaker, speaking on condition of being granted anonymity.

"You end the war by persuading the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," said Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski.

World.title: How Maroš Šefčovič talked his way to a China trade breakthrough
World.content:
The agreement, which will initially cap imports at 350,000 vehicles a year, marks a significant concession from Beijing, whose carmakers have been flooding the European market with increasingly competitive vehicles.

For Šefčovič, who negotiated last year’s tariff truce with Donald Trump, the agreement suggests his strategy of engagement backed by the threat of tougher trade measures may be starting to pay off.

Šefčovič agreed to launch the trade dialogue at a meeting with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Brussels in late June.

By focusing initially on cars — an area where the EU has leverage as one of the few major markets still open to Chinese manufacturers — the Slovak commissioner hoped to secure a confidence-building win before tackling thornier questions, from critical raw materials to China’s vast industrial overcapacity.

At the same time, he worked to coalesce European governments behind a parallel effort to strengthen the bloc’s trade defenses, reinforcing his negotiating position with the threat of tougher action to bring down the EU’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China.

The hybrid deal, however, is only the opening move in a much bigger contest.

World.title: Philippe, Glucksmann, Retailleau : les temps forts du Sommet sur la compétitivité économique de POLITICO
World.content:
Une vision rejetée quelques instants plus tard par Raphaël Glucksmann. “Je ne vois pas du tout en quoi cet objectif [de 2035] était une erreur”, a rétorqué le tout nouveau candidat du PS et de Place publique. L’eurodéputé plaide pour que les constructeurs automobiles se concentrent sur le développement de l’électrique. “C’est ça l’avenir”, a-t-il insisté, jugeant que l’Europe a “un énorme sujet de naïveté vis-à-vis de la Chine”.

Deux positions renvoyées dos à dos par Bruno Retailleau, qui a rappelé que le groupe du Parti populaire européen, dans lequel siègent les eurodéputés LR, s’était opposé à l’instauration de cette règle lorsqu’elle a été votée au Parlement européen. “Ma position, elle est très nette, elle n’a pas changé, ça fait des années que je le demande, je dénonce cet accord”, a insisté le candidat des Républicains. Il aurait préféré voir “imposer le principe de la neutralité technologique”, via un “cadre très exigeant”, mais progressif pour les constructeurs.

Sur la question des échanges commerciaux avec Pékin, le Vendéen rejoint la position d’Edouard Philippe en s’affichant en faveur de “vrais droits de douane” sur les importations chinoises. “A partir du moment où les règles ne sont pas loyales, on doit pouvoir les compenser”, a défendu Bruno Retailleau.

Energies

Autre dissonance entre les candidats : l’énergie. Pronucléaire, Edouard Philippe a insisté sur la nécessité de “défendre” et “favoriser” l’atome, tout en ajoutant que le “risque associé à [son] exploitation” est “réel”. Si, par mesure de sécurité, il fallait interrompre la production des centrales nucléaires françaises, il faudrait que d’autres technologies puissent prendre le relai et produire de l’électricité, a-t-il exposé, mentionnant les énergies renouvelables. Sinon, la France pourrait se retrouver dans une “situation qui peut-être terrible”, a-t-il prévenu. Le candidat Horizons est par ailleurs favorable à la construction de tous les réacteurs EPR2 envisagés par l'exécutif.

Du côté de Bruno Retailleau, le discours est beaucoup plus mesuré sur les renouvelables. Le candidat LR a confirmé vouloir couper leurs subventions s’il était élu, tout comme il compte abandonner la programmation pluriannuelle de l'énergie (la PPE3), définie par le gouvernement Lecornu. Prudent, Bruno Retailleau l’est aussi sur le développement des EPR2. Alors que la construction de six nouveaux réacteurs a déjà été décidée, “on verra” pour les huit autres prévus, a-t-il temporisé.

Vision de l’Europe

Face aux menaces en matière de défense, sécurité ou IA, Raphaël Glucksmann a répondu qu’il fallait “sortir de l’intergouvernemental” et que l’Union européenne devait assumer sa puissance dans le rapport de force avec la Chine ou les Etats-Unis.

World.title: France should seek rebate on EU contribution, says presidential candidate Retailleau
World.content:
European leaders are meeting in Brussels on Thursday and Friday to discuss the bloc’s long-term budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework, which is pitting the so-called frugal countries against those who want a bigger EU budget. France sits in neither camp.

Retailleau singled out structural funds — money that is invested in poorer European regions — as an area where savings could be made.

“We’ve given billions to countries so they would catch up with us. Well they have, and in a couple of years they’ll probably have a higher standard of living. Sorry, but stop,” he said.

However, Retailleau, who is trailing center-right presidential candidate Edouard Philippe and far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen in the polls, did not put a figure on the rebate he would demand if he came to power. Le Pen, who is the front-runner ahead of next year’s presidential election, and her party have proposed slashing France’s yearly contribution by €11.1 billion as early as next year.

Retailleau said he would seek “a negotiation,” rather than unilaterally impose a lower contribution, as Le Pen says she would do.

“I’m not going to behave like Marine Le Pen, I’m pro-European,” said Retailleau.

Retailleau argued that France’s defense and nuclear deterrence investments should also be included in the country’s contribution calculation, because the concept of forward deterrence benefits France’s European neighbors.

World.title: ‘A foreign attack on EU territory’: MEPs call EU to shield ICC from US sanctions
World.content:
EU lawmakers urged the bloc’s executive to robustly defend the International Criminal Court against U.S. sanctions in a letter sent to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Tuesday and obtained by POLITICO.



“We formally call for the urgent deployment of all instruments at our disposal to protect the International Criminal Court from the consequences of these sanctions,” reads the letter, signed by 58 MEPs, led by ECON chair and S&D lawmaker Aurore Lalucq and EPP Dutch lawmaker Dirk Gotink.



They ask the Commission boss “to draw a clear line towards the US administration.”

The Trump administration has repeatedly threatened to demolish the ICC “brick by brick.” Washington has already sanctioned several judges, including judges from France, Italy and Slovenia, after the court issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

U.S. sanctions announced on Friday risk to cut off the whole ICC from the financial system, which runs on the dollar, and from the majority of tech service providers.



Lawmakers said the sanctions are "an attack by a foreign power on an entity on EU territory, using our own financial system.” They want the Commission to activate a legislative shield known as Blocking Statute, that would prevent EU firms from complying with the U.S. sanctions as soon as a 180-day grace period ends.

After a meeting in Luxembourg, foreign affairs ministers agreed to seek pragmatic solutions to make it possible for EU firms to continue to work with the Court, according to two diplomats. MEPs called for a fiercer reaction.

“The survival of the values the European Union upholds is at stake, as is Europe’s autonomy and credibility in protecting its citizens and entities against foreign sanctions,” their letter reads. “This is about the survival of the Union itself.”

World.title: Poland arrests second man over threats to Prime Minister Tusk
World.content:
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk speaks during the opening session of the Warsaw Security Forum in Warsaw, Poland on October 12, 2026. | Wojtek Radwanski/ AFP via Getty Images

The 46-year-old suspect allegedly posted messages calling for the killing of Donald Tusk on Facebook and TikTok.

Polish police arrested a man accused of calling for the murder of Prime Minister Donald Tusk and parliament speaker Włodzimierz Czarzasty, the government said Tuesday, marking the second arrest in connection to threats against senior politicians in three days.

Police detained the 46-year-old suspect Monday in Oborniki, western Poland, government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said on X.

Prosecutors charged him Tuesday with inciting murder and insulting Tusk, Czarzasty and an unnamed journalist at public broadcaster TVP Info, local prosecutor Katarzyna Sill-Szułczyńska said on RMF FM radio.

World.title: Lights, bells and liability: Europe’s privacy regulators crack down on smart glasses
World.content:
Privacy regulators are putting forward a united front on smart glasses, as privacy concerns about the wearable technology have multiplied since videos made with them have begun spreading online without the knowledge or consent of those being filmed.

The statement is not legally binding but will guide how privacy regulators in Europe assess whether smart glasses users and manufacturers are complying with EU privacy rules like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

The regulators said smart glasses manufacturers should implement a combination of transparency measures to make other people aware that they are being recorded.

The measures may include lights or sounds when users are recording, requiring smart glasses users to activate them with an audible voice command, sending notifications to the smartphones of people nearby and other design "clues" to help people spot smart glasses.

The group of privacy regulators said that not only should users of smart glasses respect other people's privacy but that the devices' manufacturers and people providing connected apps or services may also be responsible for making sure they comply with privacy rules.

The GDPR applies to companies and organizations, and doesn't apply when people process personal data in a household context. The regulators said this household exemption should be "narrowly interpreted" when it comes to smart glasses, and would not apply when someone shares photos or videos of others "to an indefinite number of persons on a public social media account."

World.title: Cornell University suspends frat parties over gang rape allegations
World.content:
Cornell University in the US has suspended all fraternity parties amid mounting backlash over its handling of an alleged gang rape at a frat house in 2024.

 

In September, a lawsuit filed by a woman known as Jane Doe alleged that she had been "plied with alcohol and drugs to the point of intoxication" by several fraternity members before being sexually assaulted.

Protests have broken out across the US to show support for Jane Doe as the university faces accusations that it did not sufficiently punish the men involved. The fraternity was suspended after Jane Doe initially reported the incident and the college disciplined a number of students, but no criminal charges were filed.

In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said he was "deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered" and that "this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community."

"All parties and social events in Interfraternity Council (IFC) houses at Cornell will be suspended for the remainder of the 2026-2027 academic year," his statement continued, adding that this would allow time for a "thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue."

Cornell, which is based in Ithaca, New York, will operate a "zero tolerance" policy for violations of the rule, with any fraternity holding an in-house party or social event to be suspended.

"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," Kotlikoff said.

The university has also appointed former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct a "comprehensive independent review" of the university's response to the rape allegations.

But Kotlikoff said on Tuesday that it was "clear that we cannot wait for these findings to take action."

Other measures to be enacted by the elite Ivy League institution include the appointment of a dedicated case manager to support people reporting sexual misconduct and bringing in New York State Police to allow the force's criminal investigators to investigate any future allegations of sexual assault on campus.

World.title: Violence in Paris as tens of thousands turn out for student protests across France
World.content:
Violence erupted in Paris on Tuesday amid largely peaceful demonstrations across France, as tens of thousands of people joined a student protest movement sweeping the nation.

 

At the Place Vauban, next to Les Invalides in the capital's 7th arrondissement, people threw bottles, fireworks, and stones at police whilst officers fired water cannons and teargas as they sought to disperse the crowds.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 11 police officers had been hospitalised in Paris on Tuesday, which he described as a "particularly gruelling" day for local law enforcement.

"I wish to reiterate my firm stance against violent individuals who attack the police," he added in a post on social media.

The police also fired stun grenades on Tuesday, as one officer confirmed to Euronews. The use of stun grenades has come under increasing scrutiny in France, with the government suspending the use of a specific type after a 15-year-old pupil lost his hand during a police operation outside a school earlier this month.

According to authorities, an estimated 161,500 people joined Tuesday's rallies across the country, while 41,500 took to the streets of Paris. Unions put the figure considerably higher, at around 480,000 nationwide.

Although many protesters interviewed during previous student demonstrations expressed support for peaceful protests, some questioned on the fringes of Tuesday’s clashes argued that violence could be seen as a legitimate response to police brutality.

"This is the education system rising up, students and teachers. There is absolutely no response, no willingness to engage with our demands. All we get from the police is violence, so there’s violence in response too, because no one is listening to us," one protester told Euronews.

He added that in his view, the fact that rioters had destroyed shop windows or set bins alight was not an issue, arguing that insurances would pay for the cost of these damages.

France's protests and school blockades began in Paris’s suburbs in mid-September before rapidly spreading across the country, with grievances including teacher shortages, poor facilities, and overcrowded classrooms.

Ahead of separate mass demonstrations scheduled for Saturday over the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices, some individuals said they hoped the student movement would unite with a broader social movement.

"Anger which has been building up for years is coming together, and the student movement was the spark that lit the fuse. We’re here now, and we’ll see what happens on Saturday," said a protestor.

Another acknowledged that "masked individuals" had thrown objects including stones at the police on Tuesday, but said that he believed using tear gas was disproportionate.

"I just experienced tear gas and it ripped my eyes out", he said.

Students chant during a march to protest against under-resourced schools in Paris, Tuesday Oct. 13, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Rights groups have accused police of using excessive force as they have responded to protests around France.

Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty International France, has called for authorities to ensure young people attending the demonstrations are kept as safe as possible.

"Authorities must ensure their safety and security and protect and facilitate the exercise of their right to demonstrate peacefully," she said. "Any policing response must be lawful, necessary and proportionate, and authorities must avoid unnecessary and excessive use of force."

Stanislas Gaudon, national secretary for Alliance Police Nationale, a major French police union, previously told Euronews that police remained focused on ensuring security around the perimeter of schools.

"When there are acts of aggression and the use of force, it's a question of determining the proportionality and the legitimacy of the act," Gaudon said.

"If this is done against individuals who have fired at police officers or thrown acid, then the use of force to disperse is necessary. I don't like using the term 'repression' or 'suppression' of student protests. That's not the issue. If there is no disturbance in the public space, then there is no legitimate use of force by law enforcement," he added.

Greta Thunberg joins Paris protests

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg also made an appearance at a protest in Saint-Denis, in the northern suburbs of Paris, on Tuesday.

Speaking to reporters outside a high school, Thunberg said: "Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us."

"As we've seen here, schools are not getting investment that they need," she continued. "It just gives the signal to young people that you are not prioritised in our society."

World.title: EU advances Ukraine accession as Hungary lifts veto, paving way for Zelenskyy-Magyar meeting
World.content:
The EU Council has agreed to open two additional accession clusters with Ukraine after Hungary lifted its veto, bringing the total number of opened clusters to four out of six.

 

The decision follows an agreement on the rights of Hungary’s ethnic minority in Ukraine, a long-standing demand from Budapest.

The breakthrough, alongside the opening of two additional accession clusters, could pave the way for a first bilateral meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar in Brussels this week, potentially marking a turning point in relations between the two neighbouring countries.

Hungarian and Ukrainian diplomats are working to arrange the meeting, which could take place on the sidelines of the EU summit, sources told Euronews. However, no date has been set and the meeting has yet to be officially confirmed.

Magyar also raised the possibility of meeting Zelenskyy in a media interview last weekend.

Hungary has criticised Ukraine’s education and language laws since they were adopted in 2015 and 2017, respectively, as those restricted the use of minority languages in schools. The dispute triggered repeated diplomatic tensions, with Budapest under Viktor Orbán blocking Ukraine’s EU accession progress.

Since Magyar’s election victory in April, the new Hungarian government has taken a more pragmatic approach, seeking concrete guarantees for the Hungarian minority while signalling its willingness to let Ukraine’s European integration move forward.

Budapest agreed in June to open the first two accession clusters but made further progress conditional on Kyiv strengthening legal protections for Ukraine’s ethnic Hungarian minority.

Following talks with Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán in Luxembourg on Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the two sides had agreed on the next steps and welcomed progress in implementing their bilateral commitments.

What changes under the new minority law?

One of the key provisions establishes a special legal status for schools where more than half of pupils are taught in a minority language that is also an official EU language. Schools that qualified for this status when the law entered into force can retain it as long as at least 20% of their pupils continue to study in that language.

The law also expands the use of eligible minority languages in school activities and communication, and adds safeguards for native-language education when schools are reorganised or closed.

Pupils taught in eligible minority or indigenous languages will also be able to request translated questions in external examinations, except in language and literature subjects.

Crucially for Kyiv, Ukrainian remains the language of state education. The new provisions strengthen minority-language education without reversing Ukraine’s broader policy of promoting the state language.

The changes build on reforms introduced in 2023, extending protections to minorities whose languages are official languages of the EU. Russian remains outside the scope of the new safeguards.

Beyond the accession talks

Opening the next two clusters is another step in Ukraine’s lengthy accession process, but it does not guarantee membership. Kyiv must still complete extensive reforms, and closing each cluster requires unanimous agreement among EU member states.

Even though Hungary’s objections appear to have been resolved, other EU countries could still obstruct progress.

Agriculture is expected to be one of the most contentious issues in Ukraine’s accession negotiations. Some member states fear that integrating Ukraine’s large agricultural sector into the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy could put pressure on European farmers, subsidies and market competition.

For now, the agreement between Kyiv and Budapest is a significant diplomatic achievement and ends a long-running feud between the two neighbours.

World.title: Ronaldo waves Saudi flag scarf after missile alert delays Asian Champions League match in Riyadh
World.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo waved a scarf bearing the Saudi flag after Al-Nassr’s Asian Champions League victory on Monday, following a missile alert that delayed kick-off by an hour in Riyadh.

 

Al-Nassr beat Uzbekistan’s Neftchi Fergana 3-1 in the AFC Champions League Elite at Al-Awwal Park.

Ronaldo draped the scarf around his shoulders as he joined his teammates to applaud supporters. Before the game, he had also kissed the Saudi national emblem on his shirt.

Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued its warning about 15 minutes before the scheduled start. Players waited in dressing rooms while spectators remained seated.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired towards the capital. Civil Defence later announced that the danger had passed.

Al-Nassr later shared a quote on its Arabic X account from Ronaldo’s June 2025 interview with the club: “I’m Portuguese, but I belong to Saudi Arabia.”

He made the comments after extending his contract until 2027, having joined Al-Nassr in January 2023.

The 41-year-old’s goal in the 42nd minute on Monday took his career tally to 981, leaving him 19 short of 1,000.

Angelo Gabriel had opened the scoring before Alisher Odilov pulled one back for Neftchi in the second half. The visitors later had a player sent off and conceded an own goal.

The victory was Al-Nassr’s first of the campaign after a 4-0 defeat by Al-Ain in their opening game.

Deadly attacks on Riyadh airport

Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people over the weekend, according to Saudi authorities. Thirteen died following Saturday’s strike, which injured more than 300 people, and a further attack on Sunday killed one person and wounded 11.

The airport remains closed. Saudi officials told the Associated Press, speaking on condition of anonymity, that an investigation was examining how missiles and drones breached the kingdom’s air defences.

Yemen has seen renewed fighting after four years of relative calm. Forces allied to its internationally recognised government launched a Saudi-backed offensive against the Iran-aligned Houthis earlier this month.

Al-Ahli Saudi FC defender Merih Demiral also offered condolences at a press conference on Sunday. The Turkey international described Saudi Arabia as his second home.

“My thoughts, prayers and heart are with them,” he said.

World.title: Russian strike injures dozens at Rivne University as ballistic missiles hit Kyiv
World.content:
At least 25 people were injured after a Russian strike hit an educational institution in Ukraine's Rivne on Tuesday, local authorities said.

 

Police said two people who are in a serious condition are undergoing surgery, while three more people were being treated by medical staff.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said five ballistiv missiles also hit civilian infrastructure in the country's capital Kyiv, adding that Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about the attack.

Zelenskyy characterised the barrage on the capital as “particularly vile,” and emphasised that receiving intelligence from Ukraine's partners on such ballistic missile attacks “helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues.”

"This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed — when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning.

Strikes on Kharkiv kill 4, injure 41

Zelenskyy said that in addition to four deaths in a strike on an apartment building in Kharkiv, 41 people were wounded in the city in one evening alone.

A woman was wounded in a Russian strike on a private home in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, the Kyiv city military administration said, while a Russian drone hit a residential building in the village of Murovane, near the western city of Lviv, during a morning attack Tuesday, Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said.

One person was killed in the Fastiv district of the Kyiv region and at least two others were hurt in a Russian attack on the area, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration.

Russia's war in Ukraine hasn’t seen major shifts on the ground since last year, but Ukraine is struggling to fend off Moscow's intensified aerial attacks on cities that include speedy ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones.

Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening. Among the damage was a residential building in the northeastern city of Kharkiv that was destroyed, killing four people despite an all-night rescue operation, he said.

Russia has increasingly used attacks on civilian infrastructure such as energy facilities to deny Ukrainians power, heat and running water during the 4 1/2-year war, hoping to wear down public support for Ukraine’s response to Moscow’s full-scale invasion.

Tuesday's strikes came ahead of a key summit of the European Council in Brussels on Friday, 16 October, where Zelenskyy is expected to attend.

World.title: Secret lies in hospitality: Porto tops ranking as Europe's most welcoming city, Lisbon close behind
World.content:
Portugal is often considered one of the most welcoming and hospitable countries in the world, with international studies and surveys repeatedly placing the Portuguese people at the top of tourists’ favourites. It is therefore no surprise that Porto has been awarded the title of "Europe's friendliest city".

 

The distinction comes from readers of Condé Nast Traveller in the Readers’ Choice Awards 2026 (source in Portuguese), which also place the city of Lisbon in second position in this category.

The vote aims to identify cities where "hospitality is at its warmest" and "you find locals eager to help, whether you’re trying to make sense of a neighbourhood restaurant’s menu or looking confused on the metro".

The recognition now given to the Invicta, as Porto is known, "reflects the significant rise in Porto’s popularity as the ideal city-break refuge, both for lovers of good food and for culture enthusiasts", the magazine explains, also highlighting the city’s authenticity and relaxed atmosphere.

"Unwind in a stunning square lined with azulejo tiles or share petiscos – small portions of local delicacies – with residents in a neighbourhood restaurant", Condé Nast encourages, "and you will quickly realise how generous hospitality has made Porto a destination many of us end up returning to time and time again".

Lisbon appears in the next spot. "Few European cities are as picturesque as the sun-drenched Portuguese capital, famous for being built on the seven hills that punctuate the banks of the River Tagus", the magazine notes, describing it as "a wonderful city of winding alleys, soulful fado and creamy pastéis de nata".

"But what really ties it all together is the people. A youthful, inclusive atmosphere pulses through its steep neighbourhoods, and there are plenty of opportunities for travellers to get involved too. Experiencing the vibrant café culture is unmissable, where groups gather to savour their ritual morning espressos, or visiting during the Festival of Saint Anthony to see the cobbled streets fill with open-air parties", the publication recommends.

In the European ranking, the top five is completed by mentions of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, Stockholm in Sweden and Valletta in Malta.

World.title: Europe’s satellite sovereignty push faces funding test as EU space budget cycle ends
World.content:
National telecoms authorities, EU policymakers and Barcelona-based satellite company Sateliot met at the European Parliament in Brussels on Tuesday to discuss how radio frequencies and fresh money will decide who controls the communications Europe relies on from orbit, with the bloc’s current seven-year space budget expiring in 2027.

 

Euronews was at the event, organised by Sateliot, whose spacecraft act as mobile phone masts in space, connecting Internet of Things (IoT) devices such as sensors and trackers where ground networks don’t reach.

The EU’s €14.8 billion space programme for 2021-2027, which funds Galileo, the bloc’s satellite navigation system, and Copernicus, its Earth observation service, ends next year along with the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the EU’s seven-year budget.

For 2028-2034, the European Commission wants space funded from a new European Competitiveness Fund, a single pot for strategic industries that would set aside €131 billion for defence and space.

EU leaders are due to discuss the next budget at the European Council meeting on Thursday and Friday.

The Commission’s defence industry and space department, DG DEFIS, closed bids on 29 September for a four-year, €55 million framework contract for management and legal support on three fronts: IRIS², the EU’s planned secure satellite constellation, space surveillance and tracking, which monitors objects in orbit, as well as analysis of the space economy.

More calls under Horizon Europe, the EU’s research and innovation programme, follow in 2027, while EUSPA, the EU Agency for the Space Programme, and the European Space Agency (ESA), an intergovernmental body separate from the EU, keep running tenders.

Spectrum and sovereignty

Much of the debate centred on spectrum, the radio frequencies that satellites and mobile networks need to transmit.

In May, the Commission proposed a single EU-wide licence for mobile satellite services, which link satellites directly to phones and other devices, in the 2 GHz band, whose current rights expire in May 2027. It would specifically reserve part of the band for European operators and a secure system linked to IRIS².

European Parliament Vice-President Javier López hosted the meeting and the Commission’s digital department, DG CONNECT, was represented by Gerasimos Sofianatos, head of the radio spectrum policy unit.

"This discussion could not come at a better moment considering the current geopolitical tensions and the debate surrounding technological competition", said López in his opening statement.

"A Europe that controls its own network and data is a Europe that can act independently and make its own decisions [...] satellite connectivity is a perfect example of an area where we must achieve strategic control", López added.

Speaking to Euronews after the event, the CEO and co-founder of Sateliot Jaume Sanpera stated that "we have to build and support European champions that can compete globally in the space sector," adding that "today half the world wants to work with European companies in defence and space because we are more predictable."

In September, the ESA selected Sateliot to contribute to IRIS²’s Low-LEO layer, a testing ground in low orbit where new government services are tried out before any are added to the main system. The ESA plans in-orbit test missions from 2027 to 2029.

Through its RESCUE-NET project, Sateliot will also study how 5G connectivity from space can keep public authorities connected when ground networks fail. The ESA signed 18 contracts worth €20 million in total with nearly 80 companies for this phase.

From SpaceX to PLD Space

For small satellites, reaching orbit still largely means flying American.

On 1 October, Sateliot sent five satellites built by Spanish small-satellite maker Alén Space into orbit on Transporter-18, a rideshare mission by Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX that carries spacecraft for many customers, taking its total launched to 11.

The extra satellites double its daily passes over any given point, the company says.

Asked by Euronews whether Europe can expand its fleets without relying on non-European launchers, Sanpera said that he is optimistic and mentioned that there are currently four or five companies in the race to fill that gap.

FILE. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket with a crew of four launches from pad 40 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Cape Canaveral, Florida, 1 Oct. 2026 AP Photo/John Raoux

The CEO of Sanpera also explained that the firm's next launch will be in July 2027, again in collaboration with SpaceX, but the one after that will be with PLD Space, a Spanish launch company based in Elche.

That launch in late 2027 will not only be entirely European, but it will also feature Sateliot's first two Tritó satellites, a larger next generation designed to offer 5G direct-to-device services to ordinary phones.

They will fly on Miura 5, a small orbital rocket built by PLD Space that has yet to fly.

Back in August, PLD won a conditional €158.9 million contract under ESA's European Launcher Challenge, which backs new European rockets, and it plans a debut launch from Europe’s spaceport in French Guiana by the end of this year.

Meanwhile, Sateliot, which is raising €150 million from investors, comprising €100 million in equity and up to €50 million in debt, aims to grow its constellation to more than 500 satellites.

World.title: Qatar’s emir vows that country will emerge stronger as he outlines national strategies
World.content:
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani said on Tuesday that his country "will emerge from this crisis more resilient and better equipped to adapt to global changes," outlining the country's national strategies which now also focus on diversifying the economy towards the "non-hydrocarbon sectors," in addition to the traditional model of liquefied natural gas global supply which Qatar wants to increase.

 

In a speech to the nation at the opening of the Shura Council’s annual session in Doha, Sheikh Tamim made it clear that "Qatar was attacked on its territory by Iran, in a blatant violation of its sovereignty, the provisions of international law, and the principles of good-neighborly relations."

“Qatar has always preferred to resolve disputes through negotiation and diplomatic and peaceful means," Sheikh Tamim added.

"Our commitment to dialogue and peaceful solutions does not mean being complacent about defending our country," he said. "Our right to defend our sovereignty does not conflict with our determination to prevent a wider war."

Iran has consistently maintained that it was only targeting US interests among its neighbours during the war.

Against the backdrop of widening conflicts across the region, he stressed the need for the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries to cooperate, stating that "the security of the GCC states and the protection of their sovereignty and stability are non-negotiable."

Sheikh Tamim urged "to redouble our efforts to secure navigation in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and to protect energy and water facilities, as well as civil infrastructure."

Sheikh Tamim also outlined the country's response during the war and its strategies going forward, based on long-term planning before the crisis and the measures Qatar implemented to adapt to the war's consequences.

He addressed "the extraordinary events" that impacted the country and the region, which "demonstrated (...) our ability to respond to crises efficiently and responsibly" and that "resilience isn't born in the moment of crisis; rather, it is the result of the planning that precedes it."

"In this crisis, Qatar has shouldered three responsibilities simultaneously: protecting its sovereignty, fulfilling its role in energy security and the global economy, and keeping the doors of diplomacy open," Sheikh Tamim said.

Based on these responsibilities, Qatar's Emir outlined "four key elements" that formed the country's strategy in addressing the crisis: "first, defending the homeland firmly without being drawn into war; second, maintaining essential services, supply chains, and economic activity; third, contributing to efforts to secure a ceasefire and reopen waterways; and fourth, urging negotiations and seeking opportunities to return to talks to reach peaceful resolutions to the conflict."

Sheikh Tamim acknowledged Qatar's key role in global energy systems, supplying about one-fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas (LNG), and said that "any disruption affecting it is quickly reflected in markets and consumers everywhere."

"The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, together with the direct damage inflicted on some energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City, disrupted a significant portion of the country’s exports," the Qatari emir said.

Signalling a key development, Sheikh Tamim said Qatar absorbed the shock by focusing on the "non-hydrocarbon sectors", which "continued to grow with their contribution reaching approximately 80% of real GDP."

He explained that the "non-hydrocarbon sectors" alternative "reflects the resilience of the national economy and its ability to sustain growth under exceptional and complex circumstances", and that "the stock of foreign direct investment continued to grow."

He revealed that "the total revenues declined by 42% during the first half of the year, while public expenditure fell by 14%, without compromising essential services or development priorities," as "the state did not succumb to panic."

"Instead, it continued to look to the future with confidence in the national economy," Sheikh Tamim said.

"We decided not to reduce essential services and opted to maintain our developmental priorities, in order to sustain Qatar’s ongoing economic momentum," Sheikh Tamim said.

"The policies adopted by the state prior to the crisis — including strengthening reserves, reducing public debt, budgeting based on conservative oil price assumptions, and developing non-oil revenues — have enabled us to absorb the repercussions of this crisis thus far."

Moving forward, Sheikh Tamim said the Gulf country's "aim is not to return to the pre-crisis situation, but rather to use the recovery as a springboard to accelerate economic diversification and strengthen national capabilities."

"Our duty is to always strive for the best, but we must also be prepared for the worst-case scenarios, and everyone—institutions and citizens alike—must take responsibility," the emir told the nation.

He outlined the country's plans for the energy sector, which include the expansion of the North Field Gas project to increase LNG production capacity, the progress of the Golden Pass project in the US and QatarEnergy's increased investments and international partnerships, "alongside the development of petrochemical industries, solar energy projects, and efforts to strengthen water security."

He also outlined the country's focus on food security, agriculture, technology, institutional efficiency, investment in education "to face the challenges of our time" and in digital transformation.

Sheikh Tamim said the Palestinian cause remained a priority for Qatar, declaring that "what has happened in the Gaza Strip is undoubtedly a genocide, and those responsible must not escape accountability."

He warned of "the dangers" resulting from Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank, "not to mention the repeated raids on the Al-Aqsa Mosque, and countless violations of the provisions of international law, the UN Charter, and international humanitarian law."

Sheikh Tamim's criticism in his national speech underlined Qatar's ongoing firm position towards Israel's actions in Gaza and Lebanon. Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has lashed out frequently at Qatar, calling it "a hostile state".

Beyond Gaza and the Gulf, the emir reaffirmed Qatar's continuing role in mediating political agreements to resolve the crises in Sudan, Libya, Yemen and Somalia.

World.title: Houthis launch fresh wave of missiles across Saudi Arabia
World.content:
10/14/2026 October 14, 2026 Aramco offices catches fire after suspected Houthi attack

The complex in Dhahran serves as a major operation for Aramco, which is the world's largest oil company Image: Jiji Press/picture alliance

Saudi Arabia said that an attack on the headquarters of oil state oil firm Aramco sparked a "limited fire."

The fire at the building at Aramco's complex in the eastern city of Dhahran resulted in no casualties or deaths, the country's Energy Ministry said.

A company source told the Reuters news agency that a ballistic missile struck the top floors of an office building.

The complex in Dhahran serves as a major operation for Aramco, which is the world's largest oil company.

Hours earlier, Saudi authorities said they had intercepted several missiles, including over the capital city Riyadh.

World.title: Cornell suspends frat parties after gang rape case
World.content:
Cornell said no parties will be held at frat houses until the end of the academic year. The university is trying to mend its reputation following its handling of a gang rape case in 2024.

Cornell University has suspended all parties at frat houses until the end of the 2026/27 academic year, the university announced on Tuesday.

This comes after the case in which a woman alleged to have been drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, with the university's reaction to the gang rape allegations now attracting criticizm from around the nation and overseas.

The new measures include a new "zero tolerance" policy for violations, which would result in an immediate suspension of a chapter.

University President Michael Kotlikoff said these measures were to "provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life" at Cornell, while also determining how it can safely continue. The university has more than 20 active fraternities that are organized under its Interfraternity Council.

It is not clear whether the suspension also includes parties that take place outside the campus.

More support for victims

As part of the measures, Cornell is to hold talks with students and faculty experts about the "the development of safe social alternatives" to Greek life party culture, as well as investing the money needed to support the initiatives' establishment, Kotlikoff said.

The Cornell president also said the institution will be adding a case manager to its Office of Civil Rights to support people that report sexual misconduct to help in navigating the process.

Campus police, which has full law enforcement authority but is controlled by Cornell, are largely the ones responsible for looking into crimes committed at the university. However, Kotlikoff announced that Cornell will work closely with New York State Police to allow an investigation independent of the school.

The case triggered widespread protests across the US Image: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Decision not to prosecute criticized

The 2024 gang rape allegations were initially investigated by the campus police, which then passed its initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who did not prosecute — a decision that was lader met with widespread criticizm.

The woman filed a lawsuit in September, in which she claimed she had been drugged and sexually assaulted by several fraternity members after attending a party at the Chi Phi house in October 2024.

According to the lawsuit, messages saying she was sexually available were sent among fraternity members without her knowledge.

The Chi Phi fraternity house, where the woman was allegedly assaulted Image: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

After learning about the case, Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students, without any criminal charges being filed.

All seven men mentioned in the lawsuit have denied the allegations.

After the case was made public and triggered wide-scale criticism, the investigation is now in the hands of New York Attorney General Letitia James. The university's response will be reviewed by former Deputy US Attorney General Sally Yates.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: OpenAI says employee caught planting listening device
World.content:
A Saudi national employed by the artificial intelligence lab has been arrested after a listening device was planted in a company conference room.

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, said Tuesday one of its employees was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was found in one of its San Francisco offices.

A 35-year-old Saudi national working as an engineer was arrested on Friday, a week after the device was discovered in a conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

After the device was discovered, the company reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee. A federal investigation is ongoing.

The suspect, who appeared in court on Tuesday, has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

The criminal complaint did not specify what the suspect might have wanted to do with the recordings. It did add, however, that the suspect used a tool to inquire about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Will AI destroy humanity? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How was the device found?

OpenAI said the device was discovered a few days after it was allegedly planted by the suspect.

"We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," a spokesperson for the artificial intelligence company told the Associated Press.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the spokesperson added.

According to the US Justice Department, the suspect wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and hid it inside a television located in an "executive conference room."

He was seen on camera near the room several times despite not having authorization to sit in meetings there. After this was noticed, another camera was installed in the room that captured the suspect on film checking on the stashed device.

World.title: Vatican confirms Pope Leo underwent surgery for lung cancer
World.content:
The pope has had part of his lung removed and is recovering after surgery. Leo has been unusually candid for a pontiff about his health issues, disclosing the surgery to thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.

Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung that later was reported to be cancerous, the Vatican said, adding the pope "woke up normally" after the procedure.

"The procedure was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned," said a brief Vatican statement.

The Vatican ​said in a medical bulletin that he lower lobe of Leo's right lung was removed, and he was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common ​form of lung cancer.

The Vatican said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.

The surgery at Rome's prestigious Gemelli hospital, which has been the main site of treatment for popes for decades, lasted about three hours. Leo's recovery is expected to ​take about a week, the statement added.

According to oncologists, Leo has an excellent prognosis since the cancerous nodule was caught so early.

A Vatican source cited by AFP news agency said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread further.

Shift in transparency

Leo, 71, disclosed the health issue to thousands of worshippers at a prayer service on Sunday, making a marked shift in the level of transparency about his health compared to his predecessors.

In the past, the Vatican has often been accused of making confusing or extremely vague statements about popes' health, if revealing at information at all.

All of the pontiff's engagements have been cancelled through October 20. He is still likely to take a planned trip to South America in November.

World.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: Former gang leader Duane Davis sentenced to 40 years
World.content:
Former Los Angeles gang leader Duane "Keffe D" Davis was found guilty of ordering the killing of hip-hop icon Tupac Shakur

Duane "Keffe D" Davis was sentenced by a Las Vegas court on Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur over 30 years ago.

Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25.

Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.

"You don't get to take a man from his family. You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur," Judge Carli Kierny told a Las Vegas court while handing down the sentence.

What happened the night of the shooting?

On the night of the shooting, the rapper and his entourage got into a brawl with members of a rival Los Angeles street gang at the MGM Grand Casino during a boxing match. One of those beaten in the brawl was Davis's cousin.

Davis said he sought retaliation, and hours after the fight while riding around Las Vegas in a Cadillac, he located Shakur at a red light in the passenger seat of a BMW.

Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur.

Tupac Shakur was killed at 25 during the height of his career as a hip hop artist Image: Death Row Records/dpa/AFP/picture alliance

The question of who actually pulled the trigger has never been conclusively decided. Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.

The killing went unsolved for years until Davis gave interviews and wrote about his role in the shooting in a 2019 tell-all memoir.

Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that Davis was trying to profit off the killing, and deserved the maximum sentence.

Davis' lawyer said he plans to appeal the verdict.

Shakur was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.

World.title: Germany news: Left-leaning Berlin coalition talks break down
World.content:
Skip next section Why have the Berlin exploratory talks broken down within a week?

The breakdown in the exploratory talks can be traced back to concerns about the often highly critical stance on Israel adopted by some members of the Left Party, coupled with criticism of the appearance of a figure linked to organized crime at an election night party.

The Left scored well with parts of Berlin's population, not least the young and communities with more people of migrant backgrounds, with an unusually stern line on Israeli wars in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East by the often muted standards of German politics.

But comments from its more outspoken members and controversies like an organized crime boss attending an election-night after-party led to questions — particularly in some newspapers and from the conservative Christian Democrats — about whether center-left parties could work under the Left's leadership.

In a bid to settle this, the Greens, SPD and Left drafted a joint statement on antisemitism, Israel's right to exist and maintaining a distance from organized crime before starting their talks.

But the text subsequently faced criticism from within the Left's own ranks.

On Tuesday, as 44 Left Party members of the new Berlin parliament met, they instead signed off on a different text more closely aligned to the party's past internal position papers.

"We stand by Israel's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Israel. Equally we stand by Palestine's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Palestine," the Left Party's text read.

Among other things, this omits a reference in the joint text to Israel's right to exist being "non-negotiable," and to listing potential sanctions for transgressions potentially extending as far as being ejected from the party.

The CDU — which emerged as the second-largest party in the vote, well adrift of the Left on 18.8% — argue that the SPD and Greens should negotiate a coalition government with them instead.

Chancellor Merz had also weighed into the discussion, saying that the allegations of impropriety facing the Left Party cannot be "dismissed with a piece of paper." In the meantime, the party's state lawmakers appear to have disavowed that piece of paper anyway.

World.title: Ukraine allies in Poland after Starlink sabotage, Trump diesel deal
World.content:
Germany's Johann Wadephul said hybrid plots like the Starlink fire showed Europe was "in Russia's crosshairs." The UK's Ed Miliband said Trump's Russian diesel deal led to a "very difficult few days" diplomatically.

The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.

This came as investigators in Germany were chasing down suspects for a fire at a Starlink station in Poland, and as Ukraine's European allies scrambled to deal with US President Donald Trump's latest lurch into Vladimir Putin's lap.

What did the ministers say about Russian diesel and Ukraine?

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until midterm elections.

"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said, noting the new package of EU sanctions imposed on Monday.

"We are keeping our course," he said, adding that Europe was asking the authorities in Washington to do the same.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said sanctions should continue being imposed on Russia's economy as attacks on Ukraine persist Image: Jörg Blank/dpa/picture alliance

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband arguably found even clearer words.

"Within the bounds of diplomacy we should acknowledge that it's been a very difficult few days," Miliband said in the Polish capital that's just a few hours' drive from Ukraine's western border.

Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, meanwhile, said he was counting on "our MAGA president" — a reference to Andrzej Duda of the rival PiS party whom Trump has often praised — to use his "friendship" with Trump to do two things.

"Number one: to secure a permanent US base in Poland. And, number two: to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor, and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression, and you end the war by convincing the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," Sikorski said.

Norway's Espen Barth Eide said it was important to focus on the actions of the last four years, also welcoming Monday's latest round of Russian sanctions.

"I feel that what we've done over the last years ... all of this is a very strong signal that Europe, together with Canada and — on most good days — also with the US, we are sending a very clear message to Putin," Eide said.

Facing criticism at home as well, Trump on Tuesday said that the US was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine. He also said that other countries would be buying Russian diesel as part of the deal he announced, without being deemed to breach US sanctions, rather than the US buying it itself. This contradicted or possibly corrected his earlier statements.

The first two Starlink arrests took place in the small German town of Nürtingen in the southwest, far from Poland's borders Image: Enrique Kaczor/dpa/picture alliance

Wadephul: Starlink sabotage shows Europe 'in the crosshairs' of Russia

Wadephul also told reporters during his visit that he had spoken with his opposite number Sikorski about the investigations into a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month.

Two people with Turkish citizenship were arrested in Germany in the southwestern town of Nürtingen, not far from Stuttgart, on Monday. Based on comments from Polish officials, they are suspected of connections with organized criminality but are thought to have been working on behalf of Russia.

Wadephul said that this and other hybrid incidents across the continent showed that "we are in Russia's crosshairs."

The satellite-based Starlink internet service is used extensively by Ukraine's military and so the fire was thought to be targeting accessibility across the border in the warzone.

"We're being attacked and it's not just happening in Ukraine but all across Europe," Wadephul said. "That means we must strengthen our cooperation."

But he also said that the arrests in Germany, which will likely lead to an exatradition process, showed how the security systems were working — both at the policing and intelligence-gathering levels.

He said he did not believe Russia would succeed in "dividing us" with such campaigns, saying that instead he expected they would galvanize European allies.

A private Polish broadcaster meanwhile reported two further arrests in Germany on Tuesday, although German authorities did not immediately comment on them.

Miliband and Sikorski, who spent many of his younger years in the UK, also held a joint press conference in Warsaw on Tuesday Image: Neil Milton/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

Miliband praises Zelenskyy, but says 'let us take seriously' energy ceasefire idea

UK Foreign Secretary Miliband praised Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for showing "extraordinary leadership ... in the most difficult of circumstances" since Putin's 2022 full-scale invasion, shortly after Trump's call — mirroring Russian messaging — for presidential elections in war-torn Ukraine.

However, Miliband also said the notion of an "energy ceasefire" raised by Trump — seemingly unilaterally — was nevertheless worthy of consideration given the attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the onset of winter.

"So let us take up this idea of the full energy ceasefire and let us seek with President Trump to hold Putin to this full energy ceasefire, because that is what we need," Miliband said.

Miliband noted how Zelenskyy had expressed a willingness in theory, even if Russia was yet to do so.

Wadephul added that, if possible, any such efforts to broker a partial ceasefire should also seek to incoporate grain exports and shipments in the Black Sea, particuarly to North Africa.

"This is still necessary. And let us please not forget this and urge Russia also to be ready to enlarge the ceasefire, not only for the energy sector but also for the Black Sea. Because this is needed to stop a lot of people in North Africa from falling into hunger," he said.

World.title: Ukraine and the US: What's next after Trump's diesel deal with Russia?
World.content:
Donald Trump plans to allow the purchase of Russian diesel, drawing criticism at home and abroad. What is behind the US president’s decision and what should Ukraine do next? DW spoke with experts.

The diesel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin has sparked anger in Ukraine. Under the agreement, Moscow is allowed to supply Russian diesel fuel to global markets. The US news website Axios reported the move came in response to Kyiv's failure to comply with Washington's demands to stop attacks on oil refineries in Russia.

Trump also declared that it was time "for Ukraine to get a new president."

The agreement to sell diesel was announced while talks between Ukrainian, US and European representatives were taking place in Miami.

"I think our team is simply being used as a cover. That is definitely not fair," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists shortly afterwards, describing Trump's decision as "a weak decision by strong partners."

From the Oval Office to Miami

This is hardly Kyiv's first crisis in its relationship with the Trump administration. In February 2025, Trump told Zelenskyy in the Oval Office "you don’t have the cards."

The White House confrontation was followed by a suspension of weapons deliveries and intelligence-sharing agreements. According to media reports, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to suspend intelligence sharing during the talks in Miami, too, citing Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as the reason. US officials have denied the reports.

Memories are rekindled of the February 2025 spat between Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Donald Trump and JD Vance Image: Jim Lo Scalzo/UPI Photo/IMAGO

The current tension recalls the dispute in the White House at the time, says Mykhailo Honchar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" in an interview with DW. However, he says there is no reason for Ukrainians to panic.

"Last year, too, there were threats and suspensions of intelligence sharing, as well as disruptions in weapons supplies," he said. "Then the Americans realized how much this was hurting them, too, and reluctantly resumed everything."

Is Trump looking for a 'scapegoat?'

All the experts interviewed by DW see a connection between Trump's threats toward Ukraine and the US midterm elections on November 3. In the midterms, all seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one third of Senate seats are up for election.

Ivan Us of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv expects a crushing defeat for the Republicans. He says the main reason will be high fuel prices.

"Donald Trump wants desperately to distract attention from the fact that high prices are linked to his war with Iran and the problems in the Strait of Hormuz. He needs a scapegoat for this. And he has decided that Ukraine will be it," the expert said.

Mykhailo Honchar sees Russia as the main beneficiary of Trump's deal with Putin: "This whole diesel deal looks like a disguised request from Putin to Trump to exert influence on Ukraine."

Honchar also links the agreement to a possible sale of the foreign assets of Russian oil company Lukoil. According to The New York Times, potential buyers of these assets include investors with ties to Trump.

Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How can the crisis be resolved?

Oleksandr Kraiev of the Ukrainian think tank Ukrainian Prism warns against taking drastic action.

"Slamming the door in anger will certainly not help us. In that case, security assistance and intelligence sharing will be off the table. We cannot afford that. It may be difficult, and sometimes even repulsive, but we have to maintain contact with the Americans," the expert said.

At the same time, Ukraine could work with Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and France to make deliveries of Russian diesel fuel "simply unrealistic." After all, the tankers would have to pass through these countries' territorial waters on their way to the United States, and the partners have already said they would not allow this.

Ivan Us advises against reading too much into the harsh rhetoric.

"You can say whatever you want in public, as long as you carry on as before," he said of the possible relationship between Kyiv and Washington.

Ukrainian diplomats should work with US Republicans and the MAGA movement. Trump's agreement with Putin is already being criticized in those circles, with some raising concerns that Russia could use the proceeds from the diesel trade to support Iran.

Us also does not rule out a legal challenge to Trump's decision. Republican Senator Tom Tillis told NBC that the president was likely violating a 2022 law prohibiting imports of Russian oil and other energy products.

Ivan Us considers US threats to cut Ukraine off from intelligence or weapons to be little more than "fearmongering" ahead of the elections.

"The US makes such statements not because it intends to take action, but to make the markets believe that it is about to exert pressure and thereby drive prices down," Us said.

What will change after November 3?

The three experts agree that Kyiv should ride out the situation until after the US midterm elections on November 3. Oleksandr Kraiev says he is sure that Trump may back down on this issue after the elections, since abandoning Ukraine would mean showing weakness toward China.

Mykhailo Honchar points out that Trump's deal with Putin is already being criticized by Republicans in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. In addition, Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has introduced a bipartisan bill named after former US President Ronald Reagan that would block purchases of Russian oil.

"Despite all the threats, and perhaps even some attempts to impose temporary measures against Kyiv, it is unlikely that Trump will go any further. The situation should not be portrayed in apocalyptic terms," Honchar said.

He added that Trump's pressure was also bringing Ukraine and its European partners closer together.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

World.title: El Rey, en Ceuta: “La soberanía y la integridad territorial no son negociables y, ante cualquier riesgo, nuestra obligación es su defensa”
World.content:
El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

Felipe VI defiende en la ciudad autónoma que “cualquier amenaza” a la frontera “es una amenaza al conjunto de la UE”

A última hora de la tarde de este martes, tras darse un baño de cariño y afecto por distintos puntos de la urbe de Ceuta, Felipe VI ha culminado su primera visita a la ciudad autónoma con un discurso muy contundente. Dentro del hotel Parador, el Rey ha calificado de “violación de nuestra frontera” el cruce multitudinario de finales de julio, ha defendido la “soberanía” y “la integridad” de la ciudad, y ha subrayado la “obligación” de defenderlas. Todo dos meses y medio después de la entrada masiva que ha puesto en jaque a la urbe africana. El monarca ha reivindicado además su papel como “jefe del Estado”, algo que no suele hacer en este tipo de alocuciones, y ha mantenido que “la violación de nuestra frontera sigue teniendo un enorme impacto en España entera”. “No os vamos a dejar solos ni indefensos”, ha prometido a los ceutíes, después de que miles de vecinos se acercaran a saludarle por las calles donde ha transcurrido el viaje.

También ha mencionado a Marruecos, con quien ha mostrado “la responsabilidad de mantener una buena relación de vecindad”, pero basado en los “respeto mutuos” entre ambos países. Felipe VI ha pronunciado sus primeras palabras a las 19.30, ante miembros de la sociedad civil ceutí convocados para el acto celebrado en el hotel, donde pernoctará esta noche antes de viajar mañana miércoles a Melilla, y en una sala donde ha sido recibido con el himno nacional y entre gritos de “¡Viva el Rey!”.

“Aquella violación de nuestra frontera por una inmensa multitud de personas fue un shock para todos, especialmente para vosotros, y sigue teniendo un enorme impacto social, político, económico y sicológico en vuestras vidas, en la ciudad y, en buena medida, en España entera, pese a que desde entonces hayan retornado la mayoría de las que entraron y muchas otras hayan sido internadas en los centros de acogida”, ha expresado el Rey durante su discurso. “Ceuta y Melilla son una parte irrenunciable de la realidad política y nacional que es España. La soberanía y la integridad territorial de nuestro país no son negociables: son indiscutibles. Y ante cualquier riesgo, nuestra obligación es su defensa y preservación”, ha añadido. “Ceuta es España…, y Ceuta es Europa. Por tanto, su frontera, como la de Melilla, lo es de la Unión. Cualquier amenaza que sufra, es una amenaza al conjunto de la Unión Europea", ha remachado Felipe VI, desatando en ese punto del discurso el aplauso intenso de los presentes.

Los Reyes llegaron al Parador tras un visita que arrancó a mediodía de este miércoles e incluyó una ceremonia en el Palacio del Ayuntamiento, ubicado en el centro histórico, junto a las autoridades locales y mandos militares; un encuentro con niños y profesores de un colegio público situado en un vecindario de clase media, en el Campo Exterior; y un homenaje a las víctimas mortales de la entrada multitudinaria, celebrado en el cementerio musulmán de la barriada periférica de Sidi Embarek, donde yacen los restos de decenas de fallecidos. Durante todo el periplo, los Felipe VI y la reina Letizia han estado acompañados del presidente de la ciudad, el popular Juan Jesús Vivas, que ha sido muy aclamado a cada paso que daba con ellos. También por el ministro de Política Territorial, Ángel Víctor Torres, al frente del mando único, que por el contrario fue abucheado en uno de los momentos de la visita, durante el saludo oficial en el balcón del Ayuntamiento. Primero hicieron acto de presencia los Reyes, después se sumó el presidente Vivas y, finalmente, el ministro Torres.

Ya a última hora de la tarde, los Reyes llegaron al Parador para pronunciar Felipe VI sus primeras palabras oficiales en la ciudad autónoma. “No os vamos a dejar solos ni indefensos”, prometió a los ceutíes después de que miles de personas hayan acudido a los distintos puntos por donde ha transcurrido el periplo de los Reyes para mostrales su afecto. “Nos ha abrumado, nos toca el corazón”, expresó el jefe del Estado saliéndose del guion en el Parador La Muralla, que toma el nombre de la infraestructura monumental que separa en parte el centro monumental del Campo Exterior. En el mismo hotel dormirán los Reyes, lo que supondrá también un paso muy relevante, pues será la primera vez que un jefe del Estado pase la noche en suelo ceutí. En 2007, bajo el Gobierno de José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, Juan Carlos I y la Reina Sofía visitaron la ciudad pero no pernoctaron.

Unas 80.000 personas entraron desde Marruecos a Ceuta entre los días 30 y 31 de julio. Dos meses y medio después, el Gobierno central acoge a miles de migrantes en 10 recursos improvisados con 7.400 plazas. El Ejecutivo ceutí tiene además filiados con 2.827 menores extranjeros no acompañados. En paralelo, 12.000 personas han retornado al país vecino desde el 10 de agosto, la gran mayoría de “manera voluntaria” por el paso fronterizo de El Tarajal. “Quienes entraron irregularmente en nuestro país deben, como regla de principio, regresar a su lugar de origen, lo antes posible y por los cauces legalmente establecidos. Mientras estén entre nosotros deberán ser tratados siempre con dignidad y humanidad, y con todas las garantías previstas por nuestras leyes”, ha expresado Felipe VI. “Pero también se les debe exigir un respeto escrupuloso de las normas de convivencia ciudadana y de los derechos y libertades de los ceutíes. Que cuando miremos atrás, hacia estos días tan difíciles, podamos hacerlo con la tranquilidad y la satisfacción de haber hecho las cosas bien”.
