World.title: Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote, officials say
World.content:
STRAIT. Ships and tankers in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Musandam, Oman on April 18, 2026.

Tehran is moving toward a closure of the strait to vessels violating its restrictions, with one official adding, 'It will be complete closure soon'

Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.

Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.

Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.

The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.

The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.

“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials said.

The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said.

Iran using spotters

A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official said.

Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.

Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy.

The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November’s midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.

US President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote.

The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.

The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic.

In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data.

There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on October 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization.

“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.

Attacks over an expanded area

As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said.

Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days.

The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections.

“Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said.

“Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz.”

The Pentagon and Iran’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Complete closure of Hormuz soon, says Iranian official

Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving toward a situation in which no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. “It will be complete closure soon,” one of the officials said.

In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained “severe”, the second-highest level.

“IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing,” JMIC said. – Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] How the Philippine Left lost its way
World.content:
In his Vantage Point column on September 1, 2026, “What’s left for the Philippines’ Left?,” Val Villanueva proposed some explanations for the demise of the revolutionary Left in the Philippines. One is that the ideology of fighting for socialism went out of fashion globally, with China and Vietnam’s turn towards capitalism. Another is that the Left’s position on EDCA and Pax Silica has aligned it with China geopolitically, thus discrediting it as well as allegedly revealing its ignorance of the economic benefits that could come to the country. In short, global developments have left the Philippine Left behind.

My sense, however, is that the principal cause of the Left’s decline lies in three things: its misreading of domestic political realities after the collapse of the Marcos dictatorship, a bloody internal purge that took several thousand lives, and a very deep split in the leadership of the revolutionary movement.

The way these factors came together is illustrated in the life of former New People’s Army (NPA) cadre Eddie Quitoriano, whose memoir published by Ateneo de Manila University Press, just came out. Let me share a review I did of that book as a way of illustrating why the Left’s decline was really a complex—and tragic—process.

At the launch of his book Deeper Ground, Darker Shadows** in Manila a few weeks ago, Eddie Quitoriano asked, “How did the NPA’s image change from being the ‘Nice People Around’ to one of being only interested in imposing revolutionary taxes and obtaining weapons?”

This was Eddie’s diplomatic way of asking, “How did the Philippine revolution lose its way?”

Answering that question was undoubtedly a key motivation for writing his memoir. In the process of fleshing out his life in over 300 pages, he provides the reader a fascinating personal odyssey that is meshed with a larger, tragic odyssey, that of the national democratic movement. Eddie as an individual reaches his Ithaca, which is reconciliation with a family he had neglected out of devotion to the revolution. The movement, however, has not, and is still adrift, growing more marginal to Philippine politics by the day.

This is a book that should be required reading for the global left, for it is a sobering affirmation of the truism that efforts to realize good intentions, if not grounded in a firm belief in the intrinsic value of individuals, balanced by good institutional checks, and guided by plain common sense, can go badly awry.

Cadre

The offspring of a struggling family in Mindanao, the Philippines’ second biggest island, Eddie grows up in a frontier area peopled by Christian settlers, indigenous peoples, and Muslims. It is the early seventies and, like many in his generation, he is repelled by Ferdinand Marcos Sr.’s declaration of martial law and attracted to the national democratic revolution radiating outwards from Manila to the rest of the country. He is drawn into activist circles, resulting in his being railroaded from the seminary where he has been training to be a Catholic priest. Recruited into the reestablished Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP), he proves his mettle as an organizer, one who is able to skillfully navigate both the perils of encounters with the military and internecine conflicts within the fledgling party.

With the establishment of the party’s Mindanao Commission and the growth of the CPP’s armed wing, the New People’s Army, in the movement’s most promising expansion area, Eddie becomes a seasoned NPA fighter and trainer, even as he fathers a family and, along with his wife, Agnes, rotates in and out of military and police detention. His performance attracts the attention of Romulo Kintanar, the chief of the NPA and a fellow Mindanaoan, and he and his family are brought to Manila for his integration into the people’s army’s General Command.

In the first part of the book, the excitement of revolutionary organizing and the dedication of CPP and NPA cadres come across despite the author’s understated style of writing and his reluctance to tell the reader about his talents and capabilities. Still, there are things that bother him that he registers. One is the lack of warmth with which he is received by “Tagalog” cadres in Manila; indeed, their reluctance to extend personal assistance contrasts with the spontaneous solidarity of comrades in Mindanao. Another is a disconcerting distrust among the top leadership of the party and NPA, which leads to non-sharing of vital information like his pending assignment to overseas work. The third is the most alarming, which is news from home about an internal purge taking the lives of many veteran cadres in Mindanao beginning in 1985.

The voyage out

But before he can wrap his head around what came to be known as “Kampanyang Ahos,” or “Garlic Campaign,” he is sent off on a mission to raise money and purchase arms abroad by Kintanar, who comes across in these pages as a dynamic, take-charge personality. Over the next seven years, the mission brings him to Syria, North Korea, Nicaragua, Libya, Cuba, Yugoslavia, Greece, Yugoslavia, the Netherlands, Vietnam, to name just a few stops.

He is unable to procure weapons, but does get some money, and is able to arrange for the training of NPA combatants in Pyongyang and Libya. In the process, along with top leaders of the party and NPA, he gets to meet the mercurial Libyan chief Muammar Khadaffy, who gives the NPA one million dollars, and the ailing North Korean leader Kim Il-Sung, who promises weapons but wants assurances the NPA can work out a way of receiving them, which it can’t.

Since his mission is not sanctioned by the party leadership but only the NPA General Command, it is not surprising that Eddie eventually gets entangled in the transnational feud between Kintanar in Manila and the party leadership in exile domiciled in Utrecht, the Netherlands, led by Joma Sison, whom Eddie initially accords the respect due to one who has been a key founder of the party and its prime ideologue. The feud stems from jurisdictional, political, ideological, and personal conflicts. An explosion waiting to happen, animosities accumulate and erupt over the mixing of counterfeit dollars provided by the Japanese Red Army (JRA) for NPA operations with Khadaffy’s gift of real dollars. US authorities have spotted the counterfeit dollars, resulting in a major headache for the NDF’s international representatives. Along with another comrade, Eddie is tried by what he describes as a kangaroo court in the Dutch City of Maastricht, with Sison leading the prosecution while denying his own role in authorizing the use of fake dollars for revolutionary ends. Admitting his own role in the foolhardy enterprise, Eddie is dismayed by obvious efforts by others to make him the fall guy.

Play Video

Stormy voyage back…

Judged guilty and “banned” from again setting foot in Western Europe, Eddie is on his own, subsisting on funds periodically given to him by a Japanese Red Army contact codenamed “Nadia,” who is later revealed to be the legendary Fusako Shigenobu, founder of the Japanese Red Army (JRA). His travels bring him to, among other places, Havana, where hospitable Cuban comrades arrange for cosmetic surgery. He is on the run from US and international police authorities owing to the counterfeit dollars affair and needs a new nose to look like someone of Native American descent from the Andes. The Cuban surgeon botches the first operation, forcing him to return for a second, which succeeds. As he explains, “I had to disappear. I was no longer with the CPP or the NPA and I wasn’t prepared to join the JRA, but I wanted to survive, even as a different person if need be.”

Surprisingly, at a time that he is deserted by his own party, it is the JRA that remains faithful to Eddie, generously providing cash for his subsistence and travels even when meaningful reciprocal support for “joint actions” from the increasingly disorganized NPA General Command is no longer feasible. The grateful Eddie does try to repay the favor by scouting for and securing safehouses in Latin America for the JRA, which is finding its Eastern European safehouses becoming less and less secure with the collapse of socialist governments there at the turn of the nineties.

Eddie hints at casual encounters with the opposite sex on the winding way back home, but if he does indulge in them, like Odysseus he does not allow any Circe or Calypso derail him from what has now become his obsessive goal of reaching hearth and home.

After an odyssey of nearly seven years, Eddie finally gets back to the Philippines in 1993. No longer with the party and NPA, his priority is to provide his two children and wife with the stability that his revolutionary commitments deprived them when they were growing up. He is able to fend off the military’s efforts to send him to prison, but he cannot avert his eyes from the tragedy that has engulfed the movement he has cut ties with.

…to the heart of darkness

It turned out to be a stroke of luck that Eddie was absent from the Philippines during the period 1986 to 1993. For it was during this period that the CPP literally descended into madness. The scale of the purges in Mindanao that he had first heard about when he left in 1986 shocked him upon his return. Thousands of trained cadres of the party and NPA had been executed by their own comrades owing to the panic that swept the ranks that were triggered by unverified rumors that the military had been able to infiltrate its agents into the movement. Ironically, methods of summary justice CPP cadres had employed against “bad elements” in the barangays or villages were now turned against their own comrades. Mindanao was turned into a howling wilderness in just a few months in 1985 to 1986 by Kampanyang Ahos, and, failing to absorb the lessons of a purge that went out of control, party and NPA units in Luzon stumbled into the same bloody process, with the purges known as Operation Missing Link and Project Olympia, which Robert Francis Garcia, a victim, documented in his classic 2001 account To Suffer Thy Comrades.

When Marcos was overthrown in February 1986 and Corazon Aquino assumed power, the NDF was immobilized and stood on the sidelines, partly because it had adopted a policy of boycotting the rigged polls that triggered the mass insurrection against the dictator. But the bigger reason was that it was in no position to intervene because its ranks had been depleted and demoralized by successive purges.

The bloodletting at the base took place in parallel with a fierce struggle at the top for the leadership of the party, with Sison regaining unchallenged control of the party and NPA and driving out those he labeled military adventurists like Kintanar and as well as other factions that questioned his leadership or rejected a return to the classic Maoist strategy of protracted people’s war. Filemon Lagman was assassinated in 2001, Kintanar in 2003, and Arturo Tabara in 2004, though the NPA admitted only to the killing of Kintanar. All had been top leaders of the CPP. In 2005, the names of 14 “counter-revolutionaries” or, as we joked then, candidates for execution, were published by the CPP journal Ang Bayan (among them my own, most likely because I was among the first to do an empirical investigation and publish an analysis of the purges).

Purges are not, of course, uncommon in revolutionary movements. Still, there are those like the Vietnamese Communist Party, that have been able to evolve a collective process to resolve intra-party disputes relatively peacefully. During the Chinese Revolution, Mao Tse-tung dealt with his rivals not by executing them but by relieving them of their positions and isolating them in “criticism-self-criticism” sessions designed to get them to “reform.” Among those famously subjected to this treatment were influential cadres such as Zhou En Lai and Deng Hsiao Ping, who was purged twice.

Stalin, of course, executed thousands of his Bolshevik comrades and their factional followers, but this took place long after the triumph of the Russian Revolution in 1917. The uniqueness of the purges in the Philippines was that the mass executions took place before the left even had a real chance to come to power. As Patricio Abinales aptly put it, the purges resulted in “the revolution devouring its own children before victory.” Indeed, the purges eliminated thousands of trained, loyal cadres who would have been indispensable actors had the movement been in a position to take over the state.

A distant reckoning

The tragedy has been compounded by the fact that none of those who led the purges, whether they later aligned with Sison’s “reaffirmist” line or against it by joining the “rejectionist” camp, have stepped forward to take responsibility for the purges, hoping perhaps that memory of the bloody campaigns would be erased with the passage of time. It’s been 40 years since the killings, yet the collective refusal to own up to the collective madness persists. This is understandable, though inexcusable, since most of those in national or responsible regional leadership positions in the then still unified party knew about the ongoing purges but did little or nothing to halt them, though some of them did apologize to the incredulous relatives of the victims. “Kahos (purge) only stopped when there were no more comrades to execute,” Eddie writes.

Eddie is right that the actual number of cadres whose lives were taken will never be really known, though a hint was provided by a party document that acknowledged that in the immediate post-Marcos years, the number of party members abruptly dropped from 9,000 to 3,000. For him, the real measure of the scope of the purge is the “silence of the NPA guns and the collapse of guerrilla fronts and party organizations.”

Having been central in building the party and NPA infrastructure in Mindanao, an endeavor that took years, Eddie is understandably aghast at a campaign that demolished it in just a few months. It is only when he talks about the question of accountability for Ahos that bitterness seeps into Eddie’s writing. People responsible for the purges “have not been held to account because they continue to perform essential duties for the organization. Some have found new lives in government, academia, or the private sector. I am sure they know what happened and what their role was but choose to pretend they have done nothing wrong.” One can sense a smoldering desire to name names instead of the pseudonyms that people went by, but out of a remnant of comradely respect, he refrains from doing so.

The moral high ground surrendered

Revolutions succeed for a variety of reasons. But one of the ingredients of success is that among the people, the revolutionaries are seen as holding the moral high ground. Ahos and the other purges demolished that for all sections of the Philippines left, and it is doubtful that in the foreseeable future they will be able to reclaim that once quaint popular description of them as “the nice people around.”

The question, however, might arise among some readers: How reliable is Eddie’s account? Fairly reliable, I would say. It’s not just the level of detail and complexity with which he describes his experiences, which could not have simply been conjured out of thin air. Just a few pages in, you realize that what you’re reading is not a polemical ideological tract nor an account by someone with an axe to grind but an honest attempt by one who spent 20 years in the revolution as an ordinary cadre to find an answer to one question, one that is asked by many who came into political maturity during a memorable era and became part of something bigger than themselves: Was it all worth it?

Like the response to Eddie’s query of how many young lives were snuffed out by the purges, the answer to this question is not likely to be definitively settled. But to again become a real force in the country’s politics, the revolutionary left must reckon with rather than avoid its past. – Rappler.com

Walden Bello, a retired professor at the University of the Philippines and the State University of New York at Binghamton, is the author of Global Battlefields: My Close Encounters with Dictatorship, Capital, Empire, and Love (Ateneo de Manila University Press, 2025).

**Deeper Ground, Darker Shadows: The Making of a Mindanao Rebel (University of Wisconsin Press 2025 and Ateneo de Manila University Press 2026)

World.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove part of lung
World.content:
POPE'S HOSPITAL.A man prays before the statue of the late Pope John Paul II outside Gemelli Hospital, where Pope Leo is hospitalized in Rome, Italy, October 13, 2026.

Experts emphasize the need for more information regarding the tumor's size and potential spread to lymph nodes to assess the prognosis and treatment options

VATICAN – Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung during surgery on Tuesday, October 13, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin.

The 71-year-old pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said.

The surgery to remove a small growth discovered during a recent routine health check lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications, according to Leo’s lead surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, and personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone.

“In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” they said, indicating that the aim was to eliminate all cancerous tissue.

The pope was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital earlier on Tuesday for the procedure. The Vatican had said his recovery was expected to take about a week.

Leo regained consciousness normally after the operation and returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, the medical bulletin said.

The Vatican said earlier this week that the pope was expected to remain in hospital for about a week. All his public events have been cancelled until October 20.

A medical expert said more information was needed to assess the pope’s condition, including the size of the tumor and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, details the Vatican did not immediately provide.

“While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment,” said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital.

“If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative,” Liu said. “But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis.”

Leo left the Vatican shortly before 1 pm (1100 GMT) on Tuesday and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy traveled about 9 km north to the hospital.

Upon arrival, Leo shook hands with several officials and walked past a crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted “Auguri” (best wishes), before entering through the main entrance.

Elected by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, Leo is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues.

The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025.

Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Monday, October 12, maintains a busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, though it was unclear whether the trip would still go ahead.

The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics and has no deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the Vatican’s bureaucracy continues its work, holding off on decisions that require papal approval.

Born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, Leo served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he contracted typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru, and was hospitalized.

He recounted the experience in his only major interview as pope, published in a book by Penguin Peru. Leo said the pain was so severe that he asked God to let him die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that “We need you here (on Earth),” he said.

“I never looked back,” Leo said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sara Duterte amid trial: ‘I will not resign. I will never resign.’
World.content:
VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte waves to supporters as she arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court for the arraignment of her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.

'Whether or not I become the next president of our country remains to be seen,' says Duterte

There have been allegations here and there against Vice President Sara Duterte.

She has an ongoing impeachment trial that could oust her from the vice presidency and prevent her from running for president in 2028. There are alleged deliveries of millions of pesos to her as claimed by former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.

And there’s this claim about her alleged link to companies that do business with China. Cale88 Food Corporation, tied to Duterte and husband Mans Carpio, allegedly received remittances from Chinese state-owned firms.

So, is resignation the answer to all her problems?

“No, no, no. I will not resign. I will never resign from the Office of the Vice President,” said Duterte during a chance interview with reporters on Tuesday, October 13.

Even before, Duterte’s defense lawyers said resigning is not option for the Vice President: “Never pa namin napag-usapan ng ating Bise Presidente ‘yung resignation (The Vice President and I have never talked about resignation). So, I don’t think we even have to discuss that issue,” said defense spokesperson and counsel Michael Poa.

A resignation, until now, would be a gamble for Duterte. There’s no assurance that her resignation will stop the Senate impeachment court from continuing her trial.

House prosecutors have been firm that a Duterte resignation won’t stop the trial, and by extension, the impeachment court’s judgment.

“Even if she resigns, for example, it will not absolve, it will not even terminate the impeachment trial because the only way to terminate the impeachment trial is for the court to finally reach a decision,” said House prosecution Zia Alonto Adiong earlier.

Duterte remains to be the most popular presidential aspirant because based on Pulse Asia’s September survey, she received a 50% voter preference rating. This is perhaps what keeps her holding on to her presidential dream.

But this number does not guarantee her political survival. If she gets convicted, it will mean nothing nor be of any use.

And at the rate things are going, the odds might no longer be in Duterte’s favor.

Play Video

First, the Senate impeachment court already adjusted the voting threshold — it will count only the votes of senator-judges who are “legally and factually capable” of participating in the proceedings at the time of the vote.

This is bad news for Duterte because with 20 active senators at present, two-thirds of the denominator would mean 14 (the required number of conviction votes). And this rule, so far, still stands because the Supreme Court dismissed the three petitions challenging the decision to adjust the threshold.

Second, the prosecution already dropped three of four articles of impeachment against her. The prosecutors said their evidence on her alleged unexplained wealth is sufficient to convict Duterte.

“We believe that evidence is substantial and compelling, and warrants the respondent’s removal from office for culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust,” lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro said.

What could this mean? It’s possible the prosecution has the numbers to convict her — and the dropping of the three articles is a telltale sign that the end of her vice presidency is coming.

“Whether or not I become the next president of our country remains to be seen. Hindi natin alam (We don’t know). And perhaps my purpose has always been bigger than the position itself,” said Duterte. – Rappler.com

World.title: Prosecution drops 3 of 4 cases vs Sara Duterte | The wRap
World.content:
Here are today’s headlines – the latest news in the Philippines and around the world:
