World.title: Azerbaijan's insurance sector capital exceeds prudential requirements
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. Azerbaijan's insurance sector had total capital of 312 million manat ($183.5 million) in the first half of 2026, compared with required capital of 205 million manats, indicating that the sector's capital position remained above prudential requirements.

According to the Financial Stability Report published by the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), 15 insurance companies and one reinsurance company were operating in the country during the reporting period. Of the insurance companies, five provided life insurance services and 10 specialized in non-life insurance. The sector also included 23 insurance brokers and 459 insurance agents.

Total insurance premiums rose by 6.2%, or 51 million manat ($29.9 million), year-on-year in the first six months of 2026 to 867 million manats. Life insurance accounted for 60% of premiums, while non-life insurance made up the remaining 40%.

Life insurance premiums increased by 8.8%, or 42 million manat ($24.7 million), to 516 million manat ($303.5 million), while non-life insurance premiums rose by 2.6%, or 9 million manat ($5.2 million), to 351 million manat ($206.4 million). Voluntary insurance products were the main drivers of growth in both segments.

Compulsory insurance premiums fell by 23%, or 45 million manat ($26.4 million), to 150 million manat ($88.2 million). In contrast, premiums from voluntary life insurance rose by 14%, or 61 million manat ($35.8 million), to 483 million manat ($284.1 million), while voluntary non-life insurance premiums increased by 17%, or 35 million manat ($20.5 million), to 235 million manat ($138.2 million).

Concentration in the insurance market remained high. At the end of the reporting period, the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) for life insurance fell by 119 points to 6,822, while the index for non-life insurance rose by 593 points to 3,813.

Premiums ceded to reinsurers also increased, rising by 23%, or 14 million manat ($8.2 million), year-on-year to 74 million manat ($43.5 million). They accounted for 8.6% of total premiums. Of the premiums ceded, 4.9%, or 3.6 million manat ($2.1 million), came from life insurance, while 95.1%, or 70.7 million manat ($41.5 million), came from non-life insurance.

Insurance claims also increased significantly during the reporting period. Payouts rose by 27.3%, or 118 million manat ($69.4 million), compared with the same period last year, reaching 550 million manat ($323.5 million). Of this amount, 402 million manat ($236.4 million) related to life insurance and 148 million manat ($87.05 million) to non-life insurance. Life insurance payouts increased by 32.5%, while non-life insurance payouts rose by 14.5%.

The insurance sector's assets increased by 5.8%, or 123 million manat ($72.3 million), in the first half of the year to 2.26 billion manat ($1.3 billion). Bank funds accounted for 37% of assets, government securities for 31%, non-government securities for 7%, accounts receivable for 10%, and other assets for 14%.

The sector's liabilities rose by 10%, or 151 million manat ($88.8 million), to 1.65 billion manat ($970.5 million). Insurance premium reserves accounted for 68% of liabilities, reserves for insurance claims for 23%, and other liabilities for 9%.

Insurance companies' investment portfolios expanded by 9.7%, or 140 million manat ($82.3 million), from the end of last year to 1.6 billion manat ($941.1 million). Investments consisted mainly of government and corporate securities, as well as bank deposits. Investment portfolios accounted for 76% of the assets of life insurance companies and 64% of the assets of non-life insurance companies.

The report also outlined the sector's liquidity indicators. At the end of the first half of 2026, the sector held 1.2 billion manat ($705.8 million) in high-quality liquid assets, against expected cash outflows of 793 million manat ($466.4 million) and expected cash inflows of 301 million manat ($177.05 million).

The sector's liquidity ratio (ILR) stood at 237%. The ratio was 206% for life insurance and 315% for non-life insurance.

Accounts receivable for insurance premiums increased by 9%, or 11.6 million manat ($6.8 million), from the beginning of the year to 140 million manat ($82.3 million). Receivables in life insurance fell by 6.1% to 48.5 million manat ($28.5 million), while those in non-life insurance rose by 19.2% to 91.6 million manat ($53.8 million). Receivables accounted for 6.9% of the sector's total assets.

The insurance sector's net profit rose by 11.9%, or 10 million manat ($5.8 million), year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to 90 million manat ($52.9 million). Life and non-life insurance companies each recorded profits of 45 million manat ($26.4 million).

At the same time, the sector's loss ratio increased by 4 percentage points to 89%. The loss ratio for compulsory motor third-party liability insurance rose by 6 percentage points to 115%, while the ratio for motor vehicle insurance increased by 2 percentage points to 87%.

The report noted that the sector's total capital fell by 69 million manat ($40.5 million) from the end of last year to 312 million manat ($183.5 million), taking dividend payments into account. Required capital increased by 1 million manat ($588,235.29) to 205 million manat ($120.5 million). Despite these changes, the sector's total capital remained above the required level.

World.title: Drive-by shooting at house in Melbourne's western suburbs
World.content:
Detectives are investigating a drive-by shooting at a house in Melbourne's western suburbs overnight.

Victoria Police said several shots were fired from a vehicle at the house in Flinders Place, Caroline Springs at around 12.45am.

The front of the house is marked with numerous bullet holes. (ABC News: Tara Whitchurch)

Four people inside the property at the time were not injured.

Police said the offenders fled in a silver Toyota Corolla, which was later found burnt out in Deer Park.

A crime scene has been established and police said the investigation into the incident was ongoing.

A vehicle at the house was sprayed with bullets. (ABC News: Tara Whitchurch)

Neighbours told the ABC they heard two separate rounds of gunshots in the middle of the night.

They said the occupants of a vehicle fired shots at the house before speeding off.

A Victoria Police vehicle in front of the home in Caroline Springs. (ABC News: Tara Whitchurch)

A vehicle arrived and parked at the house a short time later and remains at the property.

The neighbours said it was not the first time the house had been shot at.

Police have asked anyone with information or footage of the shooting to contact CrimeStoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: 'Stranded patients' in NSW hospitals prompts call for change
World.content:
New South Wales must think outside the box to stop the number of "stranded" aged care patients in hospitals from spiralling out of control, the state's productivity commissioner says.

According to recent data from NSW Health, the number of people who occupied hospital beds while awaiting placement in aged care facilities had jumped almost 40 per cent over the past year, from 761 to 1,063 patients.

A new report from the NSW Productivity and Equality Commission, released on Wednesday, estimated that figure could reach more than 7,000 in 10 years if aged care and community care services failed to keep pace with Australia's ageing population.

The report, which was commissioned by the state government, said an extra 2,600 aged care beds would be needed each year to meet future demand, but NSW was projected to deliver only 660.

It said the costs associated with patients stranded in NSW hospital beds were estimated to exceed $1 billion annually.

Patients waiting for aged care beds in hospitals has risen by 40 per cent in a year. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

NSW Productivity and Equality Commissioner Peter Achterstraat told the ABC more funding was required for aged care support and health prevention, but other alternatives could be explored.

"We need to look outside the box. There may as well be a third alternative, such as intermediate care where people can go to facilities which are not an acute hospital but not quite an aged care facility," he said.

Peter Achterstraat emphasised the need for intermediate care. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Mr Achterstraat said previous research conducted by the commission found that keeping patients in hospital beds was costing $1,000 a night, compared with "just a few hundred dollars" at an aged care facility.

"If an elderly person is at home and they have an accident or something and they need to go to the hospital … normally they'd be ready after five days to go home," he said.

"But in many situations they can't go home because they need someone at home to change the bandages or to administer medicines.

"So they stay in hospital, they can't go home and there's no aged care facilities available for them because there's a shortage … there are over 1,100 people in New South Wales hospital beds today who shouldn't be there."

NSW government responds

Ryan Park says the state government will provide interim support services. (ABC)

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said the state government would provide interim services, but argued aged care was traditionally the responsibility of the Commonwealth.

In early September, state and territory leaders called for the Commonwealth to expand its Support at Home package to help stranded patients return home sooner.

The productivity commission is also calling for the service to be expanded, estimating there were more than 100,000 Australians waiting to access funding for at-home support services in March 2026, with average waits of about 12 months.

Mr Park said the state government would introduce a $28 million pilot program, which could include funding for short-term services such as clinical care, wound care and symptom management, personal care, as well as domestic assistance.

"It is a significant reform because we're essentially stepping into a space [that is] traditionally the responsibility of the Commonwealth, but I can't see hospital beds continue to be taken offline each and every day," he said.

Funding not in line with building new aged care homes

The commission's report found Commonwealth government funding for new aged care homes had not kept up with rising construction and operating costs.

It said the federal government was not providing sufficient returns to recover the up-front costs of new homes; the biggest barrier to increasing supply.

Bed block costs $3m per day in Queensland It didn't take long for 80-year-old Gwen to lose her ability to walk.

"Meaningful and sustained reductions in stranded patients will require the Australian Government to ensure the capacity of aged care services keeps pace with population needs," the report said. "The Australian Government should increase residential aged care funding to efficient levels that support development feasibility, long-term investment confidence and the supply response needed as the population ages."

Federal Aged Care and Seniors Minister Sam Rae's office has been contacted for comment.

Other recommendations include establishing a dashboard to track stranded patients in NSW hospitals, ensure aged care funding supports demand, expanding community based services, as well as setting up a cross-agency delivery team to coordinate action on aged care supply and stranded patients.

World.title: Storms 'swirling like a tornado' leave trail of destruction in parts of NT
World.content:
Central Australian businesses and residents are assessing damage from severe, tornado-like storms that swept through parts of the Northern Territory.

Rain, hail and winds at speeds of nearly 100km/h hit the outback town on Monday afternoon, ripping roofs from houses, knocking down trees and powerlines and covering roads with leaf litter and mud.

The Double Tree Hilton suffered significant damage. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Double Tree Hotel general manager Todd Grierson said multiple parts of the Alice Springs building were extensively damaged after footage circulated online of rain blowing in under the front doors and water pouring through the ceiling above the reception desks.

"There is just so much more throughout the building ... from our tenancies, to our beauty salon, other restaurants, our ballroom and meeting areas and back of house too," he said.

"But thankfully, the way any direction of this storm has hit us, hasn't had any effect on our guest rooms."

Cleaning up at the Double Tree Hilton. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Mr Grierson estimated the repairs would cost more than half a million dollars to complete.

Alice Springs cafe The Roastery threw out thousands of dollars worth of food, after widespread power outages.

Owner Kim Hopper said the cafe received a delivery on the day of the first storm, but food safety rules meant they had to discard many products.

Kim Hopper says thousands of dollars worth of food was discarded. (ABC Alice Springs: Mitchell Abram)

"Our staff are there at the moment just documenting it all and tipping hundreds of litres of milk down the sink," she said.

"It'd be thousands to replace that cost, but it's a loss of the sales as well...we'll be doing an insurance claim on that, and luckily we've got that in place."

'Unbelievable' storm widespread

About 20 kilometres east of Alice Springs, Undoolya Station copped a lashing, with owner Ben Hayes saying the storm was devastating.

"It was swirling, it was like a tornado. It didn't know where it wanted to go, it was just coming every direction. I've never been in a storm like that before in my life," he said.

"It was unbelievable lightning. I don't know what the hell's been hit around here, whether any of these trees have been hit, but a lot of them are screwed up."

Ben Hayes in front of his historic storeroom. (ABC Alice Springs: Charles Geary)

Mr Hayes said there had been significant damage to infrastructure on the cattle station, including a lean-to collapsed onto a house, smashed windows, a chook pen blown away and the roof of an historic store room ripped off by wind.

"There's a lot of history in this room and [my wife] Nicole's rattling it all out, drying it out, trying to save as much as we can," he said.

"We've got a few shipping containers up the dump with a lot of these records left to go in there, until we can find somebody to help put a roof on this thing for us."

The storeroom contains historic documents, which have been relocated to a storage container for safe keeping. (ABC Alice Springs: Charles Geary)

Meanwhile, cattle stations near the Northern Territory-South Australian border were battered with large hailstones.

Lyndavale Station, 250 kilometres south-west of Alice Springs, recorded hailstones the size of golf balls.

World.title: Nine roller-coasters close across US, Canada after man dies during ride
World.content:
Nine roller-coasters have been closed across the United States and Canada as new information emerges about a man who was ejected from his seat and fell to his death at a Georgia theme park.

Warning: This story contains eyewitness accounts of the incident, which may disturb some readers.

Witnesses watched in horror as 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was ejected from his seat, appearing to hover above the car before striking several people and falling to his death at Six Flags over Georgia.

The nightmarish death prompted Six Flags to temporarily close nine similar roller-coasters across North America.

Six Flags over Georgia is just north-west of Atlanta. (AP: Mike Stewart)

Police and a state agency that oversees ride inspections are investigating, but many questions remain, including how the man fell out and whether there were problems with his restraints.

Mr Kariem, a school employee from Atlanta, was killed while riding Goliath, the park's tallest roller-coaster, which features a first hill measuring 61 metres.

"It looked like he was hovering because the car was moving underneath him," said Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars pass overhead.

The man fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mr Mendenhall said, before being ejected from the ride on its final turn.

"It felt like slow-motion, but it happened in an instant," he said.

"I was just praying in those moments. I was praying: 'God, please let him stay in that car.'"

Goliath towers above the entrance at Six Flags over Georgia just outside Atlanta, the state's capital city, with a series of hills and turns.

It does not take riders upside down.

There are no seat belts. Instead, riders are restrained with lap bars that pull down over their legs and waists.

In a theme park industry that is constantly introducing new thrills, it is far from the world's tallest, fastest or wildest coaster.

One family watched as the man flew out of the roller-coaster

Investigators and park employees told investigators that Mr Kareim was thrown from the roller-coaster, but officials have not released any other information about the people who were hurt.

Mr Kariem worked as the information technology manager at a public charter school and, before that, as a technology teacher.

Police and state officials are investigating the incident. (AP: Mike Stewart)

In a statement, the Wesley International Academy said it was devastated, and Mr Kariem's "dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did".

Summer Bates, who was at the park with her husband and three children, saw Mr Kariem fall.

"One thing I think that will stick with us is the sound of his body coming down," Ms Bates said.

Ms Bates said she and her family rode Goliath earlier in the day.

"My older two children rode on the car ahead of us," she said.

"I noticed they kept trying to push their [restraints] down tighter.

"I assured them that they were OK. But once my husband, youngest child and I loaded into our cart and headed up the incline, I quickly understood why my older two were messing with theirs.

"It just didn't feel secure and tight."

Amusement ride oversight varies by state

In the US, roller-coasters and other rides at major amusement parks such as Six Flags are not regulated by the federal government.

That responsibility falls to the states.

Georgia's Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees annual ride inspections, is "conducting an in-depth and comprehensive review," of what happened, said Garrison Bennett, a spokesperson.

In California, the state approves new rides and ones that have been modified and either directly inspects them or relies on an annual inspection by the owner.

Florida's largest theme parks are exempt from state safety inspections, unlike smaller venues and fairs.

Instead, the largest theme parks, such as Walt Disney World and Universal, conduct their own inspections and have their own protocols.

Six Flags closes roller-coasters elsewhere

The roller coaster closure comes a month after lawsuits alleging riders suffered serious brain injuries emerged at the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain. (AP: Jae C. Hong)

Six Flags Entertainment Corp temporarily shut down roller-coasters at six of its theme parks in the US and Canada.

The parks were already scheduled for seasonal midweek closures on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Those rides include a second coaster named Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California; Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Illinois; Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey; Fury 325 and Thunder Striker at Carowinds in North Carolina; and the rides Leviathan and Behemoth at Canada's Wonderland in Ontario, Canada.

The company did not say why those specific rides were shut down or what would be done before they reopened.

Bolliger & Mabillard, the Swiss company that manufactured the coaster and many others worldwide, said it was actively investigating and would not comment "until we have a better understanding of what happened".

"Our thoughts are with the family and those affected," a spokesperson said.

AP

World.title: High Court rules in favour of prisoner trying to freeze her eggs
World.content:
The High Court has ruled in favour of a Queensland prisoner who is trying to freeze her eggs whilst serving time in custody.

Rachel Smith was part way through a 10-year jail sentence for drug trafficking, when she applied to Queensland Corrective Services (QCS) for approval to receive a privately funded Oocyte cryopreservation procedure.

QCS automatically refused her application, citing Queensland laws, which they said prohibits inmates from accessing "assisted reproductive technology".

Smith challenged the decision in the Supreme Court and then again in the Court of Appeal, with her lawyers arguing that egg freezing did not fall under this definition, as it was only a "preparatory" step.

After failing to convince the Queensland appellate judges, she sought leave to appeal in the High Court.

Queensland Corrective Services was ordered to pay Smith's legal costs. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Following a hearing in Canberra last month, on Wednesday five High Court judges allowed her appeal.

They ruled the decision made by QCS in 2024 should be quashed and that the matter return to the department for determination "according to law".

QCS was also ordered to pay Smith's legal costs.

World.title: Students risk 'cognitive outsourcing' if AI overused, schools warned
World.content:
Schools and teachers across Australia have been warned to use AI "sparingly" in the classroom or risk students' lifelong learning outcomes.

In fresh advice to educators and government released today by the government-owned Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO), CEO Dr Jenny Donovan said there was a risk AI could cause disruption to student learning.

"It can become a distraction, and it can disguise the fact that children are using it as a crutch rather than actually a tool to learn," she said.

AERO is a national education research body and has reviewed studies in Australia and overseas to provide advice on the risks and benefits of AI, as schools rush to keep up the rapidly advancing technology.

CEO of the Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO) Dr Jenny Donovan warns AI is becoming a crutch to student learning. (Supplied)

Dr Donovan said AI could create an illusion of learning, with studies overseas showing students using AI were unable to replicate results when deprived of the technology in an exam setting.

"It's called cognitive outsourcing. It's when you rely on the tool to do the thinking for you, and there are real risks for students, because they are novice learners," Dr Donovan said.

"If they're never required to do that thinking for themselves, or if they don't do enough of it, they never build up the knowledge that they need to be able to become independent, creative, critical thinkers."

How different states approach AI in schools The NSW government is suggesting a ban on take-home assignments for senior students after an influx of cheating using AI. But a leading expert says that is not the only issue.

Dr Donovan said AI should be avoided completely in the first three years of primary school and only be used carefully after that, in combination with established teaching practices like explicit instruction.

"It's really important that students have foundational knowledge, that they can draw on, that is embedded in their long-term memories that has actually been learned and absorbed by them," she said.

"If they don't get that knowledge in place, if it's masked by the fact that they've always resorted to AI or other props, then they're not going to be able to develop in their knowledge and their thinking as they move through their lives."

AERO warns AI should be completely avoided in first three years of schooling. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

Dr Donovan said AI was important to introduce in high school as it would be part of later higher education.

She said some school jurisdictions like NSW had developed generative AI tools that could guide students through reasoning rather than providing direct answers or essays on command.

Dr Donovan said tools like this were appropriate for students and warned parents against giving students "unfettered access" to tools like ChatGPT at home.

"Try not to let students use AI at home too much if you can. There's a reason that some of the jurisdictions went down the path of developing a bespoke version of ChatGPT," Dr Donovan said.

"They were able to make sure that the students still had to do the brain work for themselves, that they couldn't just subcontract their learning to the devices."

While AI will be important to use in high school, AERO warns parents to limit the use of it at home. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

The advice comes amid a growing backlash to education technology with Education Minister Jason Clare warning too much screen time was contributing to recent poor results from Australian students in global PISA testing.

"These results and PISA over the past show us students who use screens a lot score lower than those who don't," Mr Clare said.

"Students need to learn digital skills. That includes how to use, and how not to use AI. But it does point to the need to wind back the amount of screen time in schools. A bit of a digital detox."

World.title: Court dumps Plibersek heritage decision that halted $1b gold mine
World.content:
The Federal Court has overturned a Commonwealth decision that halted a billion-dollar gold mine in New South Wales.

Regis Resources launched legal action against then federal minister for environment and water Tanya Plibersek in November 2024, challenging the validity of an Aboriginal Protection Order she granted over part of its McPhillamys Gold Project near Blayney.

The order applied to 400 hectares of the site, including an area where the company wanted to build a tailings dam, which is used to hold mining waste.

It was made after the mining project received approval in 2023.

At the time, Ms Plibersek said the order would protect the headwaters and springs of the Belubula River and that the company could construct its tailings storage elsewhere.

But Regis Resources disputed this, saying the decision impacted a critical area of the project development site and meant the project was "no longer financially feasible".

The Section 10 Aboriginal Protection Order made (in yellow) over part of the McPhillamys Gold Project site (in grey). (Supplied: Regis Resources)

Justice James Stellios has presided over the Federal Court challenge and held two days of hearings in December 2025.

He delivered his judgment during a short sitting today, which found that Regis Resources was successful in the judicial review and the minister's "declaration is invalid".

The Aboriginal Protection Order was granted after Wiradyuri elder Aunty Nyree Reynolds lodged an application to protect the area under Section 10 of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act in 2020.

Tanya Plibersek granted the Aboriginal Protection Order over part of the McPhillamys mine site in 2024. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The court heard the application was supported by the Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation (WTOCWAC) and referred to a Dreaming story called the Blue Banded Bee.

Justice Stellios told the court that this information "constituted a new application" and should have been referred to the government reporter for consideration and to carry out a public consultation process.

"Consequently, the declaration made by the minister was made without authority," Justice Stellios said.

"The court's decision and my reasons say nothing about the merits of the claim ... whether it's a significant area or under threat of injury or desecration ... those are matters within the authority of the minister ... not the jurisdiction of this court."

Regis Resources took the office of the federal environment minister, now held by Murray Watt, to the Federal Court. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Justice Stellios said the appropriate remedy was for the proposal to be sent back to the federal minister for environment and water, now held by Murray Watt, for redetermination.

He ordered the parties to provide written submissions on costs to be submitted by October 27.

'Committed' to mine

In its 2026 annual report to shareholders published in August, Regis Resources said work was "well advanced" on an alternative tailings facility.

"We remain committed to McPhillamys, which has the potential to become not only a long-life, low-cost operation but also the core of a significant new mining hub, with multiple associated growth opportunities," the report said.

The company said it was aiming to have a final investment decision on the project in the first half of 2028.

The ABC has contacted the WTOCWAC, Regis Resources and Mr Watt for a response.

World.title: 'A lot of emotion:' First round of redundancies to hit Whyalla steelworks
World.content:
The first of more than 250 workers to accept redundancies at the Whyalla steelworks will finish up this week — but those who want to stay are still facing an anxious wait.

The permanent closure of the blast furnace last month will reduce the plant's direct workforce from 1,700 to 1,200, while at least another 300 contractor roles will also be affected.

Australian Workers' Union organiser Shane Karger said he expected about 270 direct employees to accept "genuine redundancies" by the end of this month.

The first group of those will exit by this Friday.

Mr Karger said following that, voluntary redundancies and early retirement scheme applications would be processed.

Genuine redundancy occurs when a worker's role is no longer required, for example, those who were working at the blast furnace.

He said voluntary redundancies would go to workers in departments that would reduce their numbers but not shut down entirely.

Shane Karger said it's been a emotional time for workers in Whyalla. (ABC News)

Mr Karger said the final number of redundancies should be known by November.

"[That] will then sort out how many positions are up for redeployment," he said.

Even for those who stay on, it is unclear what the future will look like.

The steelworks has been in administration since early last year, with the announcement of a buyer expected by the end of 2026.

Mr Karger said unions have been working with administrators KordaMentha to make the process as fast and smooth as possible.

"There's been a lot of emotion," he said.

" There's those that are young, they've got a mortgage … they're now thinking 'what the hell am I going to do now?' "

"You've got other workers that are looking forward to a well-earned rest after a very long career at the steelworks."

The steelworks was forced into administration in February last year. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Several contractors have confirmed to the ABC that they have already laid off staff, with more than one closing down entirely.

'I haven't felt secure'

Jack Taylor, 30, has done manual labour at the steelworks for 10 years but will clock off for the final time this week.

His was one of the roles being cut and he has opted not to apply for redeployment, instead accepting a redundancy.

"It was a big decision to make," he said.

"I own my house here in Whyalla so going for redeployment [would have] meant I'd have a chance of keeping a job, having income coming in."

Jack Taylor accepted a redundancy. (ABC News)

Mr Taylor said years of uncertainty over the future of the steelworks had taken a toll.

"The whole time I've been there … I haven't really felt secure," he said.

"We've been through administration two times.

"I'm just a bit over all of it, to be honest."

He plans to apply for fly-in-fly-out jobs in the mining sector, and hopes to stay in Whyalla.

"I've got my family, the footy club, all my friends and that here," he said.

World.title: Greens claim Labor’s tax bill contains private school fee loophole
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Greens claim Labor’s tax bill contains private school fee loophole Brittany Busch October 14, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Greens are demanding the government hike taxes on parents paying for private school fees through trusts, arguing there is a loophole in the budget reforms. Labor needs the support of the Greens in the Senate to pass the tax on trusts, with the Coalition staunchly opposed to any tax hikes. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has already been forced to walk back a number of measures in the May budget after unforseen consequences copped backlash. Greens economics spokesperson Nick McKim says his party has serious concerns. Alex Ellinghausen But the Greens are concerned the government has gone too far in the carveouts, and will kick the bill to a Senate inquiry after Chalmers introduced the legislation to parliament on Wednesday. The minor party wants to interrogate an exemption to the proposed 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, which would exclude money paid to charities.



While the bill does not name which entities will be exempt, some private schools hold charitable status, potentially excluding disbursements to them through trusts from the 30 per cent tax. Related Article Trusts Small business trusts get stamp duty escape hatch in Chalmers’ latest tax tweak Greens economic spokesman Nick McKim said the party had serious concerns about the exemption. “It seems as if it will be possible for people with trusts to pay private school fees or donations to private schools, and not be subject to the 30 per cent minimum tax,” the senator said. “People with trusts, in general terms, are quite well-off, and we don’t think they should get a benefit that is not available to people who don’t have trusts – because money that goes into trusts is tax-free, but people who don’t have a trust are paying income tax.



“You need to be wealthy enough to afford a fancy accountant, or at least some accounting advice, which is not available to everyone.” McKim would not say whether the change was a red line for the party, but said it would consider the evidence in the inquiry. “Once we’ve been through that process, we’re happy to sit down with the government and have a conversation.” Loading The government is not expected to move on the Greens demands, given the arrangement has always been a feature of trusts.



But it poses a challenge to the government, which needs Greens’ support to pass the reforms. Related Article Updated

Federal budget Widows and divorcees protected as Labor reveals details of tax backdown Chalmers touted the changes in the House of Representatives on Wednesday morning, saying the trust reforms were the latest tranche in Labor’s budget which was about making the tax system fairer and more sustainable. “We know there are legitimate reasons to use trusts, including succession planning and asset protection,” Chalmers said. “But the flexibility provided by discretionary trusts allows some people to plan their tax affairs in ways that aren’t available to most workers and families.”



Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson was scathing of the bill and demanded an inquiry, accusing Labor MPs of failing to understand how small businesses that rely on trusts to structure their tax affairs work. “Do not misunderstand the scale of the train wreck that is about to come. You have a problem at the moment with the legislation in front of you, where if people move structures, once they move structures, it automatically ... triggers a stamp duty obligation. “The members on the other side of this chamber did not have the courage to send this legislation to an election and that is the point of why we need this inquiry.” More to come. World.title: Trump’s America and Wall Street are in a dangerous spiral
World.content:
BusinessMarketsBonds Opinion Trump’s America and Wall Street are in a dangerous spiral Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 14, 2026 — 12:00pm

October 14, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What would it look like if demand for government and corporate debt rose rapidly even as its cost surged? We’re seeing that play out in real time. The coincidence of record levels of government debt and government debt issuance with the biggest investment boom in history is having an increasingly visible impact on debt markets, one exacerbated by stubbornly-high inflation rates and heightened geopolitical risks. US debt levels have skyrocketed since Donald Trump returned to the White House. AP The world’s biggest debt markets are in the US, where there’s the $US32 trillion ($46 trillion) Treasuries market for government debt, a $US12 trillion-plus market for corporate debt and another $US2 trillion or so market for private credit. The spreads between the yields on US government and investment grade corporate debt have risen slightly recently, but remain relatively tight. Those on lesser-rated debt have been blowing out, with CCC and even lower rated bonds trading at double-digit percentage point margins over Treasuries.



That’s happening in an environment where the yields on government debt have been rising so, for all but the higher-rated issuers, there’s the double-whammy of increased spreads against rising benchmarks. Related Article Opinion

AI The world’s richest person is testing Wall Street’s limits The yields on the US and global benchmark bonds – US 10-year Treasuries – were at their lowest point for the year in late February, just before the US and Israel attacked Iran. From 3.94 per cent then the yield has climbed to 4.82 per cent. The move in the yields on two-year bonds has been even more pronounced, from 3.38 per cent on the eve of the war to 4.82 per cent now. The war, inflation and the expectation that the Federal Reserve Board will continue to raise US rates are part of the explanation for the rise. The other, perhaps more significant is the expansion in deficits and debt since Donald Trump regained the White House.



The deficit is now almost $US2 trillion, or 6 per cent of US GDP, and gross debt is more than $US40 trillion, or about $US4 trillion more than Trump inherited a little more than 18 months ago. Not only has the perceived riskiness of the debt increased, but there’s more debt to be absorbed, even as sovereign buyers of US debt have been backing away from the market – the share of the market has fallen steadily and substantially, led by China, since the 2008 financial crisis – and been replaced by hedge funds and other private sources. The most likely breaking point for the markets would be a moment of disappointment or doubt over the rate or potential of AI to be commercialised and ultimately generate profits commensurate with the risks being accepted by the capital providers. AP The US will roll over about $US10 trillion of maturing debt this year and, thanks to the deficit, add about $US2 trillion of new issuance. That’s a lot of supply for the market to absorb. The increased yields on Treasuries have spilt over into the cost of corporate and private debt, even mortgages, where interest rates have been rising and are now in the mid-7 per cent range, roughly a percentage point higher than at the same time last year.



The supply of corporate debt has also been swelling. So far this year more than $US2 trillion of new corporate bonds have been issued, an increase of about 25 per cent on the same period last year. Increasingly, that issuance is being dominated by companies associated with the artificial intelligence investment boom. Related Article Opinion

Global economy The four horsemen of the apocalypse are coming for the global economy Between them, SpaceX, Broadcom and Oracle alone are currently in the market for more than $US150 billion of new debt. Already this year, AI companies have raised closed to half a trillion dollars of new debt. Elon Musk’s SpaceX’s experience reflects the broader story. It raised $US86 billion of equity via its initial public offering in June and then immediately raised another $US25 billion through a bond issue. It’s now seeking a further $US40 billion. That tells you something about the rate of cash burn being experienced by the AI pioneers, and the inability of equity markets to keep up with the demand for the capital being burnt. As a group, AI hyperscalers will invest around $US750 billion this year, with expectations of another trillion dollars in each of the next two years.



Debt providers want collateral or pricing of the debt that reflects the riskiness of the borrower. SpaceX’s initial bond issue attracted an investment grade rating, albeit the second-lowest BBB grade. The longest dated of those bonds – they mature in 2056 – now trades at a spread of about 240 basis points over Treasuries, or about 85 per cent of their face value. The cost of insuring that debt against default has also blown out, with credit default swaps costing 194 basis points, or $US19,400 a year for every $US1 million of debt held. Between them, SpaceX, Broadcom and Oracle alone are currently in the market for more than $US150 billion of new debt. Bloomberg Oracle, the most leveraged of the hyperscalers, also has bonds trading with spreads well over 200 basis points and the cost of its five-year credit default swap has rocketed to more than 260 basis points, or $US26,000 per $1 million.



AI has an insatiable appetite for capital. Even the corporate bond market is being stretched to supply it. The companies have also been tapping fellow AI companies, private credit and constructing quite elaborate structures to attract capital providers. A common feature of the sector is for one of the big chipmakers, like Nvidia or Broadcom, to lend the funds to frontier labs to buy their chips, with contracts whose lives probably outstrip the useful life of the chips in question. It is also common for the hyperscalers to structure joint ventures within special purpose vehicles with private credit providers to raise the funding needed to construct data centres and equip them with the expensive chips and hardware required, leasing back the data centre’s capacity. There’s a lot of leverage within AI beyond conventional debt, with collateral that may prove illusory if AI revenues don’t eventually – and sooner rather than later – start to rationalise the scale of the investments being made. Similar threats of government and AI-related debt supply overwhelming demand are current globally, although the US is the epicentre for any potential flashpoint.



The most likely breaking point for the markets – and AI and those pursuing it – would be a moment of disappointment or doubt over the rate or potential of AI to be commercialised and ultimately generate profits commensurate with the risks being accepted by the capital providers. There’s also a concern that, having shown no interest in stabilising federal government finances, the Trump administration will look for painless ways to manage the debt levels. “Debasement,” or allowing inflation and manipulation of the Fed’s policy rate to keep rates artificially low, is often cited as a risk. Related Article Opinion

Inflation Don’t blame Ukraine: Prices go up and up, thanks to Trump’s wars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist If there is to be crisis in debt markets it is likely to start in the US and probably start within the AI sector. The sector relies on access to ever-increasing volumes of equity and debt to fund investments that have to be made long before there is even a prospect of the high risk-adjusted returns that those providing the capital anticipate.



Whether it is the escalating cost of the debt, or its availability from the increasingly risk-aware capital providers, or some external event that shakes the debt markets, the AI sector and those funding it are extremely vulnerable to the slightest of adverse developments. World.title: SBS debate ‘brings together’ childfree advocates and anti-abortion campaigners
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV SBS debate ‘brings together’ childfree advocates and anti-abortion campaigners Bridget McManus October 14, 2026 — 11:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What do three childfree advocates and three conservative commentators have in common? Not a lot. But this is why you’ll find them taking part in a debate on SBS’s youth-focused current affairs program, The Feed. The six participants will thrash out an urgent question in light of Australia’s plummeting birth rate: “Why are more people choosing a childfree life, and should having kids still be a priority?” According to the debate’s producer and moderator, journalist Elfy Scott, “there were surprising moments of agreement from both sides of the panel.” Surprising indeed, given the profiles of the speakers. Elfy Scott hosts The Feed Debate: Having Kids. SBS Promoting the childfree lifestyle are model and actor Ellie Gonsalves, who in 2023 went viral for posting 118 reasons why she doesn’t want kids; comedian and One Nation critic, Andrew Lewis; and Dita, a nurse and content creator who posts about racism and family violence. On the opposing side are single mother and anti-abortion activist Elspeth McKellar, who creates confrontational content for Joanna Howe’s organisation Bird Flip; George Mamalis, South Australian head of the late Charlie Kirk’s right-wing advocacy group Turning Point USA, who has advocated against abortion and called feminism a “death cult”; and Stephanie Bastiaan, a mother of six and head of advocacy at Women’s Forum, an organisation critical of pro-trans activism.



Elspeth McKellar, George Mamalis and Stephanie Bastiaan on The Feed Debate: Having Kids. SBS “We want to bring people together outside of those polarising algorithms, and give them the space to speak openly, but then also ensure that they’re fact-checked in that context,” says Scott. “We think it is important to be able to facilitate these conversations, even if they are challenging, and to draw people out of things that they see online, and ensure that we can give perspectives across a broad range.” Related Article Australian TV Why Marc Fennell threw himself into the ‘deep end’ of the manosphere Scott has sat in the moderator’s chair for many a passionate discussion at literary festivals. She is no stranger to provocative subject matter, having authored The One Thing We’ve Never Spoken About, exploring the stigma around mental illness, inspired by her mother’s experience living with schizophrenia. She’s also presented ABC documentaries investigating everything from psychic mediums and UFO sightings to conspiracy theories. But moderating this potentially explosive forum required “keeping everybody on track as far as the topic is concerned, and keeping the debate respectful and civil … It’s such a significant conversation right now. And we need to hear from the young people making these decisions.”



Andrew Lewis, Ellie Gonsalves and Dita on The Feed Debate: Having Kids. SBS Aimed at the 16-39 demographic, the semiannual Feed debates put millennials in charge of the agenda. Other episodes have had influencers from the left and right debating politics, socialists and property investors debating whether capitalism is expiring, and an array of prominent voices from the online sphere debating masculinity. “This is a key moment in history where we are seeing the fertility rate decline to a level we’ve never seen before,” says Scott. “We are facing unique issues – economic issues, political issues, global stability issues and climate issues. So there’s a lot for people to consider that previous generations have not had to.” Scott won’t be drawn on her personal position, adding “I am still internally debating.” But she says it is a question that is frequently raised in her social circles.



“I feel like I have had a million conversations with friends and family about it. It’s the conversation we’re all having at family barbecues. For myself, as a woman in her early 30s, it is absolutely a decision that is relevant to me, and one that I enjoy hearing every perspective on … When we’re talking about issues related to AI and climate, which do come up in the debate, those are inherently political topics. I think people are becoming more apprehensive about parenthood because of things like that.” Related Article Parenting The people who say no to being a parent, and have very happy lives She hopes the debate starts conversations among viewers of all generations. “This topic is so exposed in the media at the moment, but very, very rarely are we actually hearing from the young people themselves … And I would love for older audiences to have that exposure to people from younger generations, and the range of factors that are going into this decision. “It’s not a simple choice. And that’s what a lot of young people are feeling right now – this push and pull, regarding whether or not to become a parent.”

World.title: Block on NSW gold mine rejected by federal court
World.content:
PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Block on NSW gold mine rejected by federal court Jessica McSweeney October 14, 2026 — 11:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

NSW Premier Chris Minns has emerged victorious in a stoush over a controversial Central West gold mine after the Federal Court threw out a ban made by then-environment minister Tanya Plibersek, who stalled the mine on Indigenous heritage grounds. Federal Court Justice James Stellion on Wednesday decided to send the $1.3 billion mine proposal back to the current minister Murray Watt, determining Plibersek’s original decision lacked procedural fairness. The proposed McPhillamys gold mine would process as much as 8.5 million tonnes of ore a year. Nick Moir The decision did not make any judgment about the merits of any claims of Indigenous heritage in the area, but found Plibersek’s decision-making was flawed. That declaration prevented Regis Resources from building a tailings dam to store byproducts from mining operations at the headwaters of the Belubula River, after an Indigenous group argued the area was significant to a Dreaming story about the blue banded bee. The mining company argued that made the project unfeasible.



The declaration also triggered unrest between the state and federal governments, with the Premier Chris Minns insisting the mine must go ahead. The state government had originally approved the project. “I want that mine to go ahead, I understand that that’s not the view of the federal government, but we need the investment,” Minns said before the judgment on Wednesday. “There are more people in mining jobs in NSW today than there were when we were elected in March of 2023. We’re proud of that.” When asked if the then-environment minister had made the wrong call when she made the order blocking the mine, Minns replied: “Yes”. Plibersek’s statement of reasons for the declaration said she “could not be assured that the NSW legislative framework as it currently stands can adequately protect the specified area”.



After making the declaration, Plibersek rejected suggestions from Regis Resources that the ban killed the project, insisting the mine could still go ahead if the dam was moved. The company said finding a new site for approval would take up to 10 years, but the state government flagged it would fast-track the project. The application to protect the dam area was made by Wiradjuri-Gamillaroi woman Nyree Reynolds on behalf of the Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation. Minns told a budget estimates hearing in 2024 that the local Aboriginal Land Council had been consulted as part of the original approval process. More to come.

World.title: Trump’s ambassador to Greece resigns after allegations of improper conduct
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump’s ambassador to Greece resigns after allegations of improper conduct Matthew Lee Updated October 14, 2026 — 11:47am ,first published October 14, 2026 — 3:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US President Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday (US time) after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she will “vigorously defend” herself. Trump’s administration said earlier on Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks as US President Donald Trump listens at the White House in March 2025. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once married to California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr. The announcement, after days of comments and speculation, came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing on Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle “has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well”.



Guilfoyle’s departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. “Well, we’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he was considering firing Guilfoyle. “We’re not happy.” White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Tuesday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior US official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on her future this week. In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.



Guilfoyle addressed the allegations directly in a post on X, saying, “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.” “I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.” View post on X In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle’s lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services – public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination – that had not been paid. The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations”.



After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” But after another report appeared later, Rubio – speaking on Thursday before leaving Athens – berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them. Related Article Trump's White House Trump picks Fox News expert for next White House press secretary “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. A second US official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general (IG) was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.



The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. “This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament on Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House ‘My president ... excuse me, my husband’: Trump’s new spinner gets off to a rocky start Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens, as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law. The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Representative Robert Garcia, Democrat for California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.



Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $US100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. Related Article Updated

US politics Federal agents raid home of Democratic congresswoman targeted by Trump The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives. Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behaviour appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece.

World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland councils Mayor on edge of being kicked off council after sick-leave vote Julius Dennis October 14, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A south-east Queensland mayor is on the brink of being forced out of office after her extended sick leave was rejected by councillors. Redlands mayor Jos Mitchell has been on medical leave since May, with councillors at monthly meetings voting to either accept or reject her continued absence. The leave had initially been accepted until it was voted against by most councillors at the September meeting. Jos Mitchell has been on medical leave since May. Julius Dennis Under Queensland law, a councillor’s or mayor’s seat is vacated once they miss two or more consecutive general meetings over a two-month period.



While Mitchell has missed two meetings, she cannot lose her seat until the next meeting, according to the Department of Local Government. Should she be forced from her position, Mitchell would be the first mayor in Queensland to be ousted in such a manner. Elected in 2024, Mitchell entered a deeply divided council following the exit of long-term mayor Karen Williams two years after she made headlines for crashing her council-owned car while drunk. Mitchell has been outspoken about the council’s culture, and has made headlines for being the subject of more than 50 conduct complaints, which she has claimed were politically motivated. In August, the council’s bureaucratic arm took a swing at the mayor in a submission to a state parliamentary inquiry into councillor conduct, suggesting any councillor on extended leave should be subject to an investigation.



In May, Mitchell said she would be on medical leave for six weeks. The mayor had been taken to hospital earlier in the year after collapsing at work. Redlands led the state in OIA complaints last year. Matt Dennien “On medical advice, I have made the decision to step aside from my role as mayor for a period of six weeks to appropriately address a health issue,” she said at the time. “This is a decision I have not taken lightly, nor with any pleasure. It is, though, a necessary decision if I am to continue in this role and perform at my best.”



At Wednesday’s meeting, deputy mayor Julie Talty, who has led the meetings in Mitchell’s absence, said councillors had received a note in July asking for continued leave from meetings through October 31. Related Article Queensland councils ‘Avoiding accountability’: Council takes aim at mayor on medical leave Before the vote, councillor Jason Colley asked chief executive Louise Rusan whether the council had received a request from Mitchell to take leave without pay, which she said they hadn’t. Councillors Wendy Boglary, Lance Hewlett, Tracy Hughes and Paul Bishop voted to accept the leave, while councillors Rowanne McKenzie, Shane Rendalls, Paul Gollé, Colley and Talty voted against. A spokesperson for the mayor said the vote was disappointing.



“Many workplaces send ‘get well’ messages when people are away unwell,” they said. “Mayor Jos Mitchell has received criticism and imputations.” They drew a line between the support shown for Williams after she was charged with drink-driving and the apparent animosity towards Mitchell. “Most of the councillors voting against Mayor Mitchell’s application for leave of absence with a medical certificate were present when the former mayor drank, drove and crashed the Lexus paid for by ratepayers,” they said. “… We understand the councillors appeared supportive of that mayor from her crash in 2022 until the end of her paid term in 2024.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Next year’: Leigh Sales shoots her shot on Josh Frydenberg’s political plans
World.content:
NationalCBD Opinion ‘Next year’: Leigh Sales shoots her shot on Josh Frydenberg’s political plans John Buckley CBD columnist Updated October 14, 2026 — 11:30am , first published October 14, 2026 — 5:00am

Updated October 14, 2026 — 11:30am ,first published October 14, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Leigh Sales wasn’t the first person to ask former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg about whether Australian voters can expect him to throw his hat in at the next federal election, in the lead up to the publication of his new book. And the ABC stalwart is unlikely to be the last. In the auditorium of the NSW State Library on Tuesday evening, Sales kicked off Frydenberg’s book roadshow in earnest, but kept the question of his political plans in her back pocket for the closing minutes, after walking Frydenberg through the themes of his book in front of an audience of 300 or so people. Josh Frydenberg in discussion with Leigh Sales about his memoir A Grateful Son. Janie Barrett On the substantive issue, Frydenberg (again) said he hasn’t decided on a feverishly speculated upon return to federal politics. The former deputy Liberal Party leader said the prospect has been the subject of chat around “the kitchen cabinet” at home, and, as things stand, the view is split. “And they’re split around our kitchen cabinet because they know that if you go back into politics, you’re not going back at 50 per cent or 90 per cent because you won’t succeed. You’re going in at 110 per cent, and it’s a bloody hard life, traipsing up to Canberra for weeks on end, or if you’re holding a senior position, travelling around the country,” Frydenberg said.



“But it’s all part and parcel of what is required to succeed in politics, and so we’ll take that decision next year, bearing in mind that the election is 18 months away.” Frydenberg played coy on a political comeback when probed by Sales. Janie Barrett The former treasurer also offered up some thoughts on the upcoming Victorian election, and how he expects One Nation to fare. The party is stronger federally – and in NSW – than it is in Victoria, he supposed. But he still expects the right-wingers to pick up seats when Victorians head to the polls later this year. Frydenberg’s appearance alongside Sales marked the first public event scheduled around the Tuesday release of his new book, A Grateful Son, published by News Corp’s HarperCollins. Earlier that day, the former treasurer was joined by former prime minister John Howard at the publisher’s Sydney offices for a private get-together to toast the release. Howard gave a 20-minute speech, according to The Australian, and said those expecting Frydenberg to declare his political intentions “crazy”. Among those photographed at the get-together were Seven Group Holdings chief Ryan Stokes and wife Claire, along with Justice Michael Lee and former Reserve Bank governor Philip Lowe. Sadly, though, we’re told there was no space in the room for us! Either that or News Corp wanted to keep it in the family.



Wells’ skirmish Anika Wells′ senior staffers will advise the communications minister to have a good dinner on Wednesday night – preferably a steak, we’re told – before having an early night. After all, Thursday will be a big one. Wells would be the highest-profile absentee from a TikTok event scheduled at Canberra’s Kingston Hotel on Wednesday evening – assuming she was invited – for what appears to be the first public lobbying effort by TikTok to oppose Labor’s controversial Digital Duty of Care bill. Communications Minister Anika Wells. Alex Ellinghausen TikTok, which raked in $883.7 million in revenue from Australia in 2025 while offshoring $458 million to the Cayman Islands, has roped in former ABC presenter Jan Fran for hosting duties. The platform will also wheel out a gaggle of creators – Elle Ray and Dr Karl among them – for the sales pitch. (Here’s hoping the appearance fees were generous.)



Still, our guess is Wells won’t be sad to miss it. On Thursday, the minister will address the National Press Club to peddle Labor’s Digital Duty of Care bill, which Labor is expected to introduce that day. It introduces new obligations for social media platforms – including Instagram and TikTok – to take steps to screen out harmful content. The framework would also legislate an option for Australians to opt out of social media algorithms. As things stand, the framework doesn’t have many friends in the capital and has set off a political and lobbying whirlwind that doesn’t show any sign of letting up. Related Article Harassment Greens push to let Australians sue Big Tech in digital safety overhaul The Coalition and One Nation have branded the proposal a form of censorship. The Greens want to get a provision into the bill that would allow Australians to sue tech companies for compensation if they are harmed online. And it’s safe to say the platforms aren’t pleased, either. Wells will need to get one of the Coalition or the Greens on board to push the bill through the Senate. The minister’s office has briefed Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young on the proposal, we’re told. Coalition Senator Sarah Henderson also got a rundown from both the minister’s office and the office of the eSafety Commissioner.



Word is the government has already backed down on a controversial provision that would give the minister extraordinary powers to determine what constitutes “serious harm” on the internet. But our guess is that provision won’t be the only change once negotiations are through. Campion’s spin Vikki Campion is back. The former Coalition staffer, who is married to One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, has taken up a new gig helping out One Nation as a media adviser, starting this week. Word of Campion’s new role reached us after she was listed as the media contact for the party’s NSW leader Mike Newman on Monday, sparking intrigue on Macquarie Street over who she was working for and what it would mean for her weekly column at the Daily Telegraph. In answer to our questions, Campion said she’d be working for the One Nation NSW executive, led by president Rebecca Thompson, as a contractor. She’s previously done similar work as a contractor for the Nationals, she told us.



But the publication of an “exclusive” story on her new role in the Tele on Tuesday afternoon raised our eyebrows. It went live just hours after we asked Campion our questions. Fortuitous timing, no doubt. PM holds court The appearance of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson on the program of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s (ACCI) business leaders’ summit on Tuesday was most intriguing. But if that wasn’t enough, the senator was also one of the highest profile names on the guest list for the gala dinner that would follow, where Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was billed as the guest of honour, with a string of government ministers in tow. The summit brings together the heads of the nation’s various business lobbies and promises them a night to rub shoulders with the nation’s elected officials. The gala, as you’d expect, follows a similar blueprint.



Given Monday’s welcome drinks were sponsored by Amazon, we weren’t surprised to see the $US2.8 trillion ($4 trillion) tech giant well represented on the guest list for the Tuesday night get-together. Among them was the company’s global affairs and legal officer, David Zapolsky, along with the firm’s Australian country manager and director Matt Benham, and the company’s local public policy boss Matt Levey. Business lobbyists including Minerals Council of Australia chief executive Tania Constable were promised decent company. Chinese ambassador Liu Jinsong was among dignitaries set to sit down for dinner. Then there were bureaucrats, including Treasury Secretary Jenny Wilkinson, who was set to be joined by Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade Secretary Jan Adams and Department of Industry, Science and Resources Secretary Simon Draper. The parliamentary contingent also filled out the guest list. Teal MP Allegra Spender was set to go along, as was Environment Minister Murray Watt and Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume. Assistant Science Minister Andrew Charlton, who was on the summit program, was also on the list, as was Industry Minister Tim Ayres.
