World.title: Australia barbecued South Africa in Durban. This team’s sunset may be glorious
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Australia barbecued South Africa in Durban. This team’s sunset may be glorious Daniel Brettig Updated October 14, 2026 — 11:27am ,first published October 14, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Durban: As smoke from a post-match braai wafted over Kingsmead, Australia’s Test team could be heard singing and carousing in celebration of a 214-run mauling of South Africa. The team chant, Under the Southern Cross, was belted out twice in the dressing room (“second verse, same as the first”), about three hours after Josh Hazlewood claimed the final wicket. They had truly barbecued South Africa, the kind of performance that, by its sheer dominance, should be cause for a reappraisal of Pat Cummins’ team. Josh Hazlewood stood out with six wickets in South Africa’s second innings. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Following last summer’s Ashes defeat of England, and fuelled by a spotty 1-1 home draw with Bangladesh, there has been much written and said lately about how this ageing team has to be one in decline. That narrative has been strengthened by the lack of runs emanating from domestic ranks, culminating in the decision to recall 34-year-old Nic Maddinson for this series instead of flying over any number of young players who had been playing for Australia A in India.



In South Africa, too, there had been a degree of confidence that, having knocked off the Australians in the World Test Championship final at Lord’s last year, the Proteas were well-placed to repeat the dose on home soil, perhaps helped by the memories of the infamous 2018 series, sandpapergate and all that came with it. Commentator Neil Manthorp went as far as to suggest this was the first time in his career that South Africa entered a series against Australia as favourites. When Australia chose to bat first, as Cummins had done in the Darwin loss against Bangladesh, and found themselves 6-124 on the first afternoon, it appeared that all these suspicions of a cricket empire at sunset were not without foundation. Editor's pick Australian cricket Renshaw had the game of his life at five. Cummins says he could open next Test But what followed was strong evidence that, in fact, this team of “creaking terminators”, to borrow Rahul Dravid’s phrase, has the capacity not just to maintain their rage, but improve on the performances of the past five years. It started, of course, with new blood, Matt Renshaw. Always a gifted player who fell afoul of some harsh character assessments as a younger man, Renshaw showed with patience, technique and presence of mind that Australia do have the option of batting in a less hectic manner than has occasionally been the case in recent times.



His attentiveness to lower order batting partners in Cummins, Nathan Lyon and Hazlewood was notable, keeping them calm and focused as the likelihood of a mediocre first innings was turned into 390 – the sort of tally from which victory could be built. Loading “Renners’ method was one to wait for his balls,” Cummins said. “There’s plenty of time in a Test match, so you don’t need to overplay it. Particularly in these kind of conditions ... he laid a pretty good blueprint. Someone like a Travis Head might be more aggressive, but for other guys there is a path forward where going and grinding it out might be the best thing for the team.” To hear Cummins speak of a blueprint was significant because he wants the likes of Marnus Labuschagne and the recovering Cameron Green to find a consistent method. If they can, Australia will be able to make enough runs to bring their magnificent bowling attack into game scenarios where, as the Proteas discovered, there is no escape. Cummins spoke of ruthlessness. Matt Renshaw celebrates with teammates after taking a wicket on day four of the Test. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe



“Even sometimes where we have got that far in front, I feel like we haven’t been as ruthless as we could,” he said. “You just need to sometimes grind it out, wait for the game to come to you, and we’ve just missed those moments in the past. So that’s kind of, as a group, we look at the next evolution. That’s something we spoke about.” Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Lyon all had their moments with the ball in this match, notably in how fast the skipper bowled now that he is free of back trouble and also clear of ankle and hamstring niggles that had compelled him to bowl within himself at times in previous years. But centre stage was taken firmly by Hazlewood, who plucked eight quality wickets for the Test, with career-best figures of 6-49 as victory was secured less than halfway through the final day in Durban. Like Cummins, Hazlewood looked quicker than he had been in some time, and his combination of height, accuracy and canny manipulation of the seam were at times irresistible. Editor's pick Australian cricket Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball For evidence of that, just ask Marco Jansen, who offered what looked like a correct forward stroke, only to hear his bails trimmed with the second new ball. Two balls later, Simon Harmer received a brute of a lifter that grazed the top of his glove, having arrived far quicker and steeper than the batsman’s estimate. Even the most ardent fan of Scott Boland must acknowledge a haul of 67 wickets at 14.83 since January 2024.



“He obviously gets spoken about a lot about his consistency, but I think that undersells him,” Cummins said. “He’s really skillful with the new ball. But once you get a reversing ball he’s just as skillful, can swing it both ways. “One thing I’ve always loved about Joshy and Starcy is they’re just so happy getting into the grind. They’ll never shy away from having a bowl. It’s not always the case with Test players, whereas they, just whatever the team needs, they roll up their sleeves and go to work. A captain’s dream.” Before this game, it had been the role of Matthew Hayden to launch a strident critique of Cummins and the selectors, for “promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we’ve seen in a generation of cricket”. Hayden was once part of an ageing team that, reinforced by a few more senior players like Mike Hussey and Stuart Clark, went on a sunset tear from 2005 to 2007. On the evidence of Durban, Cummins and company are capable of something similar. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: Greens claim Labor’s tax bill contains private school fee loophole
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Greens claim Labor’s tax bill contains private school fee loophole Brittany Busch October 14, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Greens are demanding the government hike taxes on parents paying for private school fees through trusts, arguing there is a loophole in the budget reforms. Labor needs the support of the Greens in the Senate to pass the tax on trusts, with the Coalition staunchly opposed to any tax hikes. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has already been forced to walk back a number of measures in the May budget after unforseen consequences copped backlash. Greens economics spokesperson Nick McKim says his party has serious concerns. Alex Ellinghausen But the Greens are concerned the government has gone too far in the carveouts, and will kick the bill to a Senate inquiry after Chalmers introduced the legislation to parliament on Wednesday. The minor party wants to interrogate an exemption to the proposed 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, which would exclude money paid to charities.



While the bill does not name which entities will be exempt, some private schools hold charitable status, potentially excluding disbursements to them through trusts from the 30 per cent tax. Related Article Trusts Small business trusts get stamp duty escape hatch in Chalmers’ latest tax tweak Greens economic spokesman Nick McKim said the party had serious concerns about the exemption. “It seems as if it will be possible for people with trusts to pay private school fees or donations to private schools, and not be subject to the 30 per cent minimum tax,” the senator said. “People with trusts, in general terms, are quite well-off, and we don’t think they should get a benefit that is not available to people who don’t have trusts – because money that goes into trusts is tax-free, but people who don’t have a trust are paying income tax.



“You need to be wealthy enough to afford a fancy accountant, or at least some accounting advice, which is not available to everyone.” McKim would not say whether the change was a red line for the party, but said it would consider the evidence in the inquiry. “Once we’ve been through that process, we’re happy to sit down with the government and have a conversation.” Loading The government is not expected to move on the Greens demands, given the arrangement has always been a feature of trusts.



But it poses a challenge to the government, which needs Greens’ support to pass the reforms. Related Article Updated

Federal budget Widows and divorcees protected as Labor reveals details of tax backdown Chalmers touted the changes in the House of Representatives on Wednesday morning, saying the trust reforms were the latest tranche in Labor’s budget which was about making the tax system fairer and more sustainable. “We know there are legitimate reasons to use trusts, including succession planning and asset protection,” Chalmers said. “But the flexibility provided by discretionary trusts allows some people to plan their tax affairs in ways that aren’t available to most workers and families.”



Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson was scathing of the bill and demanded an inquiry, accusing Labor MPs of failing to understand how small businesses that rely on trusts to structure their tax affairs work. “Do not misunderstand the scale of the train wreck that is about to come. You have a problem at the moment with the legislation in front of you, where if people move structures, once they move structures, it automatically ... triggers a stamp duty obligation. “The members on the other side of this chamber did not have the courage to send this legislation to an election and that is the point of why we need this inquiry.” More to come. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Trump’s America and Wall Street are in a dangerous spiral
World.content:
BusinessMarketsBonds Opinion Trump’s America and Wall Street are in a dangerous spiral Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 14, 2026 — 12:00pm

October 14, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What would it look like if demand for government and corporate debt rose rapidly even as its cost surged? We’re seeing that play out in real time. The coincidence of record levels of government debt and government debt issuance with the biggest investment boom in history is having an increasingly visible impact on debt markets, one exacerbated by stubbornly-high inflation rates and heightened geopolitical risks. US debt levels have skyrocketed since Donald Trump returned to the White House. AP The world’s biggest debt markets are in the US, where there’s the $US32 trillion ($46 trillion) Treasuries market for government debt, a $US12 trillion-plus market for corporate debt and another $US2 trillion or so market for private credit. The spreads between the yields on US government and investment grade corporate debt have risen slightly recently, but remain relatively tight. Those on lesser-rated debt have been blowing out, with CCC and even lower rated bonds trading at double-digit percentage point margins over Treasuries.



That’s happening in an environment where the yields on government debt have been rising so, for all but the higher-rated issuers, there’s the double-whammy of increased spreads against rising benchmarks. Related Article Opinion

AI The world’s richest person is testing Wall Street’s limits The yields on the US and global benchmark bonds – US 10-year Treasuries – were at their lowest point for the year in late February, just before the US and Israel attacked Iran. From 3.94 per cent then the yield has climbed to 4.82 per cent. The move in the yields on two-year bonds has been even more pronounced, from 3.38 per cent on the eve of the war to 4.82 per cent now. The war, inflation and the expectation that the Federal Reserve Board will continue to raise US rates are part of the explanation for the rise. The other, perhaps more significant is the expansion in deficits and debt since Donald Trump regained the White House.



The deficit is now almost $US2 trillion, or 6 per cent of US GDP, and gross debt is more than $US40 trillion, or about $US4 trillion more than Trump inherited a little more than 18 months ago. Not only has the perceived riskiness of the debt increased, but there’s more debt to be absorbed, even as sovereign buyers of US debt have been backing away from the market – the share of the market has fallen steadily and substantially, led by China, since the 2008 financial crisis – and been replaced by hedge funds and other private sources. The most likely breaking point for the markets would be a moment of disappointment or doubt over the rate or potential of AI to be commercialised and ultimately generate profits commensurate with the risks being accepted by the capital providers. AP The US will roll over about $US10 trillion of maturing debt this year and, thanks to the deficit, add about $US2 trillion of new issuance. That’s a lot of supply for the market to absorb. The increased yields on Treasuries have spilt over into the cost of corporate and private debt, even mortgages, where interest rates have been rising and are now in the mid-7 per cent range, roughly a percentage point higher than at the same time last year.



The supply of corporate debt has also been swelling. So far this year more than $US2 trillion of new corporate bonds have been issued, an increase of about 25 per cent on the same period last year. Increasingly, that issuance is being dominated by companies associated with the artificial intelligence investment boom. Related Article Opinion

Global economy The four horsemen of the apocalypse are coming for the global economy Between them, SpaceX, Broadcom and Oracle alone are currently in the market for more than $US150 billion of new debt. Already this year, AI companies have raised closed to half a trillion dollars of new debt. Elon Musk’s SpaceX’s experience reflects the broader story. It raised $US86 billion of equity via its initial public offering in June and then immediately raised another $US25 billion through a bond issue. It’s now seeking a further $US40 billion. That tells you something about the rate of cash burn being experienced by the AI pioneers, and the inability of equity markets to keep up with the demand for the capital being burnt. As a group, AI hyperscalers will invest around $US750 billion this year, with expectations of another trillion dollars in each of the next two years.



Debt providers want collateral or pricing of the debt that reflects the riskiness of the borrower. SpaceX’s initial bond issue attracted an investment grade rating, albeit the second-lowest BBB grade. The longest dated of those bonds – they mature in 2056 – now trades at a spread of about 240 basis points over Treasuries, or about 85 per cent of their face value. The cost of insuring that debt against default has also blown out, with credit default swaps costing 194 basis points, or $US19,400 a year for every $US1 million of debt held. Between them, SpaceX, Broadcom and Oracle alone are currently in the market for more than $US150 billion of new debt. Bloomberg Oracle, the most leveraged of the hyperscalers, also has bonds trading with spreads well over 200 basis points and the cost of its five-year credit default swap has rocketed to more than 260 basis points, or $US26,000 per $1 million.



AI has an insatiable appetite for capital. Even the corporate bond market is being stretched to supply it. The companies have also been tapping fellow AI companies, private credit and constructing quite elaborate structures to attract capital providers. A common feature of the sector is for one of the big chipmakers, like Nvidia or Broadcom, to lend the funds to frontier labs to buy their chips, with contracts whose lives probably outstrip the useful life of the chips in question. It is also common for the hyperscalers to structure joint ventures within special purpose vehicles with private credit providers to raise the funding needed to construct data centres and equip them with the expensive chips and hardware required, leasing back the data centre’s capacity. There’s a lot of leverage within AI beyond conventional debt, with collateral that may prove illusory if AI revenues don’t eventually – and sooner rather than later – start to rationalise the scale of the investments being made. Similar threats of government and AI-related debt supply overwhelming demand are current globally, although the US is the epicentre for any potential flashpoint.



The most likely breaking point for the markets – and AI and those pursuing it – would be a moment of disappointment or doubt over the rate or potential of AI to be commercialised and ultimately generate profits commensurate with the risks being accepted by the capital providers. There’s also a concern that, having shown no interest in stabilising federal government finances, the Trump administration will look for painless ways to manage the debt levels. “Debasement,” or allowing inflation and manipulation of the Fed’s policy rate to keep rates artificially low, is often cited as a risk. Related Article Opinion

Inflation Don’t blame Ukraine: Prices go up and up, thanks to Trump’s wars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist If there is to be crisis in debt markets it is likely to start in the US and probably start within the AI sector. The sector relies on access to ever-increasing volumes of equity and debt to fund investments that have to be made long before there is even a prospect of the high risk-adjusted returns that those providing the capital anticipate.



Whether it is the escalating cost of the debt, or its availability from the increasingly risk-aware capital providers, or some external event that shakes the debt markets, the AI sector and those funding it are extremely vulnerable to the slightest of adverse developments. World.title: SBS debate ‘brings together’ childfree advocates and anti-abortion campaigners
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV SBS debate ‘brings together’ childfree advocates and anti-abortion campaigners Bridget McManus October 14, 2026 — 11:54am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What do three childfree advocates and three conservative commentators have in common? Not a lot. But this is why you’ll find them taking part in a debate on SBS’s youth-focused current affairs program, The Feed. The six participants will thrash out an urgent question in light of Australia’s plummeting birth rate: “Why are more people choosing a childfree life, and should having kids still be a priority?” According to the debate’s producer and moderator, journalist Elfy Scott, “there were surprising moments of agreement from both sides of the panel.” Surprising indeed, given the profiles of the speakers. Elfy Scott hosts The Feed Debate: Having Kids. SBS Promoting the childfree lifestyle are model and actor Ellie Gonsalves, who in 2023 went viral for posting 118 reasons why she doesn’t want kids; comedian and One Nation critic, Andrew Lewis; and Dita, a nurse and content creator who posts about racism and family violence. On the opposing side are single mother and anti-abortion activist Elspeth McKellar, who creates confrontational content for Joanna Howe’s organisation Bird Flip; George Mamalis, South Australian head of the late Charlie Kirk’s right-wing advocacy group Turning Point USA, who has advocated against abortion and called feminism a “death cult”; and Stephanie Bastiaan, a mother of six and head of advocacy at Women’s Forum, an organisation critical of pro-trans activism.



Elspeth McKellar, George Mamalis and Stephanie Bastiaan on The Feed Debate: Having Kids. SBS “We want to bring people together outside of those polarising algorithms, and give them the space to speak openly, but then also ensure that they’re fact-checked in that context,” says Scott. “We think it is important to be able to facilitate these conversations, even if they are challenging, and to draw people out of things that they see online, and ensure that we can give perspectives across a broad range.” Related Article Australian TV Why Marc Fennell threw himself into the ‘deep end’ of the manosphere Scott has sat in the moderator’s chair for many a passionate discussion at literary festivals. She is no stranger to provocative subject matter, having authored The One Thing We’ve Never Spoken About, exploring the stigma around mental illness, inspired by her mother’s experience living with schizophrenia. She’s also presented ABC documentaries investigating everything from psychic mediums and UFO sightings to conspiracy theories. But moderating this potentially explosive forum required “keeping everybody on track as far as the topic is concerned, and keeping the debate respectful and civil … It’s such a significant conversation right now. And we need to hear from the young people making these decisions.”



Andrew Lewis, Ellie Gonsalves and Dita on The Feed Debate: Having Kids. SBS Aimed at the 16-39 demographic, the semiannual Feed debates put millennials in charge of the agenda. Other episodes have had influencers from the left and right debating politics, socialists and property investors debating whether capitalism is expiring, and an array of prominent voices from the online sphere debating masculinity. “This is a key moment in history where we are seeing the fertility rate decline to a level we’ve never seen before,” says Scott. “We are facing unique issues – economic issues, political issues, global stability issues and climate issues. So there’s a lot for people to consider that previous generations have not had to.” Scott won’t be drawn on her personal position, adding “I am still internally debating.” But she says it is a question that is frequently raised in her social circles.



“I feel like I have had a million conversations with friends and family about it. It’s the conversation we’re all having at family barbecues. For myself, as a woman in her early 30s, it is absolutely a decision that is relevant to me, and one that I enjoy hearing every perspective on … When we’re talking about issues related to AI and climate, which do come up in the debate, those are inherently political topics. I think people are becoming more apprehensive about parenthood because of things like that.” Related Article Parenting The people who say no to being a parent, and have very happy lives She hopes the debate starts conversations among viewers of all generations. “This topic is so exposed in the media at the moment, but very, very rarely are we actually hearing from the young people themselves … And I would love for older audiences to have that exposure to people from younger generations, and the range of factors that are going into this decision. “It’s not a simple choice. And that’s what a lot of young people are feeling right now – this push and pull, regarding whether or not to become a parent.”

World.title: Block on NSW gold mine rejected by federal court
World.content:
PoliticsNSWNSW State Parliament Block on NSW gold mine rejected by federal court Jessica McSweeney October 14, 2026 — 11:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. NSW Premier Chris Minns has emerged victorious in a stoush over a controversial Central West gold mine after the Federal Court threw out a ban made by then-environment minister Tanya Plibersek, who stalled the mine on Indigenous heritage grounds. Federal Court Justice James Stellion on Wednesday decided to send the $1.3 billion mine proposal back to the current minister Murray Watt, determining Plibersek’s original decision lacked procedural fairness. The proposed McPhillamys gold mine would process as much as 8.5 million tonnes of ore a year. Nick Moir The decision did not make any judgment about the merits of any claims of Indigenous heritage in the area, but found Plibersek’s decision-making was flawed. That declaration prevented Regis Resources from building a tailings dam to store byproducts from mining operations at the headwaters of the Belubula River, after an Indigenous group argued the area was significant to a Dreaming story about the blue banded bee. The mining company argued that made the project unfeasible.



The declaration also triggered unrest between the state and federal governments, with the Premier Chris Minns insisting the mine must go ahead. The state government had originally approved the project. “I want that mine to go ahead, I understand that that’s not the view of the federal government, but we need the investment,” Minns said before the judgment on Wednesday. “There are more people in mining jobs in NSW today than there were when we were elected in March of 2023. We’re proud of that.” When asked if the then-environment minister had made the wrong call when she made the order blocking the mine, Minns replied: “Yes”. Plibersek’s statement of reasons for the declaration said she “could not be assured that the NSW legislative framework as it currently stands can adequately protect the specified area”.



After making the declaration, Plibersek rejected suggestions from Regis Resources that the ban killed the project, insisting the mine could still go ahead if the dam was moved. The company said finding a new site for approval would take up to 10 years, but the state government flagged it would fast-track the project. The application to protect the dam area was made by Wiradjuri-Gamillaroi woman Nyree Reynolds on behalf of the Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation. Minns told a budget estimates hearing in 2024 that the local Aboriginal Land Council had been consulted as part of the original approval process. More to come.

World.title: Trump’s ambassador to Greece resigns after allegations of improper conduct
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump’s ambassador to Greece resigns after allegations of improper conduct Matthew Lee Updated October 14, 2026 — 11:47am ,first published October 14, 2026 — 3:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

US President Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday (US time) after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she will “vigorously defend” herself. Trump’s administration said earlier on Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks as US President Donald Trump listens at the White House in March 2025. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once married to California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr. The announcement, after days of comments and speculation, came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing on Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle “has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well”.



Guilfoyle’s departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. “Well, we’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he was considering firing Guilfoyle. “We’re not happy.” White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Tuesday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior US official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on her future this week. In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.



Guilfoyle addressed the allegations directly in a post on X, saying, “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.” “I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.” View post on X In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle’s lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services – public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination – that had not been paid. The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations”.



After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” But after another report appeared later, Rubio – speaking on Thursday before leaving Athens – berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them. Related Article Trump's White House Trump picks Fox News expert for next White House press secretary “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. A second US official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general (IG) was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.



The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. “This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament on Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House ‘My president ... excuse me, my husband’: Trump’s new spinner gets off to a rocky start Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens, as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law. The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Representative Robert Garcia, Democrat for California, have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.



Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the US could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported – citing text messages – that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $US100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. Related Article Updated

US politics Federal agents raid home of Democratic congresswoman targeted by Trump The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives. Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the US Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behaviour appropriate for the top representative of the US government to Greece.

World.title: Mayor on edge of being kicked off council after sick-leave vote
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland councils Mayor on edge of being kicked off council after sick-leave vote Julius Dennis October 14, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A south-east Queensland mayor is on the brink of being forced out of office after her extended sick leave was rejected by councillors. Redlands mayor Jos Mitchell has been on medical leave since May, with councillors at monthly meetings voting to either accept or reject her continued absence. The leave had initially been accepted until it was voted against by most councillors at the September meeting. Jos Mitchell has been on medical leave since May. Julius Dennis Under Queensland law, a councillor’s or mayor’s seat is vacated once they miss two or more consecutive general meetings over a two-month period.



While Mitchell has missed two meetings, she cannot lose her seat until the next meeting, according to the Department of Local Government. Should she be forced from her position, Mitchell would be the first mayor in Queensland to be ousted in such a manner. Elected in 2024, Mitchell entered a deeply divided council following the exit of long-term mayor Karen Williams two years after she made headlines for crashing her council-owned car while drunk. Mitchell has been outspoken about the council’s culture, and has made headlines for being the subject of more than 50 conduct complaints, which she has claimed were politically motivated. In August, the council’s bureaucratic arm took a swing at the mayor in a submission to a state parliamentary inquiry into councillor conduct, suggesting any councillor on extended leave should be subject to an investigation.



In May, Mitchell said she would be on medical leave for six weeks. The mayor had been taken to hospital earlier in the year after collapsing at work. Redlands led the state in OIA complaints last year. Matt Dennien “On medical advice, I have made the decision to step aside from my role as mayor for a period of six weeks to appropriately address a health issue,” she said at the time. “This is a decision I have not taken lightly, nor with any pleasure. It is, though, a necessary decision if I am to continue in this role and perform at my best.”



At Wednesday’s meeting, deputy mayor Julie Talty, who has led the meetings in Mitchell’s absence, said councillors had received a note in July asking for continued leave from meetings through October 31. Related Article Queensland councils ‘Avoiding accountability’: Council takes aim at mayor on medical leave Before the vote, councillor Jason Colley asked chief executive Louise Rusan whether the council had received a request from Mitchell to take leave without pay, which she said they hadn’t. Councillors Wendy Boglary, Lance Hewlett, Tracy Hughes and Paul Bishop voted to accept the leave, while councillors Rowanne McKenzie, Shane Rendalls, Paul Gollé, Colley and Talty voted against. A spokesperson for the mayor said the vote was disappointing.



“Many workplaces send ‘get well’ messages when people are away unwell,” they said. “Mayor Jos Mitchell has received criticism and imputations.” They drew a line between the support shown for Williams after she was charged with drink-driving and the apparent animosity towards Mitchell. “Most of the councillors voting against Mayor Mitchell’s application for leave of absence with a medical certificate were present when the former mayor drank, drove and crashed the Lexus paid for by ratepayers,” they said. “… We understand the councillors appeared supportive of that mayor from her crash in 2022 until the end of her paid term in 2024.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Australia barbecued South Africa in Durban. This team’s sunset may be glorious
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Australia barbecued South Africa in Durban. This team’s sunset may be glorious Daniel Brettig Updated October 14, 2026 — 11:27am ,first published October 14, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Durban: As smoke from a post-match braai wafted over Kingsmead, Australia’s Test team could be heard singing and carousing in celebration of a 214-run mauling of South Africa. The team chant, Under the Southern Cross, was belted out twice in the dressing room (“second verse, same as the first”), about three hours after Josh Hazlewood claimed the final wicket. They had truly barbecued South Africa, the kind of performance that, by its sheer dominance, should be cause for a reappraisal of Pat Cummins’ team. Josh Hazlewood stood out with six wickets in South Africa’s second innings. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Following last summer’s Ashes defeat of England, and fuelled by a spotty 1-1 home draw with Bangladesh, there has been much written and said lately about how this ageing team has to be one in decline. That narrative has been strengthened by the lack of runs emanating from domestic ranks, culminating in the decision to recall 34-year-old Nic Maddinson for this series instead of flying over any number of young players who had been playing for Australia A in India.



In South Africa, too, there had been a degree of confidence that, having knocked off the Australians in the World Test Championship final at Lord’s last year, the Proteas were well-placed to repeat the dose on home soil, perhaps helped by the memories of the infamous 2018 series, sandpapergate and all that came with it. Commentator Neil Manthorp went as far as to suggest this was the first time in his career that South Africa entered a series against Australia as favourites. When Australia chose to bat first, as Cummins had done in the Darwin loss against Bangladesh, and found themselves 6-124 on the first afternoon, it appeared that all these suspicions of a cricket empire at sunset were not without foundation. Editor's pick Australian cricket Renshaw had the game of his life at five. Cummins says he could open next Test But what followed was strong evidence that, in fact, this team of “creaking terminators”, to borrow Rahul Dravid’s phrase, has the capacity not just to maintain their rage, but improve on the performances of the past five years. It started, of course, with new blood, Matt Renshaw. Always a gifted player who fell afoul of some harsh character assessments as a younger man, Renshaw showed with patience, technique and presence of mind that Australia do have the option of batting in a less hectic manner than has occasionally been the case in recent times.



His attentiveness to lower order batting partners in Cummins, Nathan Lyon and Hazlewood was notable, keeping them calm and focused as the likelihood of a mediocre first innings was turned into 390 – the sort of tally from which victory could be built. Loading “Renners’ method was one to wait for his balls,” Cummins said. “There’s plenty of time in a Test match, so you don’t need to overplay it. Particularly in these kind of conditions ... he laid a pretty good blueprint. Someone like a Travis Head might be more aggressive, but for other guys there is a path forward where going and grinding it out might be the best thing for the team.” To hear Cummins speak of a blueprint was significant because he wants the likes of Marnus Labuschagne and the recovering Cameron Green to find a consistent method. If they can, Australia will be able to make enough runs to bring their magnificent bowling attack into game scenarios where, as the Proteas discovered, there is no escape. Cummins spoke of ruthlessness. Matt Renshaw celebrates with teammates after taking a wicket on day four of the Test. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe



“Even sometimes where we have got that far in front, I feel like we haven’t been as ruthless as we could,” he said. “You just need to sometimes grind it out, wait for the game to come to you, and we’ve just missed those moments in the past. So that’s kind of, as a group, we look at the next evolution. That’s something we spoke about.” Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Lyon all had their moments with the ball in this match, notably in how fast the skipper bowled now that he is free of back trouble and also clear of ankle and hamstring niggles that had compelled him to bowl within himself at times in previous years. But centre stage was taken firmly by Hazlewood, who plucked eight quality wickets for the Test, with career-best figures of 6-49 as victory was secured less than halfway through the final day in Durban. Like Cummins, Hazlewood looked quicker than he had been in some time, and his combination of height, accuracy and canny manipulation of the seam were at times irresistible. Editor's pick Australian cricket Australia player ratings: The perfect 10 who shone with bat and ball For evidence of that, just ask Marco Jansen, who offered what looked like a correct forward stroke, only to hear his bails trimmed with the second new ball. Two balls later, Simon Harmer received a brute of a lifter that grazed the top of his glove, having arrived far quicker and steeper than the batsman’s estimate. Even the most ardent fan of Scott Boland must acknowledge a haul of 67 wickets at 14.83 since January 2024.



“He obviously gets spoken about a lot about his consistency, but I think that undersells him,” Cummins said. “He’s really skillful with the new ball. But once you get a reversing ball he’s just as skillful, can swing it both ways. “One thing I’ve always loved about Joshy and Starcy is they’re just so happy getting into the grind. They’ll never shy away from having a bowl. It’s not always the case with Test players, whereas they, just whatever the team needs, they roll up their sleeves and go to work. A captain’s dream.” Before this game, it had been the role of Matthew Hayden to launch a strident critique of Cummins and the selectors, for “promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we’ve seen in a generation of cricket”. Hayden was once part of an ageing team that, reinforced by a few more senior players like Mike Hussey and Stuart Clark, went on a sunset tear from 2005 to 2007. On the evidence of Durban, Cummins and company are capable of something similar. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: New York’s famous Central Park horse-drawn carriages set to be banned
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAnimal rights New York’s famous Central Park horse-drawn carriages set to be banned Laura Nahmias and Samuel A. Church October 14, 2026 — 11:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

New York City: Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the New York City Council speaker reached a deal on legislation to ban horse-drawn carriages, potentially putting an end to a Central Park staple and tourist magnet that began operating more than 150 years ago. The legislation is set for a vote on October 22 and, if passed, the ban would take effect June 1, 2028. It would require “humane disposition” of the animals, forbidding the horses’ sale for slaughter or transfer to other carriage companies. A horse and carriage in New York’s Central Park. Bloomberg Sixty-eight horse cabs currently operate in Central Park, employing roughly 150 drivers and more than 180 horses, according to industry spokesperson Christina Hansen. The new legislation lists 29 sponsors in the City Council, which is enough support for the measure to pass the 51-member body. The agreement was confirmed by council speaker Julie Menin’s office.



Horse-drawn carriages in the city have long-faced opposition from animal rights activists who argue that forcing the animals to work in urban conditions undermines their long-term health and is unsafe. While on the campaign trail in 2013, former Mayor Bill de Blasio promised to shut down the industry on his first day in office, though he ultimately failed after his plan did not secure support from City Council. But after a recent carriage-related death, concerns over the industry proved impossible to ignore. On June 17, 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan fell off a runaway carriage and died while on a family trip to the city. His death prompted carriage services to shut down for six days while drivers reviewed safety protocols. Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York. Bloomberg A poll from the Central Park Conservancy, which advocated for the ban, found that 68 per cent of New Yorkers supported prohibiting the carriages after Mahajan’s death. “This is fundamentally about public safety,” said David Saltonstall, the CPC’s vice president for government relations. “It’s about mitigating a known and growing risk that we have watched build for years, which very sadly culminated in the death of Romanch Mahajan.”



Saltonstall cited a growing list of carriage-related incidents. At least seven people – including drivers and tourists – have been injured since May 2025, according to the conservancy. Mahajan’s death is believed to be the first fatality resulting from a carriage accident in Central Park’s history. Carriage operators say the rate of horse-related injuries was still much lower than other permitted park activities, such as riding e-bikes or scooters. They also say that without carriage revenue, they’ll struggle to care for their horses and pay fees to relocate them after the ban goes into effect. Loading The amended bill would require agencies chosen by the mayor to deliver a plan to support carriage drivers, owners and stable workers by April 1, 2027. That support could include financial compensation, but the legislation requires only that the city consider compensating carriage owners, and does not promise payments. Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen pushed back against the bill in a statement, calling it “political opportunism”. He said it provided “no meaningful economic relief for workers”.



Hansen, the industry spokesperson, said taking care of her horse, Sherman, cost about $US10,000 ($14,000) a year. “There is no pool of money set aside for the future, the next 20 years of Sherman’s life,” she said. The bill also includes what Menin’s office described as stronger protections for horses – barring owners from selling or transferring licensed horses for slaughter or to other carriage businesses. Owners would have to notify the Health Department and the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare at least 10 business days before getting rid of a horse, and anyone caught running a horse-drawn carriage after the ban takes effect could face civil penalties of $US10,000. Animal rights groups say that forcing horses to work in urban conditions is unsafe an undermines their long-term health. Bloomberg “The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable,” Menin said in a statement about the deal. There are about140 carriage horses in the city at any given time, according to Conor McHugh, who manages the Clinton Park Stables, one of the three locations where most of the animals are housed. He has said that if a ban passes, the stable – which has been open for more than 150 years – would be forced to shut down.

World.title: Rugby League World Cup: The star players the Kiwis missed out on
World.content:
New Zealand's international rugby league side has had its fair share of missed opportunities over the past couple of decades and, when it comes to player selection and retention, some of the biggest names in the game have been aligned with the Kiwis - only to ultimately pull on another nation's jersey.

There are signs the tide is beginning to turn, with experienced campaigners Kalyn Ponga and Dane Gagai joining New Zealand's 2026 Rugby League World Cup squad. The path has been made clearer by changes to the eligibility rules that now allow New Zealand internationals to play State of Origin. It could mark the beginning of a new wave of dual-eligible talent choosing to represent the Kiwis.

We take a look at some of the biggest players who have slipped through the Kiwis' hands:

Jarome Luai

Junior Kiwis Junior Kangaroos v Junior Kiwis, international rugby league, New Zealand v Australia, GIO Stadium, Canberra, Australia. 5 May 2017, Copyright Image: Paul Seiser / www.photosport.nz Paul Seiser

Luai was once in talks with the Kiwis camp to represent New Zealand and, in 2017, he did just that; turning out for the Junior Kiwis in a team that was absolutely stacked with future NRL talent.

Eligible through his Māori heritage, the Kiwis could have had themselves a future four-time Premiership-winning player.

But Luai, like many others, opted to play for Samoa with the chance to play for New South Wales in State of Origin.

But with the change to State of Origin eligibility rules, could we one day see Luai pull on the black and white jumper again? Maybe - but probably not.

Nathan Cleary

Nathan Cleary son of Warriors' Head Coach Ivan Cleary cheers on the team. NRL pre season trail match, Vodafone Warriors v Sydney Roosters at Rotorua International Stadium, Rotorua, New Zealand. Saturday 13th February 2010. Photo: PHOTOSPORT Anthony Au-Yeung

The four-time Premiership-winning half and Luai's former teammate has admitted he once considered making himself eligible for New Zealand - before his parents intervened.

Cleary's dad Ivan did play for and coach the Warriors for a good part of his childhood - and he did hold a New Zealand passport.

But his parents sadly talked him out of it - "I felt I was Australian the whole time anyway" - with Cleary opting to play for Australia and of course New South Wales in Origin.

Leka Halasima

Leka Halasima, Tonga Pacific Championship Rugby League Team Field Session at Trusts Arena, Henderson, Auckland, New Zealand on Wednesday 29 October 2025. Photo: Joshua Devenie / Photosport Joshua Devenie

After bursting onto the NRL scene and making a household name for himself, Leka 'The Wrecker' Halasima was hot property when it came to the international rugby league arena with Kiwis coach Stacey Jones reportedly keen for his services.

But despite feeling torn between NZ and Tonga, the second rower/centre opted to play for his country of birth.

When asked by the New Zealand Herald back in 2025, Jones said the Kiwis "had players in our wider [30-man] squad that are in other squads. Players that were born here, or players that have grown up in New Zealand. But at the end of the day, I had to pick the best 21 and I feel like I've done that".

Dallin Watene-Zelezniak

Kiwis captain Dallin Watene-Zelezniak leads the haka, during the rugby league Test match between Kiwis and Tonga in June. Photosport

Former New Zealand captain and Warriors folk hero Dallin 'DWZ' Watene-Zelezniak is the latest in a long list of Kiwi internationals to defect.

Despite having made 13 appearances for New Zealand since 2016, Watene-Zelezniak has opted instead to pull on the red and white of Tonga for the first time ever for the 2026 World Cup.

His great grandfather Puti Tipene 'Steve' Watene was the first ever Māori to captain the Kiwis all the way back in 1936.

Addin Fonua-Blake

Portrait of NZ Kiwis player Addin Fonua-Blake. 2017 Rugby League World Cup. Turangawaewae Marae, Ngaruawahia. New Zealand. Thursday 19 October 2017 © Copyright Photo: Andrew Cornaga / www.Photosport.nz Andrew Cornaga / www.photosport.nz

Former Warriors prop Fonua-Blake would go on to become one of the best players in the game - but an often-forgotten fact is that in 2017 he actually represented the Kiwis at the League World Cup.

In what's becoming a bit of a trend, the Kiwis had the Tongan powerhouse on their books but only ended up using him once during their entire campaign.

After dropping out in the quarter-finals, it seemed Fonua-Blake had seen enough, opting instead to play for Tonga ever since.

Jason Taumalolo

Jason Taumalolo poses for a picture during a New Zealand Kiwis rugby league media session ahead of the team's departure for the Four Nations tournament in the UK. Pullman Hotel. Auckland, New Zealand. Wednesday 19 October 2016 © Copyright Photo: Andrew Cornaga / www.Photosport.nz Andrew Cornaga / www.photosport.nz

Taumalolo's defection to Tonga before the Kiwis World Cup side was named in 2017 was legendary.

He paved the way for some of the game's biggest names to defect from Australia and New Zealand to instead play for their island nations.

The rest was history, as Tonga famously defeated the Kiwis for the first time ever in the opening stages of the World Cup - kicking off the Pasifika rugby league revolution that's still going strong to this day.

Jonathan Thurston

Kangaroos' Johnathan Thurston looks on. Anzac Rugby League test match, New Zealand Kiwis v Australia Kangaroos at Eden Park, Auckland, New Zealand. Friday 20th April 2012. Photo: Anthony Au-Yeung/photosport.co.nz www.photosport.nz

When people hear the name Thurston, they think of Queensland's glory days in State of Origin, the North Queensland Cowboys' premiership run of 2015 and Australia's absolute dominance over the world in the international arena.

Although he was tempted by an offer from the Kiwis in 2004 after NZRL discovered his father was a New Zealander, Thurston opted to bide his time waiting for a call up from Australia that would eventually come in 2006.

After winning multiple World Cups and playing 38 tests, he would retire from the international game one of the all time greats 11 years later in 2017.

James Tamou

James Tamou of the Kangaroos after the game. ANZAC rugby league Test, New Zealand Kiwis v Australia Kangaroos, Eden Park, Auckland, New Zealand, 20 April 2012. Copyright Photo: www.photosport.nz www.photosport.nz

Tamou was quickly snapped up by New South Wales in 2012 amid a whirlwind of controversy as New Zealanders cried foul over the eligibility rules at the time.

Tamou was born in Palmerston North and raised in Levin, having moved to Australia with his family aged 13.

In the end it all boiled down to the NZRL not moving fast enough; Tamou had childhood dreams of playing for the Kiwis, but earlier in the year had been in conversations with then-NSW coach Ricky Stewart, who was telling him he wanted him in his squad and to pledge allegiance to Australia - and he did just that.

The ones we got back: Dane Gagai and Kalyn Ponga

Photosport NZ

Former 2017 World Cup-winning Kangaroo Gagai has changed his international eligibility from Australia to New Zealand.

He had applied to the International Rugby League (IRL) for the eligibility switch, but was initially turned down.

However, the IRL appeals committee overturned that decision, leaving Gagai, 35, available for the Kiwis for their opening World Cup fixture against the Kangaroos in Sydney on 15 October.

Gagai qualifies for New Zealand through mother Tania and has played for the Māori All Stars since 2019, because of his Ngāti Pikiāo heritage.

The IRL also recently permitted Ponga to switch his international allegiances to New Zealand and AJ Brimson to play for England, after both had represented Australia at the 2019 IRL World Cup Nines.

Changes to State of Origin eligibility rules also enabled Kiwi players Briton Nikora, Casey McLean and Addin Fonua-Blake to play in this year's series, despite not being eligible for Australia, as they had previously represented New Zealand.

World.title: New ministry MCERT proposes cutting 400 jobs in restructure
World.content:
The newly formed mega-ministry the Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport (MCERT) has proposed cutting 400 roles.

MCERT met with staff on Wednesday to announce the proposal.

It said 365 of the roles being axed were currently vacant. It has about 1700 staff in total.

The ministry hopes to deliver $50 million in annual savings by 2028-29.

Have you been affected? Get in touch with RNZ at: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

The mega-ministry was created in July, merging the Ministry for the Environment, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, the Ministry of Transport and the local government functions of the Department of Internal Affairs.

Chief executiveJeremy Lightfoot. MCERT / Supplied

MCERT chief executive Jeremy Lightfoot said no decisions had been made, and nothing was final until staff have had their say.

"We will listen carefully to any suggestions they have for doing things differently, before making our final decisions in December."

Wellington Central MP Tamatha Paul told RNZ that the city couldn't handle more public service cuts.

"We just can't afford any more cuts - and I mean that financially, but I also mean it in terms of the morale of the city."

The meeting comes after the Government's announcement in May to slash public service jobs by about 14 percent over the next three years. The changes would result in about 8700 job losses by mid-2029 - 3500 of which could be in the capital.

"We can't have thousands more workers told that their work isn't important."

Paul said the cuts would leave lives up in the air.

Minister responsible Chris Bishop. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Speaking to MCERT workers, Paul said: "You have the chance to elect a government that actually values you... and values your expertise.

"Please do not listen to this anti-public service government because they will be gone in a few weeks."

'Live within our budget'

Lightfoot said most people in the ministry would be affected in some way, and he knew that brought real uncertainty.

"I'm proud of how our people have kept delivering important work for New Zealand while the ministry formed around them. The leadership team and I have tried to give them as much certainty as we can, as early as we can.

He says the ministry must "live within our budget", which means delivering $50 million in annual savings by 2028/29.

"Nothing is final until our people have had their say. Over the next few weeks our focus is on making sure they are treated fairly, are well supported, and have clear information to base their decisions on. We'll listen carefully to their ideas for doing things differently before final decisions are made in early December."

World.title: PNG police seize high-powered weapons cache linked to an international syndicate
World.content:
Papua New Guinea police have seized a cache of high-powered semi-automatic rifles, firearm parts and manufacturing equipment in Port Moresby.

Police commissioner David Manning said the cache is linked to an international firearms trafficking syndicate.

According to Manning, police acted on intelligence shared by international partners, and following covert surveillance conducted by PNG police.

Police investigators and specialist units executed search warrants at a residence in Gerehu last Thursday (8 October).

A 7,62X39mm round sits next a a 30 round magazine and an AK-47 with a bump stock installed. AFP

Items seized include fully assembled semi-automatic rifles, rifle parts sufficient to assemble multiple weapons, magazines, 3D printing technology, accessories used for firearm assembly, and documentary evidence.

"This seizure highlights the serious threat posed by transnational criminal syndicates exploiting Papua New Guinea for the movement of illicit firearms" Manning said.

"These guns fuel violence, undermine community safety, and pose a grave national security risk. The Constabulary will not stop in dismantling these criminal networks and will continue to bring offenders to justice."

Police Commissioner David Manning ( Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary

The commissioner confirmed an adult male was arrested - the man remains in police custody pending charges.

"Investigations confirm that the arrested adult was a key coordinator in relation to the smuggling of firearms into Papua New Guinea, concealing dismantled parts in purportedly legitimate importations and transporting them via international courier services," Manning said.

World.title: Hawke's Bay student missing after high school tramping trip
World.content:
A police search and rescue operation is under way for a high school student missing in the bush in Hawke's Bay.

The student from Taradale High School was one of a group hiking to Sunrise Hut in the Ruahine Forest Park.

An email from the school to parents on Wednesday morning said the teenager was part of an overnight outdoor education trip, and became separated from the group on a hike.

"Taradale High School remains focused on supporting the student's family and school community while police coordinate the search. The students who were participating in the trip are returning to school."

Hawke's Bay Area Commander Inspector Caroline Martin said the teenager was reported missing about 7.10pm on Tuesday.

"Police were made aware a teenager had separated from their group while on a school tramping trip and was missing.

"Police, alongside Land Search and Rescue volunteers, responded immediately and conducted extensive ground searches in the Sunrise Hut area until the early hours," she said.

Martin said the search was continuing today.

"With field teams searching the area and the utilisation of specialist equipment and resources. We remain in contact with the teenager's family and the school, and are providing them with regular updates.

"Police are focused on locating the teenager. While our search is ongoing, police ask the public to avoid the area to ensure our search efforts are not compromised," Martin said..

In its email the school said wellbeing and pastoral support was available for students, staff and whānau. "Our focus remains on supporting the student's family and the wellbeing of our students, staff and school community."

World.title: Poorest could face highest power bill shock in overhaul, Consumer NZ warns
World.content:
Audio player for " Consumer warns of electricity bill shock coming " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/1894412%2Fpoorest-could-face-highest-power-bill-shock-in-overhaul-consumer-nz-warns

Consumer warns of electricity bill shock coming Nine To Noon Download MP3 10m

Consumer says some households and businesses will face large increases to their electricity lines charges from next year, when the low fixed charge scheme is fully phased out.

The looming shift has led to the chair of the Electricity Authority, John Harbord, writing to lines companies about his concern some consumers could see unusually large increases in their bill.

This is because the scheme - which began in 2004 with customers on it paying 30 cents a day - has been phased out over the last five years, and has increased to now be a maximum of $1.80 per day.

From 1 April next year there will be no obligation on lines companies to stick to low fixed charges, and Consumer's head of Powerswitch, Paul Fuge, told Nine to Noon some could move to a charge as high as $4.70 per day.

"About 67 percent of households would qualify for a low user charge, and that's households that consume less than 8000 kilowatt hours of electricity in a year, or 9000 kilowatt hours if you live in the lower South Island... on average, the standard daily fixed charge is $2.70."

Fuge said there would be "winners and losers" from the change.

"Around 40 percent, we believe, will pay more, and that's based on [Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE)] analysis from the midpoint review. And so the households that are most affected in terms of who will pay the most more - lower-income, smaller households, and particularly elderly households will be the worst off. The ones who will probably do better are higher-earning, higher-consuming households who use more electricity."

One of the rationales for the change is to make it fairer for larger families, who would use more electricity than, for example, a single person or couple.

"When they brought in the low-user regulations, the idea was it would help lower-income households. But in reality, it's an inefficient way to target energy hardship. And that's because there's a lot of lower-income households that are actually quite high energy consumers. So it was seen as particularly ineffective.

"The reason that some low-income households can be high consumers is they can have large families. Their housing is generally poorer quality and they can afford less-efficient appliances.

"Conversely, there's some wealthy households who were benefiting from the low-user charges who happen to be low users because of better housing, more efficient appliances, and they may have low occupancy."

Fuge said as it was up to lines companies how they phase out the old system, there would potentially be 50 different approaches - but they should be revenue-neutral.

Fuge said if you were on the low-user charge of $1.80 per day, the average increase you might face is 90c a day, about $335 a year.

Paul Fuge. Supplied / Consumer NZ

"What should happen is the variable price of your bill should come down accordingly - but it's unknown how that will work and if that will happen."

MBIE told RNZ the impact on the majority of households was expected to be small. Analysis had found around 85 percent of households would see an increase or decrease of no more than $9 a month, around $120 a year. However, the analysis also showed some very low electricity use households could see larger increases.

"Some of the people who are the worst affected by this are the people who can afford it the least," Fuge said.

"We've seen 20 percent increase in power prices over the last two years, so consumers are already struggling, particularly [the elderly]."

Electricity Authority chief executive Sarah Gillies said while some low-user households may face cost increases, they expected lines companies to "carefully consider the potential impact on these households".

Fuge said the result would be a postcode lottery of sorts - some will be in regions where lines companies move quickly, while others might do it gradually, easing any potential price shock.

"We don't think [the Electricity Authority is] doing a particularly good job on these things. I mean, they've had five years for the phase-out to sort this out, and we've left it to the very last minute... and so consumers are rightly concerned about what the impact will be on them."

The changes will kick in on 1 April next year.

"And we're coming down to the wire. I mean, lines companies will be working out their prices right now, advising retailers what the prices will be, and retailers will be advising price changes early next year to take effect from 1 April. So it's very late in the piece to be sort of talking about this. We've had five years, and the regulator has really been asleep at the wheel here."
