The HBO legal thriller follows the explosive divorce of tech mogul Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) and international film star Carla Duval (Sienna Miller), whose bitter split becomes a high-stakes battle over money, power, and reputation. If you like your legal dramas populated by spectacularly messy rich people, this one’s for you.

Tip Toe

Before he became a three-time Emmy winner for hosting The Traitors, Alan Cumming earned three Emmy nominations for his work on The Good Wife. Now, he’s trading his castle in the Scottish Highlands for a neighborhood where the real traitors might be living next door.

Tech.title: Everyone Hates ‘Digger.’ It’s the Perfect Climate Movie
Tech.content:
Should you see a Looney Tunes–esque satire that stars Tom Cruise in prosthetics portraying a loud caricature of an American oilman, that’s currently on track to be one of the biggest box-office failures of all time?

Absolutely yes—and it’s a movie that rewired my expectations of what a movie about climate change should be. Digger, the critically panned, exorbitantly expensive new film from Alejandro González Iñárritu, calls into question the purpose of art and even the basic purpose of telling the truth in the face of a capitalist machine churning the world toward climate disaster. The deeply uncomfortable film forces audiences to confront what kind of characters we’re the most comfortable making into climate villains.

(Spoilers ahead—if you have any plans to see the movie, I really would encourage you to do so first before reading on.)

The film stars Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell, an oil billionaire who only wears cowboy boots and lives in a mansion covered in antlers and polar bear skin rugs. At the start of the film, one of Digger’s oil-drilling platforms accidentally causes a massive iceberg to break loose, resulting in a huge methane leak. With catastrophe impending, he has to alert the president (John Goodman, putting in a performance reminiscent of his best work with the Coen brothers) as the iceberg barrels toward Europe.

The trailers play up the movie as a too-broad-it’s-painful satire of American oilmen and how a Trumpian-inspired religious-right administration would respond to a real climate disaster. Iñárritu, however, lets us in on the secret early: The farce we’re watching is actually a play within the movie, being performed in a theater with a leaky ceiling that keeps losing power. Tom Cruise is not playing Digger Rockwell, but rather an actor playing Digger Rockwell.

We eventually learn that the play, Fossil Fools, depicts events that actually happened some decades ago. From then on, you’re aware that every joke, every villainous portrayal of Digger and the president as Really Bad Guys, is for two audiences: moviegoers in 2026 and theatergoers living in a dystopian future.

From the trailers, I’d initially thought that the movie was going to be similar to Adam McKay’s blockbuster Don’t Look Up, a climate satire that drew record numbers of viewers on Netflix when it aired in 2021. Don’t Look Up puts scientists racing to inform the public about an impending asteroid collision and pushing to avert catastrophe against corporate and political interests that have other plans. McKay, at the time, said the film’s purpose was to make “people less tolerant of inaction from their leaders.” If the media—journalists, filmmakers, and the like—could correctly inform the public about the risks of climate change, the film (and its accompanying calls to action) posited, we would begin to see progress on cutting emissions.

Digger, similarly, deals with themes around climate misinformation. Digger admits he ignored alerts from his own company about the unfolding crisis on his drilling platforms. Goodman’s president and his cabinet decide to deploy a “firewall” that censors out all mentions of the climate crisis (including the phrase “Al Gore”) to control the narrative of what’s happening.

Tech.title: OpenAI and Anthropic Tell British Lawmakers: Regulate Us
Tech.content:
Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta, both of which declined to back new legislation.

The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants.

“The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework. The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.”

OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon was more cautious but still supportive, backing a statutory framework and an international convention. Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. “We don’t think basing everything on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is a good long-term plan,” he said.

However, their rivals would not follow. Asked directly whether he supported a statutory framework, Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta’s Rob Sherman pointed to Britain’s existing regulators, telling MPs they were “not writing on a blank page.”

Tech.title: The 9 Best Movies to Stream This Month (October 2026)
Tech.content:
October has rolled around, and that means only one thing: Spooky season is here! And what better way to celebrate Halloween than with some of the finest fright fests of the last 50 years?

We’re bringing you a more retro-tinged selection of the best films on streaming this month, but the mix of crowd-pleasers and cult classics offers something for horror fans of all tastes. For instance, David Cronenberg’s grotesque revamp of The Fly, buzzing onto Hulu, and Ken Russell’s Altered States materializing on The Criterion Channel, both bring uniquely visceral takes on body horror to your screens, while sleeper hit Under the Skin on Netflix offers slow-burn sci-fi scares, and Midsommar on Prime Video takes to the hills for a sun-drenched approach to folk horror.

If you fancy something a bit newer, fear not. Well, fear lots actually—Zach Cregger’s shockingly original horror debut Barbarian smashes its way onto Hulu, while Netflix brings the final chapter in the sumptuously scary Mononoke trilogy, an anime extravaganza that looks like nothing else. Plus, there’s even one post-credits stinger of an entry that’s too scary to mention here …

Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.

Barbarian

When Tess (Georgina Campbell) finds her Airbnb in a sketchy neighborhood double booked with Keith (Bill Skarsgård), you’ll probably think you know where Barbarian is headed. You don't—and you should brace yourself for everything that follows. Written and directed by Zach Cregger (in a seismic departure from his early comedy background), Barbarian constantly flips the script, regularly subverting viewer expectations of horror movie clichés at every turn.

Tech.title: The ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Filmmakers Terrified Bystanders With Their Monster Sounds
Tech.content:
Actor Seth Green—yes, that one—has seen Godzilla Minus Zero and says it’s awesome.

While introducing the New York Comic Con panel for the 39th film in the Godzilla franchise, Green stressed that the filmmakers behind the movie “have created kaiju that feel physically real and, trust me, emotionally terrifying.”

While a lot of that terror came from the work of Oscar-winning visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima, some it came from the shrieking of Godzilla and his three-headed nemesis, King Ghidorah. Those roars were the work of sound designer Natsuko Inoue and her team, who created the monsters’ outsize vocalizations by rolling speakers to the top of an outdoor dam—much to the horror of people nearby.

“There were people having a picnic, maybe people just taking a stroll,” Hisafumi Takeuchi, who also worked on sound for the film, said during the panel. “The person walking their dog, though—they had the worst time, because the dog was freaking out and barking back at us.”

Since the creatures are imaginary, getting their screams to sound realistic is essential to making them seem believable—and genuinely scary—onscreen. At first, Inoue wasn’t sure if the idea of recording at the dam would work. Those fears were quickly put to rest.

“The first time we sent that roar out on the speakers, I could see the relief and confidence in everyone's eyes,” Inoue said. “By using speakers and projecting it into the real world, capturing the reverb, the echo, the reflection of the sound back with the mic, it manifests it in our world.”

For other kaiju sound effects, Inoue’s team took an analog foley approach. To simulate Ghidorah’s dragon-like wings, for example, they flapped a rubber fisherman’s suit and mixed that noise with the sounds of an accordion-like air duct.

Getting two of Toho’s most famous monsters right was a huge undertaking, especially after the success of Zero’s predecessor, Godzilla Minus One, which brought home $114 million worldwide at the box office. Following that 2023 film’s harrowing mix of post–World War II malaise and bracing kaiju destruction will be tough, but a new trailer shown during the film’s panel at NYCC promised a sequel full of aerial dogfights and a punch-’em-up for the ages between Godzilla and Ghidorah.

Tech.title: The Apple HomeView Is Like a Giant Apple Watch for the Home
Tech.content:
It’s a big year for Apple firsts. The company launched the first MacBook Neo, unveiled its first folding iPhone in September, and installed a new CEO for the first time in 15 years. Now comes the Apple HomeView, Apple’s first smart display.

Rivals like Google and Amazon have made countless screen-enabled smart speakers since voice assistants invaded the home a decade ago. But Apple stuck with a smaller smart home ecosystem centered on its HomePod speakers, even removing the iPad as a hub device a few years ago, which forced users to buy an Apple TV or HomePod to get started. Maybe that’s why it hasn’t found much success in the home.

Announced Tuesday at an event in New York City, the 7-inch smart display arrives alongside several other new smart home devices as part of Apple’s bid to revitalize its lagging ecosystem. The HomeView costs $299 and comes in two versions—a speaker base and a wall-mounted display—both priced the same. Preorders are live, with sales kicking off on November 13.

Courtesy of Apple

A Big Apple Watch

The first thing I thought of after seeing the Apple HomeView in action is that it looks like a blown-up Apple Watch. The 7-inch square screen has multiple “faces” you can swipe through, exactly like the smartwatch. You can even customize the face’s colors and add different complications for more glanceable information.

The faces can range from a clock, your favorite photos of friends, family, or pets (you can even use shared albums) to weather updates and, yes, Snoopy animations. Swipe up for the home screen, which is more like an iPhone or iPad, with apps neatly arranged alongside widgets. Except the HomeView doesn’t run iOS or iPadOS—it runs the generically named HomeView software.

It doesn’t have an App Store. Instead, Apple has a curated selection of apps, including FaceTime, Messages, and Safari. A handful of third-party media apps like Spotify are available, and developers can bring over existing CarPlay apps. If your iPhone already has one of these CarPlay apps installed, it can automatically appear on the HomeView after setup. (There are no video streaming apps like YouTube, Netflix, or Disney+, but if those companies choose to make their apps available on the CarPlay framework, they will show up on the HomeView; for now, you'll have to consume videos by using the Safari browser.)

To get the most out of the HomeView, you need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence support (an iPhone 15 Pro or newer)—you can’t set it up with an iPad. Apple says you can still set it up with an older iPhone and access some of Siri AI's smarts (like broad world knowledge), but smarter app actions and personal context queries require an iPhone with Apple Intelligence.

Tech.title: Apple Reboots Its Smart-Home Strategy With New Hardware and a ‘Home Collection’
Tech.content:
Apple has lagged in the smart home race, which Amazon and Google have dominated for a decade with Alexa and Google Assistant (now Gemini), respectively.

But after finally revamping Siri AI this year and turning the butt-of-the-joke voice assistant into a more competitive companion—paired with a more mature Matter-supported ecosystem of smart home gadgets—Apple now has the brains to power the home system it has always envisioned.

That starts with three new devices: the Apple HomeView, the company's first smart display; the HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker; and the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K.

Apple announced the products at a media-only event in New York City, and it also revealed a slew of new smart-home gadgets made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric, including a video doorbell, thermostats, and security cameras.

Here's everything you need to know.

The Apple HomeView

The cornerstone of Apple's latest smart-home push is the Apple HomeView, a countertop gadget made up of a 7-inch square display resting on a speaker base. It operates like smart displays we've seen from Amazon and Google, but it’s an entirely new device category for Apple.

It runs what Apple calls “HomeView Software,” so while the interface may resemble an iPhone or iPad, the HomeView runs a stand-alone operating system and lacks access to the App Store. As an alternative, Apple has curated a selection of apps for the system, including Messages, Safari, and FaceTime, alongside select third-party media apps like Spotify. (If an app developer has made an app for the CarPlay standard and it's installed on your iPhone, that app can also populate on the HomeView.)

Tech.title: Can Vibe Coded Apps Replace Adobe and Microsoft? These AI Apps Hope So
Tech.content:
In this current era of vibe coding — using AI to create mobile and desktop apps — it was probably only a matter of time until someone made free versions of popular apps. That happened this month when a Reddit user announced that he did so with popular but expensive Adobe and Microsoft programs.

The person behind the project is Brandon Thomas, a software engineer who uses the handle “u/ai_art_is_art” on Reddit, where the tools first caught AI enthusiasts’ attention. Thomas has released 13 free, open-source apps on his website, called ArtCraft. These apps aim to replicate the core functionalities of Adobe and Microsoft programs, including Photoshop, Word and PowerPoint — or, as Thomas calls them, PhotoCraft, WordCraft and DeckCraft.

ArtCraft apps aim to replicate the core functionalities of Adobe and Microsoft apps. ArtCraft/Screenshot by CNET

Vibe coding has taken off for software developers and AI enthusiasts, leading to AI-made apps flooding Apple and Google’s app stores. However, significant concerns persist about the overall usefulness, security and long-term viability of vibe-coded apps. Apple removed some apps that help people vibe code this year because the apps didn’t comply with Apple’s developer rules.

More from CNET

But in the US’s current affordability crisis — and with legacy tech companies constantly raising their prices — a cheaper, AI-created alternative to Photoshop or Microsoft Word can be an attractive option for a subscription-weary consumer.

This certainly isn’t the first time a startup has tried to compete with legacy software companies like Adobe and Microsoft. Canva, Affinity and CapCut are extremely popular Adobe alternatives for content creation and editing. Google and Apple each have their own versions of Microsoft’s core business apps.

But ArtCraft’s vibe-coded apps and other potential AI-made apps allow individual users to avoid handing over their cash and data to a major tech company. Using an open-source AI model on your own device, for example, gives you more control over your data than using a cloud-based app through a subscription.

As with all apps, CNET recommends you inspect the privacy and safety policies before using them. This is especially important for vibe-coded apps.

“Vibe coding can make it super easy to swap out old software tools, but it’s legally questionable,” said CNET’s Blake Stimac, a vibe coding expert. “What works great for you as a quick fix could easily turn into a legal battlefield the second you try to share it with the world.”

Representatives for ArtCraft and Adobe did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Microsoft declined to comment.

Will vibe coding kill legacy software?

It’s unlikely that vibe-coded apps will be the sole downfall of legacy software companies like Adobe and Microsoft. But they do highlight the growing frustration with those companies, particularly as subscriptions become even more expensive and their programs become bloated with AI features.

In March, Adobe reached a $150 million settlement with the US government to resolve a federal lawsuit alleging that the software giant trapped consumers in subscription plans with hidden fees and an intentionally convoluted cancellation process. Under the terms of the agreement, Adobe will pay a $75 million civil penalty and provide $75 million in free services to affected users, though the company continues to deny any wrongdoing.

Microsoft has embedded its Copilot AI throughout its software ecosystem, despite notable user backlash. While the company recently removed a few Windows AI features due to negative feedback, it is still plowing ahead with billions of dollars in AI development.

The appeal of ArtCraft and other open-source vibe-coded apps is their ability to let individuals customize programs and avoid hefty subscriptions. The pitch is tailor-made for tech enthusiasts: If you only need limited access to these programs and can set them up yourself for free, why would you pay for Adobe Creative Cloud or Microsoft Office?

But that certainly won’t be the case for everyone. For one, many folks won’t want to take the time to figure out how to download and configure an open-source AI app. Meanwhile, businesses and professional creators will likely prefer the safety and privacy guarantees that Adobe and Microsoft offer, even if they aren’t always ironclad. Better the devil you know…

Tech.title: No Man’s Sky Headlines Apple’s New Wave of iPhone and iPad Games
Tech.content:
When Apple revealed the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max last month, there was little about anything new for gaming on the devices. But not to worry, mobile gamers: a lineup of popular indie games is coming to the company’s phones and tablets.

No Man’s Sky, Sifu and Vampire Crawlers are in the first batch of seven new games as part of the App Store’s Indie Games Week, according to a post from Apple on Monday. The titles will be playable on both iPhones and iPads and are currently available for purchase in the store, with the exception of No Man’s Sky, which will be released on Oct. 28.

The new indie titles are:

More from CNET

No Man’s Sky, developed by Hello Games, is the standout of the bunch. First released in 2016, the space exploration game launched on PC and PS4 and was met with a negative reaction from players who expected big, beautiful worlds as shown in the original trailer. The backlash was so extensive that it led to an investigation by UK regulators over possible misleading advertising. Hello Games took that criticism and kept updating the game over 10 years, not only delivering on the promises made when the game was first announced, but also surpassing them while growing its player base.

With a vast galaxy to explore, including all previous content expansions, Hello Games says No Man’s Sky can run on the iPhone 11 and newer phones, as well as third-generation iPad Air tablets and newer models. iPhone players can use the touchscreen interface or a controller, while iPad users can use a keyboard and mouse if preferred.

These games are currently not included with Apple Arcade. No Man’s Sky, 9 Kings, Yes, Your Grace 2: Snowfall and Little Kitty, Big City do have free trials available to those interested in trying out the titles.

On Tuesday, Apple launched another set of hardware, including new smart home devices, at its Welcome Home event. The Apple HomeView is the company’s soon-to-be-released smart display for controlling new smart home cameras from LG, set to release in November, but preorders are now available.

Tech.title: PC Gamers, Rejoice: GTA 6 PC Port Could See Release in Early 2027, Report Says
Tech.content:
PC gamers might not have to wait much longer to play Grand Theft Auto 6 after all, according to a new report from GamesBeat. A new leak, attributed to four industry sources familiar with developer Rockstar Games’ plans, points toward a PC port for the highly anticipated game happening within the first three months of 2027.

Despite multiple high-profile delays, Grand Theft Auto 6 for the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S is still on for a Nov. 19 release.

If the latest reporting is true, the leak is another headache for Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive. The hype cycle for GTA 6 has been plagued by controversy, including the revelations that there will be no physical discs and that core features like certain car modifications and clothing shops will be locked behind the $100 “Ultimate edition” of the game.

More from CNET

A deluge of leaks from as far back as 2022 has made GTA 6’s development cycle shockingly transparent. The latest spoilers have been shared by a hacker group known as CyberLeek, which has continued to post new footage (and shill scammy cryptocurrency), despite the best efforts of Take-Two’s legal team.

In spite of the challenges Rockstar has faced in the lead-up to GTA 6’s release, analysts report blockbuster demand for the new game, with projections ranging from $3 billion to $5 billion in revenue during launch week.

A representative for Rockstar Games did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Rockstar’s PC ports usually come out at least one year after the console release date, so an early 2027 release would be a departure from the norm. Rockstar Games

Rockstar’s PC ports have always been slow. Why change now?

Rockstar has historically ported its games to PC well after their initial console release. PC gamers waited nearly two years for an official Grand Theft Auto 5 port, and a little more than a year for a Red Dead Redemption 2 port.

Rockstar’s delayed PC ports are often attributed to a host of optimization and debugging challenges, especially because PC gamers run games on more diverse hardware. Some critics argue that the company “double-dips” on sales by creating FOMO and driving PC players to consoles first. When a port is released, the thinking goes, the PC player will buy a second company and bolster Rockstar’s sales.

Either way, there are several reasons why Rockstar might be trying to turn around this particular port more quickly than ever before.

If the development studio is planning to quickly release an online service for GTA 6, that would be a massive revenue driver – the current iteration of GTA Online rakes in more than $1 million each day, and has surpassed $5 billion in revenue over its lifespan.

If a new version of GTA Online is planned for GTA 6, having the wider base of PC players will likely be more profitable in the long term than any “double-dipping” sales practice.

Also, while consoles have always been the most profitable platform for Rockstar’s games, the market is shifting. The RAMageddon chip shortage is pushing hardware prices higher, and home consoles are becoming more expensive – and less accessible.

While these hurdles also affect folks looking to buy an off-the-shelf computer or build their own PC, the market share of PC gamers is growing nonetheless. Newzoo analysts predict that there will be more than 1 billion PC gamers by 2028.

Most PC game spending is focused on microtransactions – so if one were to release a massive live service game with the ability to purchase, say, virtual preloaded debit cards, there’s probably no better time to do so.

Tech.title: Latest GTA 6 Leak of Nude Character Is a Bad Crypto Scheme Fundraiser
Tech.content:
As it nears a month before its long-awaited release, Grand Theft Auto 6 is again the subject of a high-profile leak, this time involving nudity of another main character.

The online group Cyberleek reportedly posted new footage of one of the game’s main characters, Lucia, engaging in activities such as walking in public and skydiving nude.

While there are indications that what was leaked is not from the final game — it could be an earlier developer build modded to allow for nudity — the leakers are threatening to post the game’s entire main storyline ahead of the Nov. 19 game launch. This follows a separate leak that featured the game’s other main character, Jason, also nude for much of a 24-minute video.

More from CNET

Reports say the leaked files have been made available on sites with a $40 paywall, but clips have appeared on free websites and social media. Cyberleek said it has other footage to release with names like “Police shootout,” “Beach massacre” and “Fight Jet” ahead of a full gameplay release.

The leakers are demanding that publisher Take-Two Interactive publicly apologize for not offering physical discs and issue a physical, disc-based version of the game. However, meeting these demands is highly unlikely. The game is set to be a digital-only release, and altering the production timeline at this stage is practically impossible.

There seems to be something else behind it, though: more money. Cyberleek is urging people to pump its self-named meme coin, threatening to leak a full build of GTA 6 if the coin reaches a market valuation of $30 million. As of this writing, it has ranged recently from about $2 million to $7 million, with news of the leak adding to its volatility.

A representative for Rockstar Games, the studio owned by Take-Two Interactive that built GTA 6, did not immediately return a request for comment. But the company has been involved in investigations into previous leaks and has expressed dismay about groups trying to spoil the game.

In August, in response to leaks from the same group that included nine short gameplay videos, Rockstar posted on X that the leaks were “heartbreaking” and told players, “this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time.”

In late August, Rockstar finally gave fans a lengthy look at the game with 27 minutes of uninterrupted gameplay footage, which it made available on Netflix and YouTube. There was no nudity in that footage, but fans have been speculating how R-rated the final version of the game could get in terms of its sexual content.

Rockstar, which spent more than a dozen years developing the game, has been carefully orchestrating its rollout and working with authorities to shut down repositories featuring leaked assets.

The game will be released exclusively on PlayStation 5 consoles for $80 to $100, depending on the edition gamers purchase.

Tech.title: Samsung Smart Glasses Unveiled, and They’re Superlight
Tech.content:
Samsung won’t unveil its first smart glasses until November, but now we know what they will look like — and how light they will be. They’ll come in a variety of styles and colors and weigh only 41 grams, according to a report from tech news outlet SammyGuru.

Samsung is expected to launch the smart glasses, possibly called Galaxy Glasses, next month. They will compete in the marketplace against Meta’s Ray-Bans and AI glasses from Apple, which reportedly won’t arrive until next year. XREAL reportedly will launch its Aura glasses sometime this fall.

In November, US customers can buy the Samsung smart glasses at the Warby Parker website and Gentle Monster website, and also at Samsung Experience Stores in the US. No prices have been announced, according to the report.

More from CNET

Samsung’s glasses will include six styles from South Korean eyewear brand Gentle Monster, which partnered with Huawei several years ago for audio smart glasses, and three styles from US brand Warby Parker, SammyGuru said.

The new Samsung smart glasses will have six styles from Gentle Monster. SammyGuru

There will be six frame shapes from Gentle Monster — squared, rounder, bolder square, cat-eye, slim oval and regular oval. The various lens colors include clear, light blue, gray, brown, black, light gray, pale lilac, burgundy and cream, according to SammyGuru.

Two of the Warby Parker styles, Alden and Wren, will include colors pine, dark green and reddish-brown Saddle. Reid is offered in Jet Black, the report said.

Only 41 grams in weight

The new Samsung smart glasses will weigh 41 grams with standard lenses, lighter than the 43 grams for the lightest Meta Ray-Ban model, according to the leak. They’ll include a Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chip, 2 GB of RAM, 64 GB of storage, a 12 MP camera, 3K video at 30 frames per second, two open-ear speakers and four microphones. The battery can last up to 9 hours or up to 72 hours if also using the charging case.

The glasses are similar to Meta Ray-Bans in that there is no visual display for text messages. You’ll compose them by speaking into the microphones and hear them via the speakers.



Users will need Galaxy S, Z Fold or Z Flip phones running One UI 9 or later to use Galaxy-specific features with the glasses. To use the watch features, users will need a Galaxy Watch running on Wear OS 7 or newer.

What can the glasses do?

Samsung’s smart glasses will use Google Gemini AI and run on the Android XR operating system. People wearing them will be able to perform various tasks with the AI, including taking pictures and videos, making calls and sending texts, translating, getting turn-by-turn navigation and listening to songs and podcasts.

Fast-growing market

The demand for smart glasses is rapidly growing worldwide. Sales in the US doubled over the past year, with global shipments topping 4.2 million, according to research firm Omdia. Another analysis estimates that the global market for smart glasses will grow by more than 24% yearly until 2033.

Smart glasses manufacturers are focusing on “hands-free photo and video capture, open-ear audio and AI assistance within everyday frames,” Omdia analyst Qiran Ju said in a recent report.

Tech.title: Beats Reveals How to Buy Pokemon Portable Pill Speaker: Gotta Hear ‘Em All
Tech.content:
Put a Pokemon character, especially Pikachu, on just about anything — including a $100 Polaroid camera — and fans will take notice. On Tuesday, Beats by Dre revealed the look of its upcoming Pokemon-themed Beats Pill Bluetooth speaker, as well as the cost and where to buy it.

Beats by Dre teased the collab on Monday, but confirmed it on Tuesday. The company’s social-media post and official website revealed that the special-edition Pokemon Beats Pill speaker will be available Thursday. While we guessed on Monday there might be two different Pills speakers, it turns out there’s only one, with two Pokemon characters on it. The speaker is shown with both a Pikachu image and one of Mimikyu, a sad Pokemon who disguises itself as Pikachu.

The special-edition Pokemon Beats Pill will sell for $149.99 at Target and apple.com, and is already shown on Target’s website. It comes with the speaker itself, a removable lanyard and charm, and Beats x Pokemon stickers.

More from CNET

A new adventure begins. Unleash the energy of your music with the special-edition Pokémon Beats Pill.



Get yours 10.15 pic.twitter.com/m1lzEuMMMI — Beats by Dre (@beatsbydre) October 13, 2026

On Monday, Beats shared a teaser with the caption, “Time to catch something new,” which plays off the classic Pokemon tagline, “Gotta catch ’em all!” The 6-second video shows electrical charges in yellow and purple flashing over a shadowed Beats Pill speaker. It ends with a screen showing the Pokemon Poke Ball logo and the Beats by Dre “b” logo, with an X between them, teasing the product collaboration.

Time to catch something new. pic.twitter.com/Rt0IfTKENC — Beats by Dre (@beatsbydre) October 12, 2026

Apple bought Beats by Dre for $3 billion back in 2014.

The speaker isn’t a brand-new revelation for those who stay up-to-date on all things Pokemon. Last week, a Pokemon fan who goes by BritBrattv posted a photo to Facebook showing a bright yellow Pikachu-themed Beats Pill speaker in what appears to be a Target shopping cart, though that photo was not confirmed as official.

And former Apple CEO Tim Cook shared a video on X in August showing Pikachu visiting Apple Park.

“Today’s agenda at Apple Park,” Cook wrote. “Introduce the @Pokemon team to John, talk gaming and politely ask Pikachu to stay out of the pond. Two out of three were accomplished.” By “John,” he presumably meant John Ternus, the new Apple CEO.

Representatives for Beats by Dre and Pokemon didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Beats Pill speaker in non-Pokemon designs is priced at $129 at Target and Amazon as of Tuesday. In a 2024 review, CNET audio expert David Carnoy called the Pill “a very good compact Bluetooth speaker,” praising its sound quality and strong battery life.

Tech.title: HomeView and More: Everything Apple Announced at Its ‘Welcome Home’ Event
Tech.content:
Apple wants to have a much bigger presence in your house. On Tuesday, the company behind Macs and iPhones unveiled a sweeping lineup of new products presenting a range of options for home management, security and entertainment.

The centerpiece is the Apple HomeView smart display, which can sit on a tabletop or be mounted on a wall. In its tabletop version, with its domed base, it echoes the iconic iMac G4 from the early 2000s.

But this is a device for a new era, brimming with Siri AI and personalization features and built for household interactions.

More from CNET

“Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of worldwide marketing, said in a statement.

The products altogether represent a big new smart home push for Apple, which for years has largely left that field to be dominated by Amazon and Google. One thing that could work in Apple’s favor, said Ben Wood, chief analyst at FDM CCS Insight, is its reputation for making technology easier to use than the alternatives.

“In typical Apple fashion, setting up the new products is simple: you just hold your iPhone near the device and add it as easily as pairing new Apple headphones or Watch,” Wood told CNET via email. “That’s quite a contrast to other smart home products where you have to download a specific app, scan QR codes and more.”

Tuesday’s “Welcome Home” event took place just over a month after Apple’s September introduction of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and the folding iPhone Duo.

Here’s everything Apple just announced:

Apple HomeView

The HomeView is designed as the hub for a range of capabilities, including making FaceTime calls, playing music and managing smart home devices.

It has a 7-inch square Liquid Retina display and Apple’s A18 chip. It can also be controlled by touch or voice. Apple sees its new Siri AI as central to the experience of using the HomeView.

It can recognize up to six people by their faces and you can set up a personalized home screen for each. Like on the Apple Watch, display customization options allow for a wide range of screen designs. The Home Camera face can livestream up to nine video feeds simultaneously.

Just like an Apple Watch: You can customize the look of your HomeView, depending on your preference, from standard clocks to calendar to family to Snoopy. Apple

The HomeView works with the new Apple Home Collection devices – more on that below – as well as other Matter and Works with Apple Home accessories

The tabletop version is available in four colors: silver, starlight, rose pink and space gray

The wall mount version comes in either silver or space gray.

Preorders start Tuesday for people in the US, the UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and India, on Thursday for those in Singapore, and on Friday for those in South Africa, with availability in all those countries beginning Nov. 13. The HomeView isn’t available in EU countries because Siri AI is not available in iOS there.

The HomeView is priced at $299 for both the tabletop and wall-mounted versions. There are two dedicated wall mounts, at $60 and $80, that can be preordered starting Tuesday. A third wall mount will be available in early 2027 for $130.

Apple Home Collection

The Home Collection line of products includes smart home cameras for both indoors and outdoors, thermostats, temperature sensors, a video doorbell and a smart lock designed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. In its press release, Apple described the gear as having a “clean, minimal aesthetic.”

The lineup includes four LG camera devices:

The $250 Video Doorbell, with dual cameras (for views of visitors and packages), plus a spotlight and a chime that plays through the HomeView, HomePod and HomePod Mini.

The $400 Floodlight Cam, which has motion sensing and low-light color night vision.

The simpler $200 Outdoor Cam.

The $200 Indoor Cam – for privacy: tilts up and down for you to monitor while you’re away, and down to stop monitoring when you’re at home.

Apple emphasized the privacy aspects of the devices. For instance, the Indoor Cam will tilt down when you’re at home. Camera footage, the company said, is processed locally or via Private Cloud Compute. For those with an iCloud Plus subscription, up to 10 days’ worth of video history can be stored in encrypted form.

The collection also includes the $350 LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, which recognizes when known users approach. It can unlock automatically and can work in conjunction with the video doorbell.

Two thermostats are in the mix, one from LG and the other from Schneider. Each costs $200, and separate temperature sensors cost $40 apiece.

Availability for the Home Collection products begins in December, with certain accessories available starting in early 2027.

The new Apple TV 4K can be paired with up to four HomePod speakers. Apple

Apple HomePod Mini 2

Apple is expanding its HomePod line with the new $149 HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker, or as Apple puts it, “conversational assistant.” It’s the first major upgrade to the HomePod lineup in years.

It can sync up with other HomePods or with Apple TV. For first time, the company said, users can create four-speaker surround sound with new Apple TV 4K. Buyers can choose from five colors: pink, green, blue, white and midnight.

“When paired with the new Apple TV 4K, it delivers our most immersive home theater setup yet,” Kaiann Drance, Apple’s vice president of worldwide home product marketing, said in a statement.

Preorders for the HomePod Mini 2 begin Tuesday for people in the US and about two dozen countries and regions, with availability starting Oct. 30. Siri AI access will arrive in a future software update.

Apple TV 4K

The new Apple TV 4K has Apple’s A19 chip, which allows for up to 50% faster CPU performance and up to 2x faster GPU performance, the company said. Besides streaming shows and movies, it can also serve as a home hub – for instance, doorbell notifications will appear on the screen.

It has three built-in far-field microphones so that you can talk to Siri AI.

Preorders start Tuesday, with availability Nov. 13 for customers in the US and 29 other countries and regions. Pricing starts at $299 or $49.83 per month for six months.

CNET Principal Writer Katie Collins contributed to this article.

Tech.title: Meta’s Audio-Only Glasses Are Nicely Made. They Don’t Solve the Deeper Problems
Tech.content:
I’ve started feeling self-conscious when I wear camera-equipped smart glasses out and about. It’s not hard to imagine why. Public opinion of smart glasses seems lower than it’s ever, driven by a combination of AI fatigue, privacy concerns and a general lack of awareness of what smart glasses can do or why anyone would want to wear them. Some places are also starting to ban them.

Meta’s addressed one concern, at least, with its new camera-free line of Ray-Ban smart glasses. Getting rid of the camera completely on the Meta Ray-Ban Audio means they’re smaller and lighter, and have better battery life, too. But they’re not as cheap as I’d have expected. The two models that are available starting this week, the Clubmaster and Burbank, run from $349 to $429 — just for the frames, depending on whether they have transitions lenses or not. Meta has more affordable self-branded smart glasses staring at $249, but those have cameras onboard.

I’m not sure why Meta didn’t make self-branded, camera-free glasses, too, which could have helped bring the cost down. I’m sure those are coming in the future, but in the meantime, skipping the camera seems to be more about design, privacy and extending audio battery life.

Are they a worthwhile addition to Meta’s lineup? Here’s what I think of them so far.

They look absolutely normal and feel good: Meta’s glasses design has come a long way. Scott Stein/CNET

Wearing them: Lighter, for sure

I’ve been wearing a pair of the Clubmaster glasses, but without my prescription. That means perching them over my regular glasses or wearing them around the house without being able to see much. After all, the main thing that’s “new” here is the lack of a camera.

These glasses are definitely lighter and easier to wear, and the arms are a little smaller. They weigh between 43 and 47 grams, compared with a little over 50 grams for other Meta Ray-Bans. The front of the frames is a lot smaller on the Clubmaster model, but the half-metal design isn’t exactly my style.

Meta says battery life for constant audio playback is around six hours, a couple of hours more than the four I get from my Meta Ray-Ban Gen 2 and Scriber Optics glasses. For general wear, Meta gives the fuzzier estimate of “up to 12 hours,” versus eight hours for the others, which is harder to map out. Not using the glasses’ audio obviously makes the battery last longer.

The glasses work the same as other Meta smart glasses, with a touchpad on the right arm for tapping to start or stop playback and swiping to control the volume. I still activate it accidentally too often. A button on top activates Meta AI or can be set to launch music.

Audio is your only input and output with the Ray-Ban Audio glasses. Microphones and speakers are onboard. Scott Stein/CNET

What you can do with them

Now, what would I use these for? I already find the audio quality on Meta’s latest glasses surprisingly good, and the microphones are excellent for phone calls. The audio seems a bit louder on the Clubmaster model, although the overall quality is similar. It’s still prone to being washed out in noisy areas because of the open design, which angles the speaker audio from the temples.

Obviously, I’m not taking any photos with these. That also means the glasses can’t perform any visually aware AI tricks or provide visual assistance.

Beyond music, phone calls and anything else you’d use headphones for, Meta AI is the necessary conduit for everything these glasses can do. They still need to be paired with the Meta AI phone app, too.

Meta’s FDA-cleared hearing enhancement mode, which lets the glasses function as a type of hearing aid for mild hearing loss, costs an extra $149 or comes with a Meta One subscription. I tried the technology as best I could at Meta’s developer conference last month, but I still don’t know how well it’ll compare with hearing assistance options such as Apple’s AirPods Pro. The audio glasses should, however, support hearing enhancement for longer on a single charge.

Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses on top of Ray-Ban Scriber Optics. One pair has a camera; the other doesn’t. Scott Stein/CNET

Why now?

Meta was clearly working on camera-free glasses before this year’s wave of backlash against its camera-enabled eyewear, though concerns about wearing camera-equipped glasses in public have been bubbling for a while.

But I also wonder what these particular models mean for Meta — and for its eyewear partner, EssilorLuxottica. The company has tons of eyewear stores worldwide and already makes a pair of assistance-focused audio glasses called Nuance.

The fact that these glasses are Ray-Ban branded rather than Meta branded lingers in my mind. I think they’re part of Essilor’s expanding range of more acceptable smart eyewear and likely aimed at customers who only want audio assistance.

But they feel a bit removed from the rest of Meta’s future-forward vision, which also includes display-equipped glasses and wearable neural bands. It could open up a path to display-enabled, camera-free glasses in Meta’s future lineup. It’s also likely an effort by Meta to find more acceptable ways to bring its AI to people’s faces, with or without cameras.

The charging case can rapid-charge the glasses much like other Meta glasses models, and it protects them nicely. Scott Stein/CNET

You’re still locked into Meta AI

Meta’s current Muse Spark-based AI on the glasses responds quickly and can provide live language translation and turn-by-turn navigation, set timers and serve as a general conversational research companion. But Meta’s support for connecting other services remains limited, and the privacy improvements promised for the company’s AI services in September haven’t arrived yet.

Fully agentic Muse AI is arriving on Meta’s glasses in the next year, but it’s unclear when. Muse already has an entire connected ecosystem of services, many of which require connecting other accounts to it. Some of Meta’s higher-powered AI models are now requiring extra subscription costs.

What this all means for Meta’s AI glasses over the next year is still a little unclear. They’ll increasingly become tools for tapping into those agents, perhaps to do work or monitor parts of your life. Currently, I don’t use Meta AI for much beyond short conversations about things I want to know on the fly.

Will Meta also explore always-recording “audio memories” in the future, capturing or summarizing conversations as companies like Apple and many others are already doing or promising? And if so, how will that be handled?

What I guess this means is that camera-free Meta glasses could gain acceptance in places where camera-enabled glasses are increasingly being banned. They could also offer a more reassuring option for people who want audio AI glasses but don’t want cameras. Still, most of the glasses Meta sells have cameras, and its AI is advancing so quickly that the shape of future smart glasses could change just as rapidly. They’re solid as wearable audio, but with Google’s glasses and a host of other audio glasses on their way in the next year, Ray-Bans are far from your only option.
